label: Before you read
title: A Note on the Stories
subtitle: Where the stories in this book come from, and how they are told

runs.t: Most of the stories in this book come from twenty years I spent at a Fortune 10 company, from 2004 to 2024. I started as a store trainer. I ran stores, then districts, then a region. As a region director, I led the work at the distribution center that supplied our stores. In another part of the company I led patient experience strategy. The rest come from conversations I have had since, with leaders who were kind enough to tell me what was going wrong in their own companies.

I have withheld names, places and identifying details. That includes the company, the cities, the vendors and every colleague. Some of the people in these pages made decisions that hurt. Some of them made decisions that saved careers. None of them agreed to be in a book, and none of them needs to be. The lessons hold without the names.

You will notice that I tell most of the mistakes as "we." That is on purpose. When a region won an award for payroll control while its stores could not stay staffed, nobody broke a rule. The system rewarded the number it was built to watch. When a leader made a call that drove good people out, the incentives around that leader usually made the call look smart at the time. I was part of those systems. I made some of those calls. Blaming one person would be easier to read and less useful to you, because you would close the book thinking your company does not have that person. It probably has the system.
When a fix worked, I have tried to give the credit to the teams who did the work. They earned it.

A word on the numbers. The results in this book are my own career results, from the teams I led at that company. They are not EIP client results. Where I say "about" or "roughly," I mean it. I have used the most conservative version of every figure I could defend in front of a CFO. Where a number comes from outside research, the chapter's Notes section names the source. Where an example uses round numbers to show how the math works, it is labeled as hypothetical, and it describes no real company.

The tools I mention, Turn Tax, the Flight Risk Score, Honest Read, Hire Smart and Council View, came later, at Experience Improvement Partners. They exist because I spent years building rough versions of them by hand, on spreadsheets, because nothing else would show me what I needed to see. You do not need any of them to use this book. Every chapter tells you how to start with what you already have.

The book has four parts. Part One explains why people leave and what it costs. Part Two shows how to see a departure coming before the resignation letter. Part Three covers the fixes, from the top of the company to the first day on the job. Part Four is about making the gains last.
You can read it in order. If you do, each chapter builds on the last, and the distribution center story in Chapter 20 will pull most of the ideas together in one place.
You can also jump. If you have a specific problem, go straight to the chapter for it:
You do not know what turnover costs you.
Start with Chapter 3.
Your engagement survey says things are fine, and people keep leaving.
Chapter 5.
You want to know who is about to leave.
Chapters 6 and 7.
Your best people are the ones walking out.
Chapter 8.
You suspect the problem is a few managers.
Chapter 12.
New hires quit in the first 90 days.
Chapters 16 and 17.
You fixed it once and it came back.
Chapter 18.
You run a home health agency, a nuclear plant, a portfolio of companies or a contact center.
Chapter 22.
Every chapter ends with a box called
Take action this week

. It gives one or two steps for the CEO, the manager and the supervisor, or whichever roles fit the chapter. None of them needs a budget. Most take less than an hour. If you do nothing else with this book, do those.
Appendix A collects the tools and self-assessments in one place, so you can copy them into your own meetings. Appendix B defines the terms.

label: Introduction
title: Why I wrote this book
subtitle: Where this book came from, and why it is built the way it is

runs.t: This book was not written in an office. It was written through pain and reality.

I spent 20 years at a Fortune 10 company. I worked in retail stores, in a call center, behind a pharmacy counter and in executive leadership. I led teams of up to 3,500 people and ran a $1.2 billion P&L. In the specialty part of the business, I was responsible for $3 billion in client contract renewals.

Every one of those jobs had the same problem in a different uniform. People left, and it cost us more than anyone was counting. Pharmacists walked out in the middle of a staffing crisis. Seasonal hires quit before their first day on the phones. A distribution center lost people so fast that my stores had twelve feet of empty shelves. Clients judged us on renewals, and renewals depended on the people who answered their calls.

I did not learn retention from a textbook. I learned it by getting it wrong, watching what it cost and then working with good teams to fix it. Most of the stories in this book come from those years. I have left out the names, but none of the lessons.

blocks.text: What people told me after I left

runs.t: When I left that company in 2024, I started something small called the Six Degree Career Accelerator. It was a program to help someone get a job offer within 180 days without ever filling out an application.
It worked. Twenty-seven people went through it, and 15 of them paid. I charged my first client $500. Today the program costs $3,500, and it runs on a tight system.
What surprised me was why those 27 people wanted to move. Only five of them wanted more money.
The rest wanted out of a job that was not fulfilling them or helping them reach their goals. And many of them had a version of the same story:
I would stay if the company would just do something.
Fix the schedule. Have the career conversation. Deal with the manager. Listen.

I had spent 20 years watching people leave. Now I was hearing it from the other side of the table, from the people doing the leaving. Their reasons matched what I had seen from the inside almost exactly.
Only five of the 27 wanted more money. Most of the others would have stayed if their company had done something.

Next I became a vice president at Ciklum, a global AI solutions company. It had been around for about 20 years, worked in 14 countries and wanted to start a U.S. healthcare vertical. I spent two years helping companies find their problems and then building the solutions, usually custom AI, automation and analytics. Along the way I learned the difference between consulting and advising, and how many self-described expert advisors have never done the work they advise on.
In November 2025, I was in a meeting with a client who was putting AI automation into his operations. It was going to reduce his headcount by about 24% and save a lot of money.
Halfway through, he made a joke. Since we were using AI to cut people, did we have an AI solution that could help him keep the ones he had left?

It was an offhand comment. But I told him I did have something. It was what we had built by hand at my old company: the cost math, the checklist of who was likely to leave next, the listening, the fixes.

So I dug it out and turned it into a real plan. That was the first version of the playbook this book is built on. He liked it. He told a friend. A couple of good meetings followed, and one person told me I should write a book. I was not focused on it yet.

In February 2026, I had lunch with the number two leader at a staffing company. We were meeting for the first time. We talked about work and life and everything in between. He is a fun person to have lunch with.
Then he asked me a question. His company placed people with its clients, and those clients were unhappy that the people kept quitting. Did I have anything for retention?
I had just built it. I said yes.

I incorporated Experience Improvement Partners shortly after. He and I talked almost every day after that lunch, and his encouragement kept me going when this was still an idea on paper. His company became our first client, which let us test everything with real people and real data, and then it brought us into other clients. He has been critical to all of it.

EIP helps companies see what they lose when good people leave, and keep the ones they cannot afford to lose. We work as operators, not as consultants who have never run a shift. Our Council of current and former executives reviews every diagnosis, because one person's view is never enough.
You will see four tools throughout this book:
Turn Tax™
counts what turnover costs your company, across 13 cost categories and up to 250 variables, using your own data.
Flight Risk Score™

(patent pending) scores the risk that each person leaves in the next 90 days, from 0 to 99. It starts with 19 variables in four areas: manager relationship, career and tenure, pay, and job friction. It is tuned to each company and tested against past departures. It is a documented calculation, not AI. Supervisors never see individual scores, and the score never makes an employment decision.
Honest Read™
is a set of interviews and small listening sessions run by a third party, so people say what they would not say to their own chain of command.
Hire Smart™
builds hiring around the three to five traits your long-tenured top performers share.
None of them fixes anything alone. They tell you where to look and what it is worth. People still have to do the work.

Everyone who is part of EIP today is someone I have known and worked with before. Many of them are people I helped along the way. Watching them come together around this has been one of the best parts of my career.

Life is a team game. You get what you want only when you help enough other people get what they want. EIP's purpose is built on that, and so is this book. I have helped a lot of people over the years. It is amazing to see how much of that support is coming back.
The rest of this book is what we learned, chapter by chapter, starting with the most common explanation for why people leave, and why it is usually wrong.

label: Chapter 1
title: Exit interviews and why people really leave
subtitle: Why exit interviews produce polite fiction, and what to ask instead

runs.t: The resignations started a few weeks after a new competitor opened a large facility in our market.

At first it was one pharmacist, then another. Then it was several a week. Within six months my region had lost dozens of pharmacists. Chapter 7 tells the story of the war room we built to keep stores open while it happened. This chapter is about something else: what we got wrong about why they left.
The explanation everyone reached for was money. The new competitor must be paying more. It was easy to say in a meeting, and it pointed at someone outside our walls.
Then we started looking at where people went and what they took. Many of our pharmacists had taken pay cuts to leave. Some took cuts of up to 15%.
So we tried the obvious fix. We offered raises to bring people back.
They said no.
That was the moment the money story fell apart for me. People had walked away from more money to get something we were not giving them, and more money was not going to buy them back.
If pay were the reason, a raise would have worked. It did not.
The answer had been sitting in our own data for months.

Our annual engagement survey had flagged one item lower than all the rest: whether people had enough tools and resources to do their jobs. The natural read, and the one corporate made, was that people needed better technology.

That was not it. The cause was a staffing decision. Many of our stores had lost their lead technician role. The lead technician was the person who kept the pharmacy running while the pharmacist did the work only a pharmacist can do. Without that role, pharmacists were doing everything, all day, with a line at the counter and the phones ringing.
"Not enough tools and resources" meant "not enough people." We had read it as a request for technology because that was the kind of answer the question invited.
Our pharmacists were leaving for working conditions. The competitor offered a job they could do well without drowning. They were willing to take less to get it.

There is a related story about one of our best pharmacists, who was offered about $10,000 a year more by a federal health agency. We made her the highest-paid pharmacist. Then she told us it was not about the money. Chapter 15 tells that one in full.
The money story is not unique to pharmacists. It is built into the way most companies ask why people leave.
Picture a typical exit interview. It is someone's last day. They have turned in their badge. The new job starts Monday.
An HR coordinator asks why they decided to leave. They say it was a better opportunity. The commute. A little more money.

None of that is the whole truth. The truth might be a supervisor who only spoke to them to point out mistakes in front of the team. An equipment request submitted three times with no reply. A question about a lead role that got brushed off.
They will not say that. They might need a reference someday. They might want to come back. They do not want their last day to turn into an argument. So they give a clean story nobody can argue with.
The coordinator types "compensation" into the form, and it becomes data.
Months later, someone in a leadership meeting pulls up the exit report. Compensation is the top reason people leave. Everyone nods. A pay study gets commissioned. The cycle starts again.

The exit interview is a ritual, not a research method. It asks someone who has already decided, already signed somewhere else and has every reason to stay polite. Pay is the most socially acceptable exit story there is. It names a need without blaming anyone.
I want to be fair to pay. Pay matters. People have bills. A company that pays well below its market will lose people, and Chapter 15 is about how to have that conversation honestly.
But "money" is also the answer that costs the person leaving nothing to give. Think about it from their side.
If they say "my supervisor humiliated me in front of the team," they have made an accusation. Someone might call that supervisor. Word might get back.
If they say "the workload became impossible after they cut the lead technician," they are criticizing a decision made above their pay grade. That can feel risky, even on the way out.
If they say "I got a better offer," the conversation ends. Everyone shakes hands. Nobody is blamed.
The company likes the money answer too. It points outside. It does not require anyone in the building to change how they lead.
So both sides settle on the same story. That is what makes it so durable.
When companies believe the money story, they respond with money. Counteroffers. Retention bonuses tied to a date.
A retention bonus is like wooden handcuffs. It is just annoying enough to make someone think twice about leaving, but nowhere near strong enough to make them want to stay.

The person who takes a retention bonus while still unhappy does not become happy. They become patient. They wait out the date, and then they go. Meanwhile, they are doing the job the way people do jobs they have already left in their heads.

Counteroffers work the same way. You match the offer. The person stays. Nothing about the supervisor, the workload or the missing career path has changed. In a few months, the same recruiter calls again, or a different one does, and this time they do not tell you before they accept.

I am not saying never use a retention bonus. There are moments, such as a merger, a site closing or a critical project, when a bonus buys the time you need. But a bonus buys time. It does not fix the reason someone wanted to leave. If you do not use that time to fix the reason, you have paid for a delay.

If you do use a bonus, how you structure it matters. Paying the money up front with a payback clause is often stronger than paying it at the end. Say you hand someone $20,000 today, and they owe it back if they quit before the date. That can hold people better than promising $20,000 if they stay to the end. It can even beat a promise of $50,000 at the end. Writing a check to leave is much harder than walking away from money you never had. This is how sign-on bonuses can work well too. It is still not the reason you want anyone to stay.
A bonus buys time. It does not fix the reason someone wanted to leave.
The research backs up what operators see on the floor.

runs.t: Work Institute analyzed more than 120,000 exit interviews for its 2025 Retention Report. It found that 75% of departures were preventable, and it pointed to leadership, culture and career development as the levers.
Those interviews were run by a neutral third party, not the employer. That matters. People tell an outsider what they will not tell the company they are leaving.

Gallup's 2024 study of people who quit found that 42% said their manager or organization could have prevented it. Then it asked what happened before they left. 45% said no manager or leader talked with them about their satisfaction, performance or future in the three months before they quit. Only 17% were asked what would keep them. 36% did not talk to anyone at work before resigning.

Pay does show up. In Gallup's data, better pay or benefits was the most common thing that could have prevented a departure, at 30%. Read that number carefully. It means about 70% of preventable exits needed something other than money: a better relationship with a manager, a fix to an organizational problem, a path to advance or a workload that made sense.

blocks.title: What could have prevented a preventable departure

blocks.text: A GPS that recalculates too late

runs.t: Even when an exit interview is honest, it arrives at the wrong time.

Fixing turnover with an exit interview is like using a GPS that only recalculates after you have already missed the exit. It tells you what you should have done. It does not tell you what to do next, and it cannot bring back the person who already left.

Some companies collect years of exit data and never change anything. Others act on it, but they act on the clean story. They raise pay for a role where pay was never the main problem, and they are surprised when turnover does not move.

Exit data is not useless. It can confirm a pattern you already suspect, and it can tell you where people went (Chapter 9). But it is the last and least honest data point in a process that started long before.
Every resignation has three layers.
The result.
Someone quits. This is what the exit interview studies.
The behavior.
Before that, they start applying elsewhere, taking calls, leaving right at five and going quiet in meetings.
The thinking.
Before that, the decision forms. I do not have a future here. Nobody is going to fix this. I deserve better.
Most companies only manage the result. By the time the letter arrives, the thinking is usually weeks or months old. The window to change it was open, and nobody walked through it.
The resignation letter is not the event. It is the receipt.
Think about what that means for a manager.

At the thinking layer, nothing is visible yet. The person is still showing up and doing the work. What they need is a conversation before they have decided. That is where a Retention Talk does its best work.

At the behavior layer, the signs are there if you know what to look for. Someone who used to raise their hand stops. The people who work beside them usually see it before the supervisor does. Chapter 6 covers those signals.
At the result layer, the decision is made. You are mostly collecting the receipt.
The goal of this book is to move your attention up the chain, from result to behavior to thinking. The earlier you get there, the cheaper the fix.
At a distribution center that supplied my stores, everybody blamed one large e-commerce employer nearby for the turnover. It was hiring and it was paying more.

So we asked people who were still there where their friends had gone. Of the last 30 people who left, only 2 went to that employer. The rest went to other local employers, and the causes we could fix were inside our own building. Chapter 9 covers how to trace where your people go, and Chapter 20 tells that distribution center's full story.
The pattern is the same in both stories. The exit story pointed at someone else. The causes we could fix were inside our own walls, and the people who were still there knew what they were.

blocks.text: Ask the people who are still here

runs.t: If exit interviews ask the wrong people at the wrong time, the fix is to ask the right people at the right time. That means the people who are still with you, while they are still deciding.

A Retention Talk is a short, structured conversation with someone who has not left. The goal is to learn what keeps them, what frustrates them and what might make them go, early enough to do something about it.
Use four questions:
What makes you come back here every day?
What would make this job better?
Is anything frustrating you that we have not addressed?
What would it take for you to still be here a year from now?

The first question tells you what to protect. The second and third tell you what to fix. The fourth is the most important. It invites people to describe the conditions for staying, which is a far easier conversation than the reasons for leaving.
Start with the people you can least afford to lose.
Your high performers, your long-tenured experts and anyone who trains others. These are the people with the most options, and losing one of them can take others with them (Chapter 8).
Keep it short.
Twenty to thirty minutes is enough.
Be careful about who asks.

A direct supervisor can run a Retention Talk, and often should. But if the supervisor is part of the problem, the answers will be polite. For a deeper read, or for a team where trust is low, use someone outside the chain of command. At EIP we call that work Honest Read, and Chapter 13 covers how to run listening that people trust.
Write down what you hear, in their words.
"Wants more hours" and "is worried the schedule will never stabilize" are different problems with different fixes.
Look for patterns across people.
One person mentioning the scheduling system is a complaint. Six people mentioning it is a finding.

blocks.text: Do something within two weeks, and say so

runs.t: This is the step most companies skip, and it is the one that matters most.

Every Retention Talk should produce one specific action with a date. It does not need to be big. Fix the broken headset. Clarify the path to a lead role. Move a recurring meeting. Then, when it is done, tell the person.
A conversation with no follow-through teaches people that honesty produces nothing. The next time you ask, they will give you the clean story.
If you cannot fix something, say that too, and say why. People can live with "we looked at it and we cannot change it this year, and this is the reason." What they cannot live with is silence.
This is a hypothetical, not a client or one of my results.

Say you run a site with 200 people and start with the 20 you can least afford to lose. At 30 minutes each, the round is about 10 hours of leadership time. Six of the 20 mention the same scheduling problem, three mention a broken piece of equipment and two have been waiting on an answer about a promotion. That gives you three fixes with owners and two conversations for this week.
If one of those two stays because someone finally laid out a path, you have likely saved more than those 10 hours cost. Chapter 3 shows how to put a dollar figure on a single departure.

blocks.text: If you keep exit interviews, change them

runs.t: You do not need to stop exit interviews. You need to stop treating them as the truth.
Change the question.

"Why are you leaving?" invites the clean story. "What would it take to get you back?" goes straight to the conditions, because it is about the future, not blame. People who will not criticize their supervisor will often tell you exactly what a job they would return to looks like.
Use a neutral third party if you can.
The Work Institute data came from interviews run by a neutral party, and that is part of why it found what it found. People are more candid with someone who has no stake in their reference.
Ask where they are going.
Ask about the company, the role, the schedule and what they expect to be different. Over time, that tells you who is recruiting your people (Chapter 9).
Compare exit themes with Retention Talk themes.
Put them side by side. Where they agree, you have a strong signal. Where they disagree, trust the Retention Talks. The gap between the two is your blind spot.
Gallup found that 77% of people who quit either left within three months of starting to look, or never actively looked at all.

That second group matters. Some people are not job hunting. A recruiter calls, or a friend texts about an opening, and they say yes to a conversation they would not have sought out. If they were already at the thinking layer, that call is all it takes.

So the window is short. If the first real conversation about someone's future happens after they give notice, it is too late. If it happens once a year in a performance review, it is probably too late too.
The companies that keep their people do not have better exit interviews. They have more conversations, earlier, with the people they most want to keep, and they do something with what they hear.

blocks.text: Questions to ask your leadership team

runs.t: Before your next meeting about turnover, ask these:
When our exit data says "compensation," how do we know that is the main reason and not the polite one?
In the last year, how many of our best people were asked what would keep them, before they gave notice?
What is the most common frustration on our front line right now, and who owns fixing it?
If we offered a raise to the last five people who left, how many would come back? If the honest answer is "not many," what else were they leaving?

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Commission one round of Retention Talks this quarter, starting with the people you can least afford to lose. Put the themes next to your last exit survey. The gap between the two is your blind spot.
•  Manager: Ask each direct report the four questions this month. Bring the top two themes to your next leadership meeting with an action and a date attached to each.
•  Supervisor: Ask one person today: if you ever left, what would make you go? Make it safe to answer. Then do one thing about it, and tell them when it is done.

runs.t: If the reasons people give are not the reasons they leave, the next question is what your leadership team is looking at instead. In my region, the dashboard was full of numbers, and the one that would have told us the truth was not on it.

label: Chapter 2
title: The six numbers a CEO should watch
subtitle: Why the dashboard looked best when the stores were in the worst shape, and the six numbers a CEO should watch instead

runs.t: When I was running a region, payroll dollars were one of the main numbers we were judged on. Every region had a payroll target. Ours had not been hitting it.
Then, one period, we made it.
Everyone celebrated. Our region received its first award for payroll control.
Then I looked at why we had made the number.

We made payroll because we could not keep people. Turnover was so high that the stores could not be staffed. The hours were not being spent because nobody was there to work them. The people who stayed were covering the gaps, shift after shift.
We got our first award for payroll control when our stores were barely staying afloat.
Nobody did anything wrong by the rules we had. The system rewarded the number it was built to watch, and the number looked best when the operation was in the worst shape.
That is the problem this chapter is about.

blocks.text: You get what you pay for

runs.t: Bonusing on the wrong metric is like paying a lifeguard by how many towels he folds. Whatever you pay for becomes the job, no matter what the title says.

Nobody designs a scorecard to reward empty stores. Payroll was on the scorecard for good reasons. Labor is one of the biggest costs in any operation, and a region that overspends on hours is a real problem. But a payroll number by itself cannot tell the difference between a store that is running lean and well and a store that is running lean because half its people have quit.

When the only labor number on the page is cost, the cheapest store looks like the best store. And the cheapest store is often the one where nobody can get a day off, where the new hire is training the newer hire, and where the best person is quietly updating a résumé.

I have seen the same thing with other numbers. Overtime drops, and it looks like discipline, until you realize the people who used to work the overtime have left. A good number can hide a bad operation.
Our dashboards were full. We tracked net promoter score, service levels, an annual engagement survey and payroll dollars. Each one had an owner and a target.
Turnover was not on the list. Neither were the numbers underneath it:
Who quit in the first 90 days.
We knew how many people we hired. We did not track how many were still there three months later.
Who had been trained.
A new hire on the schedule counted as staffed, whether or not they knew how to do the job.
Individual performance and productivity.
We could see a store's results. We could not see which people were carrying it, or which ones we were losing.
So we could not see the thing driving most of our other problems.

Think about how that plays out. A short-staffed store misses its service levels, its customer scores slip and the engagement survey dips. Every one of those numbers gets its own action plan. The cause, the people walking out the door, is not on the page at all. And payroll looks good, for the worst possible reason.
Chasing a score is like watching the speedometer instead of the road. The needle moving does not mean you are headed anywhere good.

When a number becomes the goal, people steer by the number and stop asking what is happening on the road in front of them. We did that with payroll. Chapter 5 shows how the same thing happened with our engagement survey, where an 81 was a celebration and a 79 was a crisis, and the conversations that would have changed either number went untracked.
Most dashboards are like a thermometer. They tell you the temperature. A dashboard with insight is like a thermostat. It lets you change it.

Our dashboards were thermometers. They told us what had happened last period, store by store. They did not tell us why. A store's customer score was down. Was that because of the store manager, the staffing, the new hires, the pharmacy wait or a broken system? The dashboard could not say.
A thermostat dashboard does three things a thermometer does not:
It shows the cause next to the result, so a falling customer score sits next to that store's staffing and turnover.
It looks ahead, not only back, so leaders can act before the result shows up.
It points to an owner and an action, so the number leads to a conversation and not just a comment in a meeting.

Chapter 1 covered Gallup's finding that most turnover is preventable and that most people who quit were never asked about their future. Gallup has also found that managers account for about 70% of the variance in their teams' engagement.

Put those together and the case for watching turnover by manager, and early, is hard to argue with. If most of the variance sits with managers, the company average is the wrong place to look. If the window is three months, a yearly report will always be late.

blocks.text: What I tracked on my own

runs.t: Since the dashboard would not show me turnover, I built my own view. It was not complicated. It started in a spreadsheet. I tracked four things:
Staffing levels by store.
How many people each store had against what it needed.
Hires made.
How many people each store brought on.
Who was still there at 90 days.
The number that told me whether hiring was working.
Overall market turnover.
What was happening around us, so I could tell a local problem from a market one.
None of this required new software. The data existed. Nobody upstairs was asking for it.
The first thing it showed me changed how we worked.
Turnover looked high across the whole region. It was not. Three districts drove 80% of it.

blocks.title: Share of one region's turnover, by district group

runs.t: Those were the hard-to-staff stores, in areas with plenty of better places to work nearby. They were the stores where a new hire could walk across the parking lot and get a job with easier hours, and many did.

Once we could see that, we stopped spreading help evenly across the region. Before, every district got a share of recruiting attention, float coverage and my time, roughly in proportion to its size. That felt fair. It was wrong. We put staffing support where the losses were, and we let the districts that were doing fine keep doing fine.
Averages hide the reality.
A regional number told us we had a regional problem. We had a problem in three districts, and the fix looked different there.
Every company average is a blend. The job is to find out what it is a blend of.
This is an illustration of the math. Picture an energy company with 4% turnover. That looks healthy, and nobody would flag it.
Now split it by manager. Most teams are at about 1%. Three managers are at about 10%. The company does not have a turnover problem. It has three teams with one, and the average is covering for them.
That is an illustration, not a client. You can test for the pattern in an afternoon.

blocks.text: A simple way to do it

runs.t: Pull every voluntary departure from the last 12 months. You need the person's location, job title, hire date, leave date and manager at the time they left.
Pull average headcount for the same period, by the same groupings.
Calculate turnover for each group: departures divided by average headcount.
Sort from highest to lowest.
Ask how much of the total sits in the top few groups.

Do it by region, then by district or site, then by manager. If a small number of groups carry most of the total, you have found where to look. If it is spread evenly, you may have a company-wide cause, such as pay, scheduling or a policy everyone lives with.
A high number next to a manager's name is a reason to ask questions. It is not a verdict.

Some managers inherit a mess. Some are sent into the hardest stores on purpose, because they are good. Chapter 7 tells the story of a manager whose turnover looked terrible on paper, until someone asked and found he had been brought in to fix a team that was already losing people before he arrived.
The data tells you where to look. People tell you what you are looking at.

blocks.text: The interview guide that never changed

runs.t: The hiring interview guide in use when I left in 2024 was the same guide we used when I started in 2004, slightly modified. I still have one of my early copies from my days as a store trainer.
In 20 years, the jobs changed. The technology changed. The labor market changed several times over. The way we chose people barely moved.

Nobody was measuring who stayed, so nobody had a reason to ask whether the guide still worked. If 90-day turnover had been on the dashboard, someone would have asked why so many new hires were gone before their third month. Chapter 16 covers how to rebuild hiring around the people who stay and succeed.

blocks.text: The six numbers a CEO should watch

runs.t: If I could put only six numbers in front of a CEO, these are the six. Together they show what turnover costs, where it is coming from and what is about to happen.

Nobody takes a job, goes through all those steps to get the job, and quits right away for no reason. When people leave in the first 90 days, the cause is inside the company: what we promised, who we chose, how we trained them or how we supported them. That makes it one of the most controllable numbers you have.

To calculate it, take everyone hired in a given month or quarter and count how many are still there 90 days later. Track it by location and by hiring manager. When one location's new hires leave faster than everyone else's, the cause is usually local and usually fixable. Chapter 17 covers what to do in those first 90 days.
Company averages hide pockets. This cut shows whether you have a company problem or a problem on a few teams.

Track voluntary turnover for each manager's team over a rolling 12 months, and compare it with the company rate. Look for the managers well above it, and also the ones well below it. The ones well below are often doing something worth copying.

blocks.text: 3. The dollar cost of turnover, the Turn Tax

runs.t: Most CEOs can name about eight costs of a departure: interviews, paperwork, the drug test, the background check. They miss the rest.
New hires make more mistakes and work slower. A good person comes off the line to train them. Customers notice. Overtime fills the gap, and the people working it get tired.

The Turn Tax counts all of it, across 13 cost categories and up to 250 variables, using your own pay and your own operation. A turnover rate tells a CFO very little. A dollar figure gets a budget conversation started. Chapter 3 shows how to build one.

blocks.text: 4. Who is likely to leave, the Flight Risk Score

runs.t: The other five numbers describe what already happened. This one looks ahead.

It scores each person's risk of leaving from 0 to 99 for the next 90 days. It starts with 19 base variables in four areas: manager relationship, career and tenure, pay and job friction. EIP then weights them for each company, adds variables where needed and tests the result against that company's past departures. It is a documented calculation, not AI.

What leaders watch is the bands: 0 to 40 is low risk, 41 to 60 is worth watching, 61 to 80 means intervention needed and 81 to 99 is critical. Chapter 6 covers how it works and what to do at each level.
From interviews and small listening sessions run by a third party, the three things the executive team should do this week or this month to make work better for employees.

Three, not thirty. A list of thirty is a report. A list of three is a plan. The test each quarter is whether last round's three got done, and whether employees noticed. Chapter 13 covers how to run listening that produces a list worth acting on.

Losing a low performer is often a good thing. Losing a long-tenured high performer creates a ripple effect. The team often loses the person others stayed for, the one who trained the new people and the one customers asked for by name.

A company can bring its overall rate down while losing more of the people it most needs to keep. Track high performer turnover on its own. Chapter 8 covers why your best people are also your biggest risk.

blocks.text: How often to review each one

runs.t: These are EIP's recommendations, based on how often each number can change and how fast you can act on it. Adjust them to fit how fast your business moves.

rows: Monthly, by location and hiring manager
Any location where new hires are leaving faster than last quarter
Monthly, with a deeper quarterly review
Each senior leader for their own managers
Managers well above the company rate, and why
Quarterly, rebuilt yearly or when pay or headcount shifts
The dollar trend, and which locations drive it
Growth in the Intervention needed (61 to 80) and Critical (81 to 99) bands
Whether last round's three items were fixed, and whether employees noticed
Every departure as it happens, trend quarterly
Any loss of a long-tenured top performer

runs.t: One rule applies to all six. Flight Risk Scores stay with senior leaders and HR. Supervisors never see individual scores, and the score never makes an employment decision. It tells leaders where to look and who to talk to.

At EIP, we review these numbers monthly with our clients in what we call Council View, with members of our Council of current and former executives in the room asking the questions an outside operator would ask. You do not need us to start. You need the six numbers on one page, and a standing meeting where someone is expected to explain them.
Put turnover on the main dashboard.
Next to customer scores and payroll, not in a separate HR report that only HR reads.
Ask what each good number is costing you.
When payroll, overtime or service levels improve suddenly, check staffing and turnover before you celebrate.
Split every average.
By district, by location and by manager. Look for the few places driving most of the number.
Track the first 90 days for every hire.
Count who is still there, who was trained and who they reported to.
Review your interview guide.
If it is older than the jobs it hires for, compare it with what your long-tenured top performers have in common.
Watch who leaves, not only how many.
Treat every departure of a high performer as something to understand within the week.

blocks.text: Questions to ask your leadership team

runs.t: Which numbers on our dashboard would look better if we lost more people? What do we check before we celebrate them?
Can anyone in this room say, without looking it up, what our 90-day turnover was last quarter?
Where does our turnover come from? If we split it by manager, how many teams carry most of it?
When was our interview guide last rewritten, and who decided it still works?

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Look at your dashboard. Count how many of the numbers tell you anything about who is leaving. If the answer is none, ask for 90-day turnover and turnover by manager by next month.
•  HR leader: Pull last year's turnover by manager. Find the three teams furthest above the company rate. Before you draw a conclusion, ask what happened on each one.
•  Manager: List everyone you hired in the last six months. Mark who is still there and who was fully trained. Talk with the ones still there about how their first weeks went.
•  Supervisor: Pick the newest person on your team. Ask what has been harder than they expected, and fix one thing they name.

runs.t: The payroll award taught me that a dashboard can celebrate a loss. The next question is how big that loss was. Turnover is a tax every company pays, and almost nobody sees the whole bill.

label: Chapter 3
title: Turn Tax: what turnover really costs
subtitle: What turnover costs, and why your HR report only shows the tip

runs.t: Every year we hired about 2,000 people for our busiest season.

We started recruiting in August and kept going through December. Most of the hiring landed in October and November. Each person went through the same steps. We screened them. We ran background checks and drug tests. We did the paperwork. Then we trained them for weeks, because the calls they would take were not simple calls.
Day one was January 1. That was the whole point of the program. On January 1, every one of those people was supposed to be trained, in a seat and taking calls.
42% of them never made it to day one.

That is roughly 840 people. We paid to find them. We paid to screen and process them. We paid trainers to teach them and paid them to sit in the training room. Then they left before they helped a single customer.

None of it showed up anywhere as "turnover cost." The money was spread across the recruiting budget, the training budget, overtime and temp labor. Each of those lines looked normal on its own. Nobody in finance was wrong about any single line.

The next year we redesigned how we hired. We shortened the process, so good candidates were not sitting around for weeks waiting for a start date and taking another job in the meantime. We added new filters and screening questions, so the people we hired were the people likely to stay. The number dropped to 15%.
That was about 540 more trained people in a seat on January 1.
Nobody had ever added it up. That is the trouble with turnover cost. It is large and it is invisible by default.

blocks.title: Seasonal hires lost before day one
blocks.source: Author's career, about 2,000 seasonal hires a year

runs.t: I call it the Turn Tax, because that is how it behaves. Every time someone quits, you pay it. You do not get a bill. You do not get a line on the P&L that says "turnover." The cost comes out of a dozen other places, a little at a time, and so nobody manages it like a cost.

Think about how a tire goes flat. Most of the time it is a slow leak, not a blowout. The tire loses air for ninety days before it goes flat, and the car still drives the whole time. You might notice it pulls a little. You might notice the gas mileage drops. You do not pull over until the rim hits the road.

Turnover works the same way. A team that loses a few people a quarter still opens every morning. The leak shows up as a little more overtime, a few more mistakes, a supervisor who looks tired. None of it trips an alarm until the tire is flat.

In Chapter 2, I wrote about the six numbers a CEO should watch. The dollar cost of turnover is one of them. Most leaders can name about eight costs when I ask: interviews, paperwork, the drug test and a few others. Those are real. They are also the smallest part.
A recruiting fee is like the tip of an iceberg. It is the part you can see above the water. Productivity loss, manager time and new hire errors are the ninety percent hiding underneath.

Ask most companies what turnover costs and they add up job ads, agency fees and background checks, because someone already paid an invoice for each of them. The rest of the iceberg never generates an invoice.
Six costs sit underwater in almost every company I have looked at.
The slowdown before they leave.
People who are planning to go do not work at full speed in their last weeks or months. They are on the roster. They are not fully there.
The empty seat.
Someone covers it, with overtime, temp labor or a supervisor doing two jobs. The cost lands in four different budget lines, and none of them is labeled turnover.
The manager's time.
Every interview and every hour spent covering the gap is time a manager is not running the operation.
The new person's learning curve.
A replacement takes weeks or months to reach full speed, and makes the mistakes the last person already learned to avoid.
The knowledge that walks out.
Workarounds, customer relationships and how things get done. None of it is written down.
The customer.
In service work, customers feel turnover first, in errors, wait times and unfamiliar faces. Chapter 4 is about that cost.

This next part should bother a CFO. Every one of those six is paid in full, in overtime, scrap, refunds and hours a director spends interviewing. The company is not avoiding the cost by failing to measure it. It is paying the cost without knowing what it bought.
Sometimes the report does not just miss the cost. It hides the problem entirely.

During COVID, call-offs at my company were paid, but they carried no tracking code. If someone called off, they still got paid, and the system still counted them as working. On paper, our stores looked about 95% staffed.

My team did not believe it. The stores did not feel 95% staffed. Leaders were telling us they could not cover shifts. So we built our own report of who showed up and how long they worked. In reality we were closer to 60%.

Think about what that gap means. Corporate saw a healthy operation. The stores were running with four people out of every ten missing. Because the people were still on the roster, nobody upstream saw a retention problem at all, and the people burning out covering those shifts were invisible too.
Eventually a code was added. By then the damage was done.

Every company has some version of this. Your reports were built to answer a question someone asked years ago. When the numbers look fine and the people on the floor tell you they are not, go build your own count. It usually takes a few days and a spreadsheet.

When we built the Turn Tax™ at EIP, we tried to name every place the cost lands. We ended up with 13 categories and up to 250 variables. Not every variable applies to every company. A hospital and a trucking company bleed in different places. But the 13 categories show up almost everywhere.
The examples below are hypothetical. They are here to help you picture each category in your own building.
Job postings, agency fees, background checks and onboarding admin. This is the part everyone counts.
Example:
A regional bank replaces a teller. It pays for a job posting, a background check, a credit check and a drug screen. All of it is on an invoice.
HR time, manager interviews and internal coordination.
Example:
A plant supervisor spends six hours interviewing for one machine operator job, and HR spends four more. Nobody bills those hours to turnover.
Output lost while the role is vacant or ramping up.
Example:
A warehouse picker who moved 150 units an hour quits. The spot is empty for three weeks. The new hire starts at 80 units an hour and takes two months to reach 140.
Institutional knowledge, client relationships and process know-how.
Example:

The one billing specialist who knew how to fix a certain insurer's rejected claims leaves. Nobody else knows the workaround. For the next two months, those claims sit in a queue and cash comes in late.
The drop in engagement and the burnout on the people who stay.
Example:

A five-person nursing unit loses one nurse. The other four pick up her shifts for six weeks. One of them starts looking for a new job in week four. That second departure is part of the cost of the first.
Service disruption, relationship risk and revenue exposure.
Example:

An account manager at a software company leaves. Her largest client gets a new contact who does not know their history. At renewal, the client asks for a discount and gets three competing quotes for the first time in five years.
Coverage gaps, error rates and regulatory exposure.
Example:
A new forklift driver in his second week clips a rack. Nobody is hurt, but the product is lost and the incident has to be reported. The driver he replaced had not had an incident in four years.
Overtime, budget overruns and revenue tied to the vacancy.
Example:
A restaurant group covers three open line cook jobs with overtime for a month. Labor runs over budget. Nobody in the monthly review calls it turnover cost.
Delayed initiatives and competitive disadvantage.
Example:
A manufacturer plans to launch a new product line in the spring. The engineer leading the project leaves in January. The launch slips six months, and a competitor gets to the shelf first.
Executive time diverted to coverage and replacement.
Example:
A regional vice president spends two days a week for a month covering for a general manager who quit, instead of coaching his other managers.
Pipeline pressure, sourcing effort and offer negotiation.
Example:
A home health agency is always hiring for the same aide jobs. The recruiter fills the last opening instead of building a bench, so every new opening starts from zero.
Access changes, licenses and system knowledge lost.
Example:
A dispatcher leaves. IT shuts off five logins and rebuilds the routing spreadsheet she kept on her own desktop, because nobody else knew it existed.
Employer brand, review sites and candidate perception.
Example:

Three former employees of a call center post bad reviews on a job site in the same month. Applications drop. The next job posting needs a higher starting rate or a sign-on bonus to get the same number of candidates.

Go back through that list and count how many of those costs your company tracks today. Most companies I meet track the first two. A few track part of the third. The other ten are being paid and not counted.

blocks.text: What the research says it costs

runs.t: The research range on turnover cost is huge, and that range is the lesson.

items.label: of salary for jobs paying under $30,000 a year (Center for American Progress, 2012)
of annual salary to replace an employee, which Gallup calls conservative (Gallup, 2019)
of salary to replace leaders and managers (Gallup, 2024)

runs.t: The Center for American Progress reviewed 30 case studies and found a typical cost of about 16% of salary for jobs paying under $30,000 a year. Many of the studies only counted direct costs. They counted the tip.

Gallup estimates that replacing an employee costs one-half to two times their annual salary, and calls that conservative. By that math, a 100-person company with an average salary of $50,000 could be paying $660,000 to $2.6 million a year in turnover and replacement costs.
At the top of the house, Gallup's 2024 research puts the cost of replacing leaders and managers at around 200% of their salary.
Depending on the role and what you count, the answer swings by ten times or more. A national average cannot tell you what turnover costs your company. Only your own numbers can.
When we build a Turn Tax, we start with ranges like these and then replace them with a client's own data:
Frontline roles:
about 25% to 55% of annual salary per departure.
Specialized and technical roles:
about 45% to 120%.
Senior leaders and executives:
about 150% to 250%.
Those are starting points. A frontline job with a long training period and a lot of customer contact sits at the top of its range.

blocks.text: What it looked like when I did the math

runs.t: For most of my career, I could not have told you what turnover cost us. When I finally added up my own results from 20 years in operations at a Fortune 10 company, I wanted a number I could defend line by line in front of a CFO. So I used the most conservative version of every input.
There were three rules.
Count the people who stayed.

Across my region, a distribution center and the seasonal hiring program, about 2,100 people a year stayed who, at the old turnover rates, would have left. That is the difference between how many people left before and how many left after.
Use real pay.

I used the actual pay for each group at the time, not a company average. Hourly pay was converted at 2,080 hours a year. I do not print those wages here. Pay changes over the years, and what was true then is not what is true in your market now. Use your own.
Use the low end of every range.
For the seasonal hires who left during training, I counted only recruiting, training and admin, because they left before we lost any customers or knowledge.
This is how it built up.
Every line works the same way. People kept, times annual pay, times the rate.
Pharmacists.

We kept 84 more pharmacists a year than we would have at the old rate. Each one was costed at 80% of salary. Eighty percent is low for a licensed professional who carries patient relationships and is hard to replace. I used it anyway.
The distribution center.

We kept 276 more people a year, each costed at 30% of annual pay, the low end of the frontline range. That is before you count a single late truck or empty shelf. The full story of that building is in Chapter 20.
To see what your own version looks like, swap in today's pay for each group. The method holds even when the wages do not.
Add the groups together and you get more than $18 million a year in turnover cost avoided, across about 2,100 people who stayed.
At the midpoint of the same ranges, it was about $31 million a year. I use the $18 million because every input can be rebuilt line by line.
I use the $18 million because every input can be rebuilt line by line. That is the kind of number that survives a budget meeting.
You do not need 250 variables to get started. You need one role, a few numbers you already have and an afternoon.
Take a hypothetical 1,000-person company. Say 400 of those people work in one frontline job that pays $20 an hour, and that job runs at 50% turnover.
Count departures.
400 people at 50% turnover is 200 departures a year.
Get annual pay.
$20 an hour at 2,080 hours is $41,600.
Pick a conservative rate.
Use 25%, the bottom of the frontline range. That is $10,400 per departure.
Multiply.
200 departures at $10,400 each is $2,080,000 a year, for one job.
That is a hypothetical, and it is the low end. Now ask the questions that move you up the range:
How long does it take a new person in this job to reach full speed?
How much overtime did we pay last year to cover open shifts in this job?
How many hours does a supervisor spend hiring and training for this job each month?
What mistakes do new people make in their first 90 days, and what does each one cost?
Each answer either confirms the low end or pushes you up. Write down where every number came from.
Do the same for your second-highest turnover role, and then your leaders. Three roles usually cover most of the cost.

blocks.text: Present a recovery, not a cost

runs.t: Retention programs get deferred when they are presented as a cost, and costs get cut, especially in a tight year.
Change the first number on the page. Do not lead with what the program costs. Lead with what turnover already costs you every year, and how much of it you can recover.
Current Turn Tax:
what turnover costs you this year, across all 13 categories.
Recovery goal:
the share of it you and your partner agree to win back, tracked monthly.
Program cost:
compared against the recovery, not against other budget lines.
A retention program framed as a cost competes with every other cost. Framed as recovered profit, it competes with almost nothing.

Boards trust a range more than a single promise. If you walk in with one number, the room spends the meeting arguing about whether it is too high. If you walk in with three, the room spends the meeting deciding which one to aim for.

Take the hypothetical company above, with a $2,080,000 Turn Tax in one job and say the program costs $300,000. The percentages are examples. A real goal is set with your partner and tracked every month.

Even the conservative case pays for itself, and this is one job using the lowest rate. Year two usually looks better, because the program cost often drops after the first year and the recovery keeps building.

When I needed approval to raise starting pay at a distribution center, opinions would not have gotten it done. We priced the fix against the Turn Tax: a starting pay move of $1.25 an hour looks expensive by itself, and next to what turnover was costing, it was the cheaper option. Chapter 20 tells that story from start to finish.
The method works anywhere. Before you ask for money, put the cost of doing nothing on the same page.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Ask your CFO what one voluntary departure costs in your highest-turnover role. If nobody can answer in 48 hours, that is the first problem to solve.
•  CFO: Run the four-step calculation above for one job, using the lowest rate in the range. Write down the source for every input.
•  Manager: Pick three of the 13 categories you do not track today. Write down what they cost your team in the last 90 days, even roughly.
•  Supervisor: Ask the people who covered for your last departure what they had to do differently in the first month. Their answer is your team's hidden tax.

runs.t: The Turn Tax tells you what turnover costs inside your walls. The biggest part of the iceberg sits outside them, with your customers, and that is where Chapter 4 begins.

label: Chapter 4
title: Customers and turnover: fixing both together
subtitle: How fixing the workforce and the customer experience together moved NPS from 24 to 81

runs.t: When I took over customer experience in another part of the company, the on-time delivery number was 97%.
It had been near that level for a long time. Nobody questioned it, and I had no reason to either, at first.
Then I asked how it was measured.

A delivery counted as on time unless the customer complained. That was the rule. If a package showed up two days late and the customer was too busy or too tired to call, it went into the books as on time.
So we changed the measure. We tracked when the medication was promised and when it arrived. Two dates, compared against each other, for every delivery.
The figure was 81%.

Nobody had lied. The system had been built to count complaints, and most late deliveries never turned into one. Most people do not call to complain. They just remember. But for years, leaders had made decisions on a number that was 16 points too high.
If you measure the complaint instead of the event, you will always look better than you are.

blocks.title: On-time delivery, two ways of measuring it
blocks.source: Author's career, customer experience in a Fortune 10 company

runs.t: Complaint-based measures are everywhere, because complaints are easy to count. Events take more work. You have to capture two timestamps, or check every job against its promise.
A few hypothetical examples of how the same thing can be counted two ways:
A plumbing company
counts a job as "fixed the first time" unless the customer calls back. Customers who gave up and hired someone else never call back.
A clinic
counts appointments as "on time" unless a patient files a complaint about the wait. Most patients who waited forty minutes do not file anything. They book somewhere else next time.
In each case, the dashboard is measuring how annoyed people were and how willing they were to say so. That is a useful number. It is a different number from whether you kept your promise.

When you switch to counting the event, expect the number to drop, and decide ahead of time how you will talk about it. The instinct is to treat a drop like 97% to 81% as bad news. It is good news. You just learned where you stand.

blocks.text: A fresh coat of paint on a cracked foundation

runs.t: The delivery number was not the only thing that looked better than it was.
We told everyone the customer was number one. It was on the wall and in the training. Then we paid people for something else.

Average handle time was the goal. Reps were judged on how fast they got a customer off the phone. That number drove reviews, bonuses and promotions. So transfers exploded. A hard call got passed to someone else, and the clock stopped for the person who passed it. Some reps transferred calls back and forth to friends.
One rep had someone call in and sit on the line for 1 minute and 5 seconds, just long enough to count as a call. Each of those calls pulled the average down and helped earn the bonus.
It is easy to blame that rep. I blame the system. We built a scorecard that rewarded short calls, and a smart person found the shortest call possible. The company asked for the wrong thing.

Fixing culture with a values poster is like repainting a house with a cracked foundation. It looks great in photos until you feel it shift underfoot. Our poster said the customer came first. Our pay plan said the clock came first.
People believe what you pay for, not what you put on the wall.

Before you read on, pull up the scorecard for one of your customer-facing jobs. Read it the way a new hire would, someone who wants to do well and get promoted. What does it tell them to do? If the honest reading is "go fast and avoid complaints," that is what your customers are getting.

blocks.text: Almost no feedback reached the people doing the work

runs.t: The third problem was quieter.
Customer surveys reached about 1% of customers. The results rarely went back to the employee who handled the call. One rep took 2,000 calls and got one piece of customer feedback. One.

Quality review was done by hand. A supervisor listened to calls and scored them. That covered about 4 calls out of 2,000. A weak rep could look strong by luck, because the four calls pulled that month happened to be easy ones.

Think about what that means for someone trying to get better at a job. They hear almost nothing from the customer or from quality. What they do hear about, every day, is their handle time. So that is what they work on.

items.label: on-time delivery, once we measured the delivery instead of complaints
of customers answered surveys
calls were reviewed for quality

runs.t: You do not fix this by surveying more customers. You fix it by getting what you already know back to the person who did the work, often enough that it can change how they work.
A few ways to start, none of which needs a new system:
Send every piece of customer feedback to the employee it names,
good or bad, within a week. Most companies already collect it and stop it at the manager's inbox.
Review more calls or jobs, and shorter pieces of them.
Ten two-minute clips a month tell a rep more than four full calls picked at random.
Tie feedback to the drivers.
"The customer was happy" teaches little. "You told her about the delivery change before she had to call" teaches the behavior you want repeated.
The point is frequency. A person who hears about their work once a year is guessing for the other eleven months.
When I arrived there were 47 separate customer experience plans in place. Almost none of them moved the customer.
We stopped all of them.

That was not a popular call. People had put real work into those plans, and some of them were good ideas. But you cannot tell which plans matter until you know what the customer cares about. We did not know that yet. We had outcomes, like the NPS score, and nothing that explained them.

If you are running a lot of programs and the number is not moving, stopping is a legitimate move. It frees up people and attention, and it tells the organization that something different is happening. Chapter 10 comes back to this idea: diagnose before you build.
Then my team built a model of what matters to the customer.

We started wide. We ended with 50 data points of impact. Some mattered more by region, some by age, some by how long someone had been a customer. We scored each factor on its own, so we could rank what moved the experience most without one factor hiding behind another.
Four rose to the top.
On-time delivery.
Did the medication arrive when we promised? This was number one by a wide margin.
Contact when delivery changes.
If the date moved, did we tell the customer before they had to call us?
No surprise bill.
A surprise $2,000 bill mattered more to a customer than being newly onboarded.
First call resolution.
Did the first person who answered solve the problem, without a transfer?
None of the four is about a slogan or a new program. They are about whether the basic promise was kept, and whether a person on our side handled it well when it was not.
Now look at it from the workforce side. Three of the four depend on an experienced person doing the job well.

A new rep does not know how to head off a billing surprise. A rep who is planning to quit does not chase a delivery change before the customer calls. He is getting through the shift. A new rep transfers the hard call because she does not know the answer yet, and first call resolution drops.
Every driver on the list gets worse when an experienced person leaves and a new person learns on the customer. The Turn Tax category for customers (Chapter 3) shows up in these four numbers.

blocks.text: How to find your own drivers

runs.t: You do not need our model to start. You need your customer data, your outcome measure and some patience.

Say you run a hypothetical home services company. Your outcome is whether a customer books again within a year. You might list 30 or 40 factors: arrival window met, same technician as last time, price matched the quote, job finished on the first visit and so on.
List everything you can measure.
Do not filter yet.
Score each factor on its own.
For each one, compare customers who got it with customers who did not, and look at the outcome.
Rank them.

Expect a short list to do most of the work. In this hypothetical, you might find that "job finished on the first visit" and "price matched the quote" matter far more than how fast the phone was answered.
Check how each driver is measured.
Make sure you are counting the event, not the complaint.
Ask who controls each driver.
Usually the answer is a person in a specific job. Then ask how long people stay in that job.
That last question is the one most customer experience teams never ask.

blocks.text: We rebuilt the people side around the drivers

runs.t: Once we knew the four drivers, we built accurate reporting on each one. That came first, because you cannot coach to a number you cannot see. Then we changed what we asked people to do and what we paid them for.
Retraining.
Training was rebuilt around the four drivers, starting with first call resolution.
New incentives and reviews.
Reviews and bonuses moved away from handle time and toward the drivers.
Pay for new skills.
People earned more as they learned more, instead of waiting for one big promotion. Chapter 15 covers how those small pay steps worked.
Surprise and delight pay.
We added pay for going beyond what the customer expected.

Moving off handle time looked risky on paper. Individual calls did get longer. But transfers dropped, and every transfer adds minutes of reintroduction and retelling. Total time on the phone went down. Chapter 14 tells how a voice AI rollout forced that same lesson on us from another direction.
Then we worked on keeping the people who were good at it. That meant knowing who they were, asking them what got in their way and fixing it.
This was not fast, and a lot of programs promise results in a quarter.

It took about 3 to 4 months to understand the data. It took about 6 more months to build the plan. We saw progress in the first year, mostly because people knew we were watching the right numbers. When you change what gets measured, behavior starts to move before any program launches. The results hit their stride in year two.
Over two years, NPS went from 24 to 81.

That was the employee experience and the customer experience moving together. It was not retention alone, and it was not a customer program alone. The team that did the work deserves the credit. They lived with an unpopular decision to stop 47 plans, rebuilt their own training and trusted a new scorecard before it had proven anything.

blocks.title: Net Promoter Score over two years
blocks.source: Author's career, customer experience in a Fortune 10 company

runs.t: The money came from throughput.

In our business, throughput was the time from when a prescription came in to when it reached the customer's hand. Faster throughput meant faster billing and faster payment. Late orders caused problems everywhere: extra calls, reshipments, unhappy customers and cash that came in later than it should have.
Turnover slows throughput. New people work slower and make more mistakes. Every open seat pulls an experienced person off the work to cover or train.
We pulled two levers.
Keeping the good people.
Fewer experienced people walked out, so fewer orders waited on someone learning the job.
Fixing friction.
We asked what got in the way of doing an amazing job, then paid for the simple fixes people asked for. Nearly every one returned at least 3x, and some returned up to 15x.
Together, those gains added $104 million in operating profit (EBIT).

If you run a plant, the same two levers apply on a production line. The experienced operator who clears a jam in two minutes, and the new one who takes twenty, are the difference between hitting the shift goal and missing it.

The friction fixes were mostly small. People were not asking for a raise or a new building. They were asking for the tool or the process change that would let them do the job right. A 3x return on a request from the front line is better than most capital projects a company will approve all year.

blocks.text: When the person who knows you quits

runs.t: Customers with complex needs who called often got a single point of contact. One named person knew their therapies, their history and how they liked to be reached. The customer did not have to explain themselves every time they called. They asked for that person by name.
It worked so well it became a premium service the company could sell.

The risk sat on the other side. When that person quit, the customer had to start over with a stranger and explain everything again: the diagnosis, the insurance problems, the last three things that went wrong.

It is like losing your doctor or your pharmacist. You can find another one. But you have to start over and build that trust again, and some people do not bother. They go somewhere else and start over there.
That is why I say the people who stay are why customers stay. Your customer does not have a relationship with your brand. They have one with the person who picks up the phone.
Your customer does not have a relationship with your brand. They have one with the person who picks up the phone.

Every company has roles like this, even if they are not formal. The account manager. The route driver who has served the same stops for years. The front desk person who remembers names. When one of them leaves, it never shows up in the turnover report as a customer cost. It shows up months later as a renewal that did not happen.
Audit how each customer number is measured.
For every metric on your dashboard, ask whether it counts the event or the complaint. Expect at least one to drop.
Stop the plans you cannot tie to a driver.
Pause every customer program until you know which few factors move your customers. Then restart only the ones that serve those factors.
Find your drivers.
Score each factor on its own and rank them. Expect a short list to do most of the work.
Pay for the drivers, not for speed.
If first call resolution matters, stop rewarding handle time. Check what your bonuses reward against what you say you want.
Put feedback back in front of the employee.
One comment in 2,000 calls teaches nobody anything. Give each person regular feedback tied to the drivers.
Protect the people your customers know by name.
List every role where a customer would notice if that person left. Know who in those roles is at risk, and talk to them first.

That last step is where retention and customer experience become the same job. EIP's Flight Risk Score exists for that conversation: it shows who is likely to leave in the next 90 days, so a manager can talk to the people customers depend on before they go. Chapter 6 explains how it works.

blocks.text: Questions to ask in your next leadership meeting

runs.t: Which of our customer metrics would change if we measured the event instead of the complaint?
What does our frontline scorecard reward, in the words a new hire would use?
How many customer programs are running right now, and which driver does each one serve?
Which jobs control our top customer drivers, and what is turnover in those jobs?
If our three best customer-facing people quit next month, which customers would notice first?
If nobody in the room can answer the fourth question, start there.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Ask how on-time delivery, or your equivalent, is measured. If the answer involves complaints, ask for the figure based on when the delivery arrived.
•  Operations leader: Put your turnover trend next to your throughput trend for the last 24 months. Look for where they move together.
•  Manager: Pull your team's scorecard. Ask each person what they think it rewards. If the answer is speed, and you want resolution, change it.
•  Supervisor: Ask your team which customers would call asking for them by name. Tell your manager who those people are.

runs.t: All of this depends on hearing the truth from your own people. Most companies try to get it once a year, with a survey, and Chapter 5 is about what that survey hears instead.
