label: Chapter 5
title: Engagement surveys, and what to ask instead
subtitle: Why your annual engagement survey hears the wrong people, and what to ask instead

runs.t: It was September. There was cake in the break room.

It was the only month all year with birthday cake. There was a bowl of candy bars on the table. My boss called to say thank you for my hard work. It was the only recognition call I got from him all year, and it came the week before the survey launched.
Then the email went out. The subject line said we value your feedback. The first paragraph said all responses were anonymous.
Everyone on the floor knew how this worked. People had a name for it: "five to stay alive." On a one-to-five scale, a five is invisible. Nobody asks who gave the five. A two gets traced back to you.
Results came back weeks later in a beautiful slide deck. Scores were up two points from last year. Leadership celebrated. A town hall got scheduled.
Meanwhile, turnover kept climbing. The survey score and the turnover number did not move together. They were not measuring the same thing.

For years I lived inside that ritual, first as a store leader and later as a region director, when the score was one of the most public numbers a leader had. It taught me what an annual survey measures when the stakes are high and the trust is low. It measures fear.
An annual engagement survey is like a New Year's resolution. Everyone means it on day one, and by March nobody is tracking it.

The pattern is the same almost everywhere. The survey launches with energy. Results come back. An action plan gets written and presented. A few things happen in the first few weeks. Then the next quarter's priorities arrive, and the plan goes into a folder.
The trouble is not that people stop caring. A single snapshot a year cannot carry a full year of work. By the time the results come back, the people most likely to leave have often already left.

There is a second comparison I like. An annual survey is like an annual physical. Ongoing check-ins are like a smartwatch on your wrist. If your heart rate has been off for six weeks, you want to know in week one, not at your next appointment.

blocks.text: The survey hears the wrong voices

runs.t: Every survey assumes the answers represent your workforce. They do not. Three groups answer in three very different ways.
Your long-tenured people check out.
They have taken this survey every year. They have watched nothing change. So why bother? They mark it down the middle, or skip it, and they leave the comment box empty.
Your new people play it safe.
They are generally happy, and they fill it out. But they are just starting their careers and they do not believe it is anonymous. They are not going to risk being honest.
Your unhappy people unload.
Someone who already has one foot out the door has a lot to say, and the comment box is their chance to say it.

Now aggregate the comments. They skew toward unhappy people and new people. The voice you are missing is the one that matters most: the happy, long-tenured high performers who know how the work gets done and what would make it better.

And every answer counts the same. Your top performer's score weighs exactly as much as the score of someone who is already planning to leave. You would not give those two opinions equal weight in any other setting.

blocks.text: What a score cannot tell you

runs.t: Take a hypothetical team that scores 91 on engagement. On a slide, that looks excellent. But a highly engaged person can still leave for a 30% raise, for remote work or for a better boss down the street. A high score tells you people feel good about the work today. It does not tell you whether a recruiter called them last week, or whether their manager has spoken to them one-on-one in two months.
Our real number, on my teams, went from 72 to 81, and I will tell you how in a moment. The point is that no score by itself tells you who is about to go.

Try this hypothetical to see the problem in your own data. Say a 500-person company scores 78 overall. Now split the results by the most recent performance rating. The bottom group, often the most vocal, scores in the low 70s. The middle group scores close to the average. The top 100 performers score 70, and a third of them left the comment box empty.
The company-wide 78 hid the most important fact in the survey: the people the company could least afford to lose were among the least engaged.

You can run this split with almost any survey vendor, as long as the groups are large enough to protect confidentiality. If the vendor cannot do it, compare survey results by team against each team's turnover among high performers.

blocks.text: Anonymous is a promise employees do not believe

runs.t: Most surveys require a login with an employee ID or an email address. That makes them confidential, not anonymous. Anonymous means nobody can connect an answer to a person. Confidential means someone can, and has promised not to. The vendor knows who said what.
Employees understand the difference, even when nobody explains it to them.

Small teams make it worse. If your manager is the problem and your team has six people, you are not going to write that down. In our case, teams under four people got no results at all, which was meant to protect them. In practice, managers guessed who scored low anyway.

So people disguise their writing. They skip capital letters they would normally use. They avoid words they normally say. Your employees are working to hide their own voice from the survey that claims to want it.
Your employees are working to hide their own voice from the survey that claims to want it.

blocks.text: The participation rate is not what it looks like

runs.t: Survey programs love to report 80% participation. That number is often made this way.
There is a list of names.
Managers get a report of who has not taken the survey yet: go talk to these 10 people.
People get called in.
Not taking the survey becomes a performance conversation.
Some managers watch.
Some managers have sat in the office and watched the screen while an employee filled it out.
By the time a pressured employee finally takes the survey, they are annoyed. How honest do you think that answer is?
All that pressure produces good-looking results. It does not mean anyone is more likely to stay.

blocks.text: When the number becomes the goal

runs.t: There was no bonus attached to the score. There did not need to be. It was public, and everyone knew where they stood. The leader with the best engagement could win an award. A leader with bad engagement had meetings with HR and had to write a plan. The leaders with the worst scores found HR sitting in on their next region meeting. It was very clear you did not want a bad score.

Once a number is that public, people manage the number. A move from 80 to 81 got celebrated. A drop to 79 caused panic. The things that would have moved the score for the right reasons went untracked: whether one-on-ones happened, whether people had a career plan, whether pay was fair.
That is how you end up with cake in September. Nobody planned it as a trick. It is what a reasonable person does when their reputation depends on how people feel during one week of the year.

blocks.text: Where the feedback goes to die

runs.t: Even honest feedback has a long trip to make. A frontline employee with a great idea can be ten steps away from anyone who can act on it. Every step is a filter.

Leaders at the top cannot read thousands of comments, so someone summarizes them. That summary is another filter. By the time an idea reaches a decision maker, it has been smoothed into a theme on a slide. "Communication" is a theme. "Nobody tells second shift when the schedule changes" is an idea. Only one of those can be fixed on Monday.

Sometimes the summary points the wrong way. During a hard stretch for our pharmacists, the lowest-scoring survey question was about having enough tools and resources. Corporate read that as a call for technology spending. The cause was that the lead technician role had been eliminated in many stores. People did not need a new system. They needed a person beside them. Chapter 1 tells that story.
The vendors know this. Many clients paid for the survey, received the deck, put it on a desk and never held a follow-up meeting.
Perceptyx's 2026 State of Employee Listening research puts numbers on the gap.

blocks.title: What employees say happens after a survey
blocks.source: Perceptyx, State of Employee Listening, 2026, as reported by HR Dive

runs.t: 71% of employees said their organization shares survey results. 59% said action plans are created. Only 51% said the feedback led to any actual improvement.
No action is worse than no survey. When you ask for someone's opinion and nothing visible happens, you teach them that speaking up is a waste of time. Next year, they answer accordingly.

blocks.text: Why companies keep doing it anyway

runs.t: When I stopped leaning on our annual survey, I got pushback. All of it was predictable.
It costs a lot, so it has to work.
We were spending more than $1 million a year on the survey. When you spend that much, people want to see year-over-year improvement.
Leaders were judged on the score.
The number became the goal, even though it did not tie to turnover or customer results.
Everyone else does it.
Nobody wants to be the one that stopped.
It feels like action.
Running a survey feels like listening, even when nothing changes afterward.
I understand every one of those reasons. None of them is a reason to keep paying for a measurement nobody acts on.

blocks.text: What we did instead: magic wand interviews

runs.t: On my teams, we replaced most of our reliance on the survey with conversations. Today we call them Retention Talks. Back then, my teams called them magic wand interviews, because of the first question.

blocks.title: The magic wand questions
lines: •  If you had a magic wand, what part of your job would you eliminate to make things better for you?
•  What would it take to get you to go to a competitor?
•  When you go home and talk to your family about your job, what do you usually say first?
•  If you had unlimited money, what would you fix?
•  If you had unlimited resources, what would you fix?
•  If you could only fix one thing, what would it be?
•  If you had no money, but could fix one thing, what would it be? This is the one that changed everything.

runs.t: The "no money" answers were gold. They were problems we could fix quickly, without waiting for budget or corporate approval. So we fixed them, and we told people we did.
Meeting times.
We moved meetings to different times of day, because people had to pick up their kids.
Recognition.
We changed how we recognized people, including recognizing them publicly, and more than once a year.
Report colors.
Our reports were designed in color, but the printers were black and white. Printed out, every line looked the same. We fixed the colors.
Some of these sound almost silly. That is the point. They cost nothing, they were fast and they proved that someone was listening. The next time you ask, people tell you more.
You do not need a vendor to start. You need a quiet room, thirty minutes and a manager who can hold back the urge to explain.
Pick who you talk to first.
Start with your long-tenured high performers, the voices your survey is missing. They know how the work gets done and they have the most options elsewhere.
Say why you are asking.
Tell them you want to know what gets in the way, and that you will come back and tell them what you did with it.
Ask, then stop talking.
The competitor question will make some people nervous. Let the silence sit.
Write it down in their words.
Not your summary. The exact phrase.
Ask the no-money question every time.
It turns a complaint session into a list of fixes.
Sort what you heard.
Quick and free, quick and costly, long-term and free, long-term and costly. Start with quick and free.
Go back to the person.
Tell them what you fixed, what you could not fix and why. Do it in person.

One caution. If a manager is the problem, the manager is the wrong person to run these conversations. That is one reason EIP's Honest Read uses a third party for interviews and small listening sessions. Chapter 13 goes deeper on how to run listening that works, including who should be in the room.

blocks.text: The score went up when we stopped chasing it

runs.t: We fixed what people told us, in person, and closed the loop. When people see that speaking up changes things, they answer the survey differently too, because they are no longer answering out of fear.

blocks.text: Better questions, if you keep a survey

runs.t: I am not telling every company to cancel its survey. Some companies need a broad read across thousands of people. If you keep it, ask better questions and handle the answers differently.

The best-known set of engagement questions is Gallup's Q12. We first used the Q12 at a distribution center, and later in our stores. The questions are short and concrete. They ask about things a manager can do something about, like whether people know what is expected of them and whether they have what they need to do the work. That makes the answers easier to act on than a broad question about whether someone believes in the company. At EIP, those questions fit into how we run Honest Read.
Whatever survey you use, a few rules make it more useful:
Read engagement next to performance.
Break the results out for your top performers. Their score is the one that predicts whether you keep the people you most need.
Read the score next to turnover.
If engagement is up and your best people are still leaving, believe the turnover number.
Act within 30 days.
Pick one or two things from the results and do them fast. Tell people you did.
Report back by name, where you can.
"You told us the printers made reports unreadable, and we fixed it" lands. "We heard your feedback on communication" does not.
Stop making the score the prize.
Recognize leaders for keeping good people and fixing what they hear, not for the number.

blocks.text: Questions to ask before the next survey goes out

runs.t: What did we change because of last year's survey, and who was told about it?
Whose pay is tied to the score?
Can we split the results by performance and tenure?
When engagement went up last year, did turnover among our best people go down?
Who on our team will read the comments, and what will they do in the first 30 days?
If the honest answers are uncomfortable, fix that before you ask your people for another hour of their time.
Decide before you survey.
If you are not prepared to act on what you hear within 30 days and tell people what you did, do not ask.
Run magic wand interviews.
Start with your long-tenured high performers. Ask the no-money question every time.
Fix the free things first.
The no-money list is your quick-win list. Most of it needs a decision, not a budget.
Close the loop by name.
Tell the people who raised it what you did. Not a company-wide memo. A conversation.
Stop making the score the prize.
Tie recognition to outcomes like retention of your best people, not to survey points.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Ask two questions about last year's survey. What specific actions came from it? Which employees were told about those actions by name? If neither answer is clear, fix the follow-through or stop running it.
•  CHRO: Find out whether any leader's pay is tied to the engagement score. If it is, list what else that leader's pay is tied to, and ask whether the score belongs on the list.
•  Manager: Ask each person on your team the no-money question this month. Pick one answer you can fix without approval. Fix it, and tell them.
•  Supervisor: Think about the last time someone gave you honest feedback. What did you do with it? Your team remembers, and it decides what they tell you next.

runs.t: A survey tells you how people felt during one week of the year. Most companies already hold far better signals in their HR systems, and Chapter 6 shows how to read them.

label: Chapter 6
title: Flight Risk Score: finding who is about to leave
subtitle: How a Flight Risk Score finds the people who need a conversation in the next 90 days

runs.t: We built a Flight Risk Score for an oil and gas company from the HR data of about 600 people. Some of them still worked there. Some had already left.

When we presented it to their leadership team, we took every name off the list on purpose. We wanted to show how the score worked, not who was on it. The room was full of people who had run that business for years, and we did not want the meeting to turn into a guessing game about colleagues.
It turned into a guessing game anyway.

The person at the top of the list scored 82, the highest in the company. All we showed was his region. Nobody asked us to reveal anything. The executives started guessing on their own, reading the region and the role and doing the math in their heads.
Someone from HR looked at the first row and asked, "Is that Daniel?"
We said yes.
She said, "Daniel quit last week."

That was the whole exchange. I have thought about it many times since. The people in that room had worked with Daniel for years. The signs that he was on his way out were sitting in their own HR file, in data they exported every month. Nobody had put those signs together in time.
The data already knew. The company did not.
This chapter is about closing that gap: what a Flight Risk Score reads, what the bands mean, what a manager should do on the day a name shows up, and what the score is not.
By the time a resignation letter lands on your desk, the decision has already been made. The letter is the receipt. The event happened earlier, quietly, while everyone was busy hitting their numbers.

Most leaders know this in their gut. Still, almost every retention process I saw in 20 years was built to respond to the letter. Exit interviews, counteroffers and a sad email to the team all happen after the event.
Chapter 1 covered Gallup's 2024 study of people who quit. The short version: most left within three months of starting to look, and nearly half were never asked about their future before they went.

That is the window. It is short, and most companies miss it. Waiting for people to tell you they are unhappy does not work, because most people never say it out loud. They say it with their calendar, their time-off requests and their silence in meetings. Then they say it with a letter.

A turnover report is a fire report. It tells you, in careful detail, how the building burned down. A Flight Risk Score is a smoke alarm. It does not put out the fire. It gives you time to walk into the room before the fire starts.
A company that only has fire reports will always be writing about the last loss.

blocks.text: The signs are already in your data

runs.t: Every experienced manager has watched someone leave and thought, "the signs were there." They usually were, spread across different reports and never read together.

Payroll knows when someone's raise fell behind. Scheduling knows when someone started calling off. The learning system knows when someone stopped signing up for training. HR knows when their manager changed. Each system holds one piece. Nobody holds the picture.
A Flight Risk Score reads them together. It looks at four areas.
Manager relationship.
Has their manager changed recently? How often do they meet? Are teammates leaving? This area usually carries the most weight, because it is the one a company controls most.
Career and tenure.
How long they have been with the company and in the role, how long since their last promotion, and whether they are near a point where people often decide to stay or go.
Pay.
Whether pay has kept up with raises, inflation and peers in the same role. Pay rarely causes a departure on its own, but it speeds up every other reason.
Job friction.
Patterns that show up before people quit: rising unplanned absences, time off used in small pieces, overtime climbing, training dropping off and internal job applications.

The original, patent-pending Flight Risk Score™ uses 19 variables across those four areas. They are the 19 most directly tied to resignations in any industry, and most companies already export them. You need someone to line them up.
Each person gets a score from 0 to 99 for the next 90 days. A higher number means a conversation is more overdue.

When I bring up the manager relationship, executives often hear an accusation. That is not the point. The manager area carries weight because it is the lever a company holds most directly. You cannot change the labor market or someone's commute. You can change how often a manager sits down with their people, how a manager change is handled, and whether a team that is losing people gets help before the next person goes.

A new manager is one of the quietest risk signals there is. The person who hired you, who knew your story and promised you the next step, is gone. The new person does not know any of it. Nobody tells the employee that the promise still stands, so they assume it does not.

blocks.text: From the base score to your score

runs.t: The 19 variables are the starting point. They are not the finish line. A frontline warehouse worker and a regional sales leader leave for different reasons, and a score that treats them the same will mislead you.

Across all the sources a company might have, there are about 80 data points spread over 15 different systems. You need the ones that matter for your people. So we tune the score for each company in three steps.
We weight the four areas for that company.
The balance between manager, career, pay and friction shifts with the work, the workforce and the market.
We add a few targeted variables where the company needs them.
These usually come from what we hear in Honest Read™ interviews and listening sessions, and from watching who leaves over time.
We test it against the people who already left.
Before anyone acts on a single name, we run the score back over the company's own past departures and check that it would have pointed to them.
That third step matters more than the other two. A score you have not tested against your own history is a guess with a decimal point.
We do not publish the weights. They change by company, and a published formula invites people to manage the number instead of the person.

blocks.text: What the score is made of, and what it is not made of

runs.t: The Flight Risk Score is a documented, weighted calculation built by our team. It is not AI. It does not use machine learning. It does not teach itself, and it does not quietly change its own rules from one month to the next. When the score changes, a person changed it, and they can tell you why.

A black box that spits out a risk number is hard to question and easy to misuse. A calculation you can open up is one you can argue with, and that is what you want from a tool that touches people's careers. Chapter 7 goes further into where AI helps and where it does not.

A Flight Risk Score is like the check engine light on your dashboard. It tells you something needs attention. It does not tell you what is wrong with the engine. For that you need a mechanic: someone who plugs in, runs the full diagnostic, asks a few questions and tells you what it will take to fix. In this case the mechanic is the manager, with support from HR and, when a company works with us, our Council of current and former executives.

blocks.text: The signs people see before managers do

runs.t: When someone quits, their supervisor is often shocked. The people who work beside them every day usually are not.

A peer of mine in leadership meetings quit, and the room was surprised because everyone loved her. Her teammates had seen it coming. She used to raise her hand for new assignments, and she stopped. She used to be the first one in the room, and she started arriving late. She took time off at odd hours, an hour in the middle of the day, the way people do when they are interviewing.
Each one alone means very little. Together, they were a person saying goodbye in slow motion.
Those are the same patterns the score is built to catch.
Schedule changes.
More call-offs, late arrivals, early departures and schedule change requests than their own normal.
Time off in small pieces.
Someone who used to take full days starts taking an hour here and there.
Going quiet.
Shorter answers, less input in meetings, no more volunteering.
Pulling away from peers.
Skipping the lunch group or the team chat they used to anchor.
A change in performance.
A steady performer who slips for two periods in a row, alongside other signs.
Asking for references.
A request for a recommendation is a sign the market is being tested.

Notice the phrase "their own normal" in the first signal. Most managers who try to spot risk by feel compare the person to the team. The person who always runs a little late is not a signal. The person who was always early and is now late is.
Some of these signs are in your systems. Some are only visible to the people on the floor. The score handles the first kind. Your managers and the people around them handle the second.

The score is a canary in the coal mine. Miners did not carry a canary because it could fix the air. They carried it because it noticed bad air before they did, and that gave them time to act. The canary was useless to a miner who ignored it.
A raw number from 0 to 99 is hard to act on. So every score falls into one of four bands, and each band has an expected response.

rows: No immediate action needed. Keep the normal rhythm of one-on-ones.
Flag for a check-in conversation in the normal course of work.
Have a direct conversation now about what is driving the score.
This person is likely already looking. Talk this week.

runs.t: Daniel, at 82, was in the Critical band. In his case the conversation was already too late. In most cases it is not, and that is the whole reason to look.

blocks.text: How to read a first list

runs.t: The first time a company sees its scores, the instinct is to sort by the highest number and start at the top. I would walk through a first report in this order.
Start with the Critical band.
Who is in it, and which of the four areas is driving each score? Those people need a conversation this week.
Look for clusters.
Are several high scores sitting under the same manager, at the same site or in the same role? A cluster usually points to a cause in the building, not in the people.
Look at the area driving the scores, not only the scores.
If most of the Intervention band is driven by pay, that is a pay structure question for leadership. If most of it is driven by the manager relationship, that is a coaching and staffing question.
Check your top performers.
Find them on the list wherever they land. Chapter 8 explains why the people you can least afford to lose often score lower than they should until it is late.
Then look at Worth watching.
This band is where you have the most time and the most room to act cheaply.

A hypothetical makes this concrete. Say a 1,000-person company sees that a large share of its Intervention band reports to three managers who were all promoted in the last year. The score did not say those managers are bad. It pointed at a pattern. The next step is to talk to those managers and their teams and find out what changed.

blocks.text: What the score is, and what it is not

runs.t: A score of 82 does not mean someone is leaving. It means a conversation is overdue.
It is a cue to talk.
The score ranks who needs attention in the next 90 days. The conversation tells you why.
It is not a decision.
The score never makes an employment decision about anyone. People do, and the right response to a high score is attention, not action against the employee.
Supervisors never see the number.
They see who to talk to and what to raise. A score on a screen turns a person into a label. A short list with a reason turns a manager into a better manager.
It is a calculation, not a black box.
It is documented and weighted, built by our team, and tuned to each company. It is not machine learning or generative AI, and it does not learn from client data on its own.
The third point is the one companies push back on most. Executives want supervisors to have the scores because supervisors are closest to the work. I still say no.

Picture a supervisor who sees that someone on the team scored 85. Maybe that person stops getting the stretch assignment, because "they are leaving anyway." Maybe the supervisor mentions it, and now the whole team knows. The number becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
So the supervisor gets a short list and a reason: "Check in with this person. Ask about their career path." That is enough to act on, and it does not put a label on anyone.
People ask me how accurate the score is. I would ask too.

We do not quote an accuracy percentage. Every company's data is different, the score is tuned to each one, and the job is to start conversations, not to win a bet on who quits. What we do is test the score against each company's own past departures before anyone uses it, and show the leadership team how it would have read the people who already left. That is the evidence that matters to them, because it is their own.
Be careful with any vendor that hands you one accuracy figure for every company. Ask what it was measured against, whose data it came from and what happened to the people who were flagged.
When the score flags someone, the report suggests what to talk about. We list the topics in a set order.
The manager relationship.
How are things with your manager? Are you getting what you need from them?
Career.
Where do you want to be in a year or two? Do you see a path here?
The work and the workload.
How does the job feel right now? What is getting in the way?
Pay.
Last, and only if it comes up or the data points to it.

Pay is real, but it is rarely the first thing to fix. Leading with money teaches people that the way to get attention is to threaten to leave. Chapter 1 covers what I learned about money and leaving, and Chapter 15 covers how to have the pay conversation when it is the right one.

blocks.text: What to do when someone is flagged

runs.t: Scores are worthless without a response. The protocol I recommend applies especially for anyone in the Critical band.
Talk within a week.

On day one, the manager reviews which of the four areas is driving the score. By day three, they reach out with a natural reason to connect. By the end of the week, they have had the conversation. Speed matters more than a perfect script.
Make it a conversation, not an intervention.

Do not mention the score. Get coffee. Ask what makes them come back every day, what would make the job better, what is frustrating them, and what it would take for them to still be here a year from now.
The manager owns it.
HR can support. HR cannot substitute. The relationship being repaired is with the manager.
Do not lead with a counteroffer.
A high score does not mean they have an offer. Leading with money tells them that threatening to leave is how to get noticed.
Do one thing within two weeks, and tell them.
Fix something specific they raised. Then close the loop in person. That is what moves the score back down.

The fifth step is where most companies fall down. Nothing visible happens for a month, and the employee concludes the conversation was a formality. A small fix in two weeks is worth more than a big fix in six months.

blocks.text: What a good first conversation sounds like

runs.t: Managers often freeze at this point. A few practical notes.
Pick a natural reason.
A project wrap-up, a schedule change, a question about a customer. You do not need a pretext. You need a door.
Ask, then wait.
"What would make this job better for you?" Then stop talking. Most managers fill the silence with their own answer.
Do not defend.
If they raise something about you, write it down. You can explain later. Right now you are learning.
End with a commitment.
"I am going to look into that and get back to you by next Friday." Then do it.

blocks.text: Questions to ask before you trust any risk score

runs.t: If a vendor or an internal team is offering you a flight risk model, these are the questions I would want answered before I put names in front of anyone.
What does it read?
Can they list the variables in plain language, grouped in a way a manager would understand?
Was it tested on our people?
Not on an industry dataset. On our own past departures.
Can a person explain any single score?
If the answer is "the model decided," be careful.
Who sees the numbers?
If supervisors see raw scores, ask what stops a score from becoming a label.
What is the response?
A score with no protocol behind it is a report, and you already have plenty of those.
If the answers are solid, you have a tool. If they are vague, you have a dashboard that will make people nervous.

The Flight Risk Score did not start as software. It started in a room with a list of names and a pen, during the worst stretch of pharmacist turnover I ever saw. Chapter 7 tells that story, and why the conversations mattered more than the list.
The score also has a blind spot that every leader should know about: the people you can least afford to lose are the ones who hide their signals best. That is the subject of Chapter 8.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Pull your last 12 months of voluntary departures by manager. If one manager accounts for an outsized share, you already know where the score will point.
•  Manager: For each person on your team, ask which of the four areas is most likely to push them out right now. If you do not know for more than two people, you need better signal.
•  Supervisor: Name the one person you would least want to lose. When did you last have a real conversation with them, not a status update? Have it this week.
•  HR leader: List the systems that hold your manager changes, pay history, absences and training records. Count how many different people own them. That number is why nobody has read them together.

runs.t: The score tells you who. The next chapter is about where it came from, and why the most useful part of the original was never the list itself.

label: Chapter 7
title: Spotting who will leave: the operator's view
subtitle: What operators see that consultants and AI miss, and why the answer starts with a conversation

runs.t: Years before EIP, a competitor opened a large pharmacy operation near my region, and we started losing pharmacists. Not one or two. In six months, 72 of our 348 pharmacists were gone.

Many of them took pay cuts of up to 15% to leave. When we offered raises to bring them back, they said no. Chapter 1 tells that part of the story and what it taught me about money. This chapter is about what we did while it was happening.
Losing a fifth of your licensed staff in six months does not leave time for a strategy deck. It leaves you deciding, three times a week, which stores can open.
So that is what we did. We pulled together our division vice president, a small group of district leaders and me. We met for two hours every Monday, Wednesday and Friday. We called it the war room.

The first job was keeping patients served with the people we had left. Some stores ran with one pharmacist a day. We moved pharmacists to wherever they could keep the most patients served. We closed low-volume stores and kept high-volume stores open, on a rotating schedule. We set a rule that no store stayed closed two days in a row, and we put up signs so patients knew where to go.
That was the logistics. But the most important thing we did in that war room was not on the schedule at all.

Every time a pharmacist resigned, we lost more than a person. We lost the hours, the patients who knew them, and a little more of the confidence of the people who stayed. Each departure made the next one easier.

We had no tool that told us who might leave next. Nothing like it existed for our situation. We had scheduling data, payroll data and an annual engagement survey that had not seen this coming. We had no way to look forward.
So we built one by hand, and we did not call it anything.
We sat in the room with a list of names and asked one question: who is likely to quit next?
Then a well-liked pharmacist quit. She was the kind of person others leaned on. So we asked the question again. Who is next?
The answer was the intern who had listened to her for a year and a half.

No report would have shown us that link. There was no field in any system for "learned the job from this person." But everyone in that room who knew the store knew the answer the moment the question was asked. When someone people look up to leaves, the people who looked up to them start wondering why they are staying.
So we built a checkbox matrix of who was likely to leave. Each district leader took their own district: about 20 stores and about 45 pharmacists. Every pharmacist's name went down the side.

First we split the list in half. On one side were the people who were never going to leave. On the other were the people who could. Then we took the second group and marked why each person might go, with the reasons across the top and a check wherever a reason applied.

By the time we were done, each district had its top five people most likely to leave. We put those names on a big whiteboard, arranged by geography. I planned my store visits around that board, so I could stop in, say hello and recognize the work those pharmacists were doing. The district leaders made a plan to talk with every person on it the next week.

blocks.text: The list was the start, not the point

runs.t: Talking to people was the point. The matrix told us where to look. The conversations told us what was wrong and what might keep them.
A checkbox matrix is a crude tool. It does not weigh anything or test itself against history. It depends completely on the people filling it in knowing their teams. In our case they did.

What the matrix did well was force a question that nobody was asking on a normal week. Without the matrix, we would have kept reacting to resignations one at a time. With it, we had a short list of people to call before they called us.

The fixes we rolled out came from what those people told us, and from the pharmacists who stayed. They were mostly about working conditions, not pay. The team in the field did the hard work of carrying them out while covering stores with too few people.

Pharmacist turnover fell from 42% to 18% within about three months of the changes, and later went as low as 9%. The matrix did not cause that. The conversations it pointed us to, and the fixes that came out of them, did.
That matrix became the starting point for the Flight Risk Score™ (Chapter 6). The idea underneath it has not changed since the war room. Find the people who need a conversation, then go have it.

The war room showed us something else we had not wanted to see. Many pharmacists from our low-volume stores could not work in our high-volume stores. They had never been trained or tested for that pace. Our development program had looked fine on paper. Under pressure, it fell apart.
A competitor does not create your weaknesses. It finds them.
Chapter 8 picks up that thread, because it says a lot about how we were promoting people and who we were rewarding.

blocks.text: How to build a checkbox matrix this week

runs.t: You do not need software to start. If you run a team, a site or a region, you can do a version of what we did in an afternoon.
Get the right people in the room.
Two or three leaders who know the people by name and see them every week. Not HR alone, and not only senior leaders who know the team from reports.
List everyone, then split the list.

Each leader takes their own team. Sort people into two groups: those who are never going to leave and those who could. Spend your time on the second group, starting with top performers and anyone others learn from.
Set your columns.

Use the four areas from Chapter 6 as a starting point: manager relationship, career and tenure, pay, and job friction. Add one more column for influence: "someone they look up to has left or is about to."
Check what you know, and mark what you do not.
If nobody in the room knows whether a person has had a career conversation in the last year, that blank is a finding.
Pick the top five.

Each leader names the five people most likely to leave. Anyone with several checks, or with the influence column checked, belongs on that list. Put the names on one board, arranged by location, so senior leaders can plan visits to recognize those people, and every one of them gets a conversation within a week.
Assign each conversation to the right manager.
Not to HR. Not to the most senior person in the room.
Meet again.
Put the matrix next to what people said. Decide what to fix first and who will tell each person what happened.

Keep the matrix in the room. It is a tool for the leaders who use it, not a document to circulate. The same rule that keeps scores away from supervisors in Chapter 6 applies here: a list of names with checks next to them can turn into a label fast.
Do not skip the influence column. It was the lesson of the intern. Departures travel through relationships.

When you make those calls, do not open with the matrix or with the person who left. Open with the work. Chapter 6 lays out a simple order for those conversations. Fix one thing within two weeks, and tell them you did. The matrix is only as good as the follow-through it starts.

My company spent heavily on outside help over the years, including a top consulting firm. The pitch always came from senior people with experience across many industries. They were impressive in the room.

The work came from new graduates who were learning the role. Our team spent the first two weeks of each project teaching a new person our company and our industry. In doing that, we shaped the answer: this is what we think it should be.
The company got little from them. The people who knew where a plan would break were the ones doing the teaching.

I do not say that to knock consultants. Many are smart and work hard. The model is the problem. Without the field's context, a good framework gets applied to the average company's problem, which may not be yours.

There is an old line about a mechanic who only owns a hammer: every problem starts to look like a nail, even when it is a screw. A company with one retention tool, whether it is a pay study, a survey or an outside framework, falls into the same trap. It reaches for the tool it has, not the one the problem needs.

blocks.text: How to hire outside help without paying to teach it

runs.t: Ask these before you sign.
Who will be on site, and what have they run?
Meet them, not just the people who pitch.
How much of the first month is learning our business?
If the honest answer is "most of it," you are paying to train them.
Who in our field will they talk to?
If the answer is mostly corporate staff, the plan will miss where things break.

blocks.text: AI on top of a survey

runs.t: The big survey platforms noticed something we all knew. Companies collected engagement results and then did little with them. Their answer was AI-generated action items, built from the same survey feedback.
The trouble is the feedback itself. Garbage in, garbage out.
It is weighted wrong.
In my experience, poor performers leave more comments than high performers. The loudest voices are often not the ones you can least afford to lose.
It collects complaints, not solutions.
A survey asks people to rate and react. It rarely asks what they would fix or how.

Perceptyx's 2026 research shows the gap (Chapter 5 has the numbers): only about half of employees see anything improve after a survey. If the inputs are weighted toward the wrong voices and full of complaints, a faster way to turn them into action items will produce wrong answers faster.

blocks.text: An MRI in the living room

runs.t: Buying people analytics software without someone to run it is like buying an MRI machine and putting it in your living room. It is an impressive machine. It does not diagnose anything without someone trained to read the results.
Plenty of companies buy the machine. Then the results sit in a portal that a few people log into once a quarter. Nobody owns turning a pattern into a question and walking it down to the floor.
The war room had no software at all. What it had was a few people who knew how to read what they were seeing and a commitment to act on it three times a week.

blocks.text: Why a company with every tool still could not act

runs.t: My former employer had more tools and budget than almost anyone. We still struggled to keep good people. Four things stood in the way.
Size.
Under about 100 employees, an owner knows everyone: their strengths, often their families. Past 100, new people arrive that the top has never met, including future leaders.
Big-company comfort.
The big platforms and the big consulting names are the safe choice. Nobody loses a job for hiring the name everyone hires. People do lose jobs for trying something new, even when it is right.
Silos.

The person in charge of surveys cared most about surveys. As executive director of customer experience, I cared most about customer experience. Nobody owned how one connected to the other, and no tool brought it together.
The tools did not exist.

There was no company-specific cost of turnover, only broad industry estimates. There was no structured way to see who might quit, only a manager's guess. And honest feedback has to come from a third party. Asking it yourself is not the same.
The first point explains why the war room worked. For a few months, our region acted like a small company. The people in the room knew the pharmacists by name and who trained whom.
The last point is why EIP exists. We built the Turn Tax™, the Flight Risk Score™ and Honest Read™ because we needed them in the field and could not get them.
Each source brings something. The mistake is expecting any one of them to do the whole job.

rows: The field's context, and the people who know where a plan will break
Whose voice is missing, and what people would fix
Why it happened, and what is about to happen
Asking the right questions, reading the context
Patterns across thousands of people without good data

runs.t: Operators have a weakness too. The war room worked because 348 pharmacists is a number a few leaders can hold in their heads. Try that with 20,000 people and the checkbox matrix breaks. Memory fails, and quiet people disappear from the list.
That is why the answer is not operators instead of data. It is documented calculations on your own data, with experienced people in the room to ask why.
We get asked this often.
Not in the scoring.
The Flight Risk Score and the Turn Tax are documented calculations run on the company's own data (Chapters 3 and 6). Neither is AI, and neither teaches itself.
Not in evaluating people.
AI does not judge employees or processes, and it does not create the data the answers come from. The score never makes an employment decision, and supervisors never see it.
Only in an optional question layer.

If a client wants to ask questions of their own results, such as "which locations have the most people in the Critical band?", we can build a searchable library over the results. The numbers underneath still come from traditional analytics.
That is a deliberate choice. A calculation you can explain is one you can challenge. When a number is about to land on a person, someone should be able to say exactly where it came from.

blocks.text: When the data was wrong and the Council was right

runs.t: In one review at EIP, turnover by manager across ten managers showed one at 80%. On paper, he was the problem. Any report, and any algorithm reading that report, would have pointed straight at him.
Our Council asked questions first: the kind any experienced operator asks about a number like that, starting with what was happening before he got there.

The answers told a different story. He was a high performer, brought in from another market to replace a manager who had been let go for poor performance. The turnover was there before he arrived. He had been brought in to fix it.

Acting on the number alone would have punished the person solving the problem. It would also have told every other strong leader in that company: do not take the hard assignment, because the numbers will follow you.
You need people with different views asking the right questions before anyone acts. The check engine light was right that something was wrong. It was not right about what.
Data tells you the pattern. People tell you the cause.
Ask who will do the work.
Before you hire outside help, meet the people who will be on site, not only the people who pitch.
Check who your feedback comes from.
Split survey comments by performance and tenure before you act on them.
Ask for solutions, not ratings.
Ask what gets in the way of doing a great job, and what people would fix first.
Put one person over the whole picture.
Someone should own how turnover, customer experience and engagement connect.
Question every outlier before you act.
When a number points at a person, find out what happened before they arrived.
Keep AI out of decisions about people.
Use it to search and summarize. Keep scoring documented, and keep people in the decisions.
Map who learns from whom.
When someone others lean on leaves, call the people who leaned on them that week.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Pick the last outside project that cost real money. Ask the field leaders who worked on it how much time they spent teaching the team. Then ask what they would have done differently.
•  HR leader: Take your last engagement survey. Compare the comments from your top performers with everyone else's. If you cannot separate them, that is the first gap to close.
•  Manager: Name the person on your team who others learn from. Then name the people who learn from them. If that person left, who would you talk to first?
•  Supervisor: Think of the last good person who left your team. Who was closest to them? Check in with that person this week.

label: Chapter 8
title: Your top performers as your biggest risk
subtitle: Why high performers leave, why the scoreboard often rewards the wrong people, and how to keep the ones you cannot replace

runs.t: She was one of the strongest district leaders I ever worked with.
She ran a district in the wealthiest part of the city. Almost no crime, great results, high margins. She had a bright personality. Everyone, including me, saw her heading to a regional role.

Then a district opened up downtown, in the same city. It was the hardest market we had: shoplifting, gangs and crime. It was the same role, a lateral move, and she would not have had to relocate. We offered her more money and more stock.

I offered it to her as a development move. It would give her exposure to a whole different world of challenges. And we needed to see that she could lead people when things are hard, not only when things are easy.
She asked to think it over. I encouraged her to take it.
She declined.

That was her right, and she stayed a strong leader. I do not tell this story to fault her. She made a reasonable choice inside the system we had built. That is the part that bothered me. The system had taught her that a hard district was a risk to her career, and the system was right.

It showed me something about our pipeline. We were promoting people on great numbers, and many of those numbers came from easier districts. We almost never tested people in hard conditions before giving them more responsibility.

Around the same time, I won an award for developing the most people to the next level in the division, including the only promotion to the region level that year. I was proud of it. I still am. I also learned that getting someone promoted is not the same as them succeeding once they get there.
Make sure the people you promote can lead people the right way, and keep them.
This chapter is about the people at the top of your roster: why they are the most likely to leave, and why your scoreboard may be pushing them away from the work you most need them to do.
A high performer is the biggest flight risk you have. That is not because they are unhappy more often. It is because they have more choices when they are.
They are easy to find.
Their results are visible. Competitors know their names. Recruiters reach them first.
They carry more than their share.

Research by Ernest O'Boyle and Herman Aguinis across 198 groups and more than 600,000 people found that performance does not follow a bell curve. In most groups, a small number of stars produced a disproportionate share of the results.
They do not complain. They leave.
They stay professional. Their output holds up. What moves first is quiet: they stop volunteering, start answering recruiter calls and stop talking about next year.

When one of them leaves, you lose a share of your results, and often the person everyone else was learning from. Chapter 7 tells the story of an intern who became our next risk the moment the pharmacist she learned from quit. Others orbit your best people.

items.label: groups studied, covering more than 600,000 people: performance did not follow a bell curve (O'Boyle and Aguinis, 2012)
salespeople studied: the best sellers were the most likely to be promoted, and on average became worse managers (Benson, Li and Shue, 2019)
of the time, companies fail to pick the manager candidate with the right talent (Gallup, 2015)

blocks.text: Why their signals are hard to see

runs.t: High performers hide their signals well. Chapter 6 lists the patterns that show up before someone quits: schedule changes, time off in small pieces, going quiet, pulling away from peers. Your average performer shows those patterns early and plainly. Your best performer shows them late, if at all.
Their output holds up longer because they are good at the job. They stay pleasant in meetings because that is who they are. By the time their numbers slip, they usually have an offer.
What moves first is quieter, and it is usually something the company did, not something the person did:
A manager who stopped checking in, because "she is fine, she does not need me."
A promotion that went to someone else, with no conversation about why or what comes next.
A raise that did not keep pace with the market, while recruiters remind them what the market pays.
Those are exactly the things a Flight Risk Score™ reads, and it is why I tell leaders to find their top performers on the list wherever they land, not only at the top.
Not telling your best people about an open role is like the world's worst surprise party, except they are the one who does not find out. Everyone else knew it was happening.

A role opens one level up. Leadership has already decided who should get it, so nobody mentions it to the strong internal candidate. Your best person learns about the opportunity and the decision in the same email.
Maybe they were not ready. It does not matter in that moment. What they hear is: "We did not think of you." If a recruiter calls that week, they take the call.

The fix costs nothing. Tell them before the announcement. If they are not the pick, tell them why and what it would take to be the pick next time. That is a career conversation, and it may be the most valuable 20 minutes a leader spends all quarter.

blocks.text: When the scoreboard rewards the easy stores

runs.t: At my company, bonuses, raises and promotions followed store results. On the surface, that sounds fair. In practice, it was not.

Some of our stores were small locations inside other retailers' buildings. They filled about 200 prescriptions a week. A typical store filled about 2,000. Many sat in affluent areas with almost no theft, where customers paid full price. Those stores were profitable almost by default.

Other stores lost 4% of sales to theft. They had bulletproof glass and half the merchandise locked up. They sat in dying strip malls, in neighborhoods where the population was dropping 11% a year. Their targets were the same as everyone else's: last year, plus a little.
Guess who won the awards, the raises and the promotions. The easy-store managers.
The saying among leaders was "don't go downtown," because taking a hard store could end your career. Everyone knew it. Nobody wrote it down.

And the people promoted from easy stores often could not, or would not, cover the busy ones. The war room in Chapter 7 exposed that many pharmacists from our low-volume stores could not work in our high-volume stores. Our scoreboard had moved people up without ever asking whether they could handle the hardest version of the job.
Whatever you pay for is the job. If you reward easy results, your best people will learn to avoid hard work, or leave for a company that sees the difference.

My team proposed a fix. Weight performance by how hard the store is, the way college football judges a team by strength of schedule, not just its win-loss record. A team that goes 10 and 2 against the toughest schedule in the country is not worse than a team that goes 11 and 1 against easy opponents.

Leadership decided what we had was good enough. Resources were limited, and that was a defensible call on a busy agenda. It still had a cost. The old system stayed, and the result was the Peter Principle in action: people with great numbers were promoted to their level of incompetence.
No one in that story was a villain. The managers in easy stores did good work in the stores they had. The system rewarded what it measured, and everyone responded to it rationally.

blocks.text: How to build a difficulty-adjusted scoreboard

runs.t: You do not need a perfect model to start. You need to stop pretending every assignment is the same.
List the factors that make a location or team harder.
For stores, that was volume, theft, staffing and local conditions. For a call center it might be call complexity. Ask your operators. They already know.
Group your units into tiers.
Three or four tiers is enough.
Compare people within a tier first.
Rank the hard-store managers against other hard-store managers before you rank them against everyone.
Give credit for improvement against the starting point.
A hard store that went from bad to average may represent more leadership than an easy store that stayed great.
Protect the bonus for people who take the hard assignment.
If moving to a tough location means two years without a bonus, you are telling your best people not to go.

A hypothetical shows the difference. Say two store managers both hit 102% of target, one in a quiet suburb and one with heavy theft and a short staff. On a flat scoreboard, they tie. On a strength-of-schedule scoreboard, the second manager is clearly the stronger leader.

I once took a tough downtown market myself. Shoplifting and violence were part of the job. Even the streetlights were not being replaced. The targets were spread evenly across stores, with no adjustment for a strip mall whose anchor stores had closed.
I knew going in that I would probably go two years without a bonus. It could have been a career risk. I took it anyway, and it worked out.

More importantly, it changed how I led. I had come from the suburbs and did not understand how hard those stores were until I lived it. It showed me how much of a result comes from the conditions, and how much leadership it takes to hold steady in them.
Later, as a leader, I moved suburban managers into tough districts so they could see it firsthand. You cannot fairly judge someone's results until you understand what they are up against.
A stretch assignment is not a punishment or a loyalty test. It is how a strong leader learns the hardest version of the job before they are responsible for a whole region of it.

blocks.text: Make the hard assignment the smart move

runs.t: If you want strong people to say yes to the hard assignment, the system has to make yes a reasonable answer. A few ways to do that:
Hold their pay steady or better.
Do not let a move to a harder market cost them their bonus because the targets ignore the conditions.
Name the time frame.
Tell them how long the assignment is meant to last and what success looks like.
Stand behind them.
Check in more often, not less. Give them first claim on help when they need it.
Make it count.
When promotions come up, give visible weight to people who took the hard work and did well in it. Say so publicly.
The goal is a culture where "don't go downtown" becomes "go downtown if you want to move up."

blocks.text: Promoting your best is not the same as them succeeding

runs.t: Economists Alan Benson, Danielle Li and Kelly Shue studied 38,843 sales workers at 214 companies. The best salespeople were the most likely to be promoted into management. On average, they then performed worse as managers than people promoted with weaker sales numbers. Being great at the job did not predict being great at leading people who do the job.
Gallup has found that companies fail to choose the candidate with the right talent for a manager role 82% of the time.
A promotion that fails costs you twice. You lose a great individual performer, and you gain a struggling manager whose team starts looking for the exit.

I saw both sides of this. That same year I had the most promotions in the division and the highest engagement, and I am proud of both. Promotions are worth counting. They show you are developing people. But the number that matters even more comes a year later: did the people you promoted succeed, and did their teams stay? A scoreboard that ends at the promotion only tells you half the story.

blocks.text: What to look for before you promote

runs.t: When you are deciding who moves up, ask about how they lead, not only about their numbers.
How does their team feel?
Not what the leader says. What the team says, ideally to someone who is not their boss.
Who have they developed?
Name the people who are better because they worked for this person.
How many of their people stayed?
Especially the strong ones.
How did they do in a hard assignment?
If they have never had one, give them one first, with support.
Do they handle poor performance?
A leader who avoids hard conversations will lose the people who are watching.

Chapter 16 covers how Hire Smart™ finds the 3 to 5 traits your long-tenured top performers share. The same thinking applies to promotions. Know what predicts success in the role, then promote for that.
Keeping your best people does not mean keeping everyone.

Some government roles run under 1% turnover. That can mean the standards are low and people who should have been let go are still there. Low turnover is not automatically good news. It depends on who is staying.

Be careful how you pay for retention. Say you bonus a leader $100,000 for taking turnover from 50% to zero. The rational move is to fire nobody and give everyone a raise, including the people who are not performing. You will hit the target and lose your best people anyway, because they will watch poor performance go unaddressed.
The fastest way to lose a great performer is to not deal with a poor performer.

High performers notice everything. They notice when they cover for a teammate for the third month in a row and the teammate gets the same raise. Every unaddressed poor performer sends a message to your best people about what effort is worth here.
The goal is zero regretted turnover: keep the people you cannot replace, and manage the rest honestly.

That is why one of the six numbers in Chapter 2 is high performer turnover on its own line. If you only watch total turnover, a good year of letting the right people go can look the same as a bad year of losing the wrong ones.

blocks.text: How to keep the people you cannot replace

runs.t: Know who they are.
Name your top performers by role, today. If you cannot list them, you cannot protect them.
Measure difficulty, not just results.
Adjust targets and rewards for how hard the job is: volume, theft, staffing, local conditions.
Have the career conversation before a recruiter does.
Where do they want to go? What would it take to get there? When was the last time you asked?
Test people in hard conditions, with support.
Before a big promotion, give them a tough assignment and stand behind them while they do it.
Promote for leading people, not just for numbers.
Ask how their team feels, who they have developed and how many of their people stayed.
Reward the hard assignments.
If taking the tough store or the tough team can cost someone a bonus, you are teaching your best people to avoid it.
Check their pay against the market.
High performers know their worth. Recruiters remind them every week.
Of all seven, the third is the one leaders skip most. They assume the high performer is fine because nothing is wrong, right up to the day the letter arrives.
A career conversation is not a performance review. It does not need a form. It needs 30 minutes, a quiet place and a few honest questions:
Where do you want to be in two years?
What would you need from me to get there?
What would make you take a call from a recruiter?
What is one thing I could do differently as your manager?

Then write down what they said and do one thing about it within two weeks. If they want to move up, map the steps with them. If the answer is pay, take it seriously and look at the market (Chapter 15).
The last question on that list is the hardest to ask. It is also the one that tells you the most.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: List your top five performers. For each one, ask when they last had a real career conversation and a pay review against market. If either is more than 12 months ago, that person is at risk.
•  Manager: Look at who won your last round of awards and promotions. Were they the best people, or the people with the easiest assignments? If you cannot tell, your scoreboard needs fixing.
•  Supervisor: Tell your best person something specific they did well this week: the action, the impact and why it mattered. Not "great job."
•  HR leader: Pull the last three internal promotions into leadership. Check how each of those leaders' teams is doing today on turnover. Then check whether anyone measured that before the promotion.

runs.t: Your best people have options because other companies are looking for them. The next chapter is about who those companies are, and how to find out what they are offering.
