label: Chapter 9
title: Competitor Intel: who is hiring your people
subtitle: How to find out where your people go, what the competition offers them, and how to compete back

runs.t: Everyone at the distribution center had the same explanation for why people were leaving.

A big-name employer had opened nearby and was hiring. It was a large e-commerce employer, the kind of company whose name everybody knows. So when someone quit, the story wrote itself. They went down the road. Supervisors said it. Leaders said it. People in the stores I ran, who were waiting on freight that was not coming, repeated it. The implication was tidy: we were up against a giant, and there was not much we could do about it.
Nobody had checked.

We did not have a system for checking. What we had instead was something every workplace has. People who work together for four or five years become friends. They text. They see each other at kids' games and at the grocery store. So when a warehouse worker left, somebody still in the building usually knew where that person landed, and they had usually asked the two questions that matter: Where did you go? Is it better?
So we asked the people who stayed. We took the last 30 people who had left the distribution center and traced where each one went.
Two of them had gone to the big e-commerce employer. Two out of 30.

The rest had scattered. Some went to manufacturers. Some went to other local employers. Some left warehouse work altogether. And many of them were not even getting a raise. They had taken a job for the same money, or close to it, at a place that was not ours.

That changed the conversation in the building. If people were leaving for the giant, the answer was a pay war we could not win. If people were leaving for anywhere at all, often for no more money, the answer was inside our own walls.

The full turnaround at that distribution center is its own story, and I tell it start to finish in Chapter 20. This chapter is about the question we should have asked first, and the one most companies still cannot answer: who is recruiting your people, and what are they offering?

blocks.text: Most companies know how many. Few know where.

runs.t: Ask an HR team how many people left last year and you will get a number within the hour. Ask where those people went and you will usually get a shrug, or a story like the one we told ourselves at the distribution center.
A headcount tells you the size of the problem. A destination tells you the shape of it.

The exit interview will not tell you (Chapter 1). An exit interview after the decision is made is like asking someone for directions after they have already parked the car. They will be polite about it. It does not change where they ended up.

Where someone went is different. It is a fact, not an opinion, and it is usually easy to learn. Their new employer shows up on their professional profile within a few weeks. Their friends already know. If you ask with real curiosity and no hard feelings, many former employees will tell you themselves.

items.label: of U.S. employees are watching for or actively seeking a new job (Gallup, 2024)
people who left our distribution center went to the employer everyone blamed
the lowest starting pay we found at employers near that center, which paid $18.25

runs.t: Gallup found that 51% of U.S. employees are watching for or actively seeking a new job. On any given Monday, about half the people in your building would at least take the call. The question is whether you know who is calling, and what they are saying.

blocks.text: Your competitor is not who you think

runs.t: When we traced the 30, the biggest surprise was not the two. It was the 28. Our competition for those workers was not one company. It was every employer within a reasonable drive that would give them a steadier week, a cleaner building or a manager who noticed them.

This is true in almost every industry. You may think your competition for people is the company that sells what you sell. It often is not. Deloitte's 2026 analysis found that more than a third of new job postings in the power and data center sectors targeted the same set of workers. The company down the road that makes a different product can still be your biggest competitor for people.
Sometimes the competitor is not a company at all. It is the exit itself.

At one point I watched good people take pay cuts to move into entirely different industries, just to get away from one leader (Chapter 12 tells that story). They did not go to a rival. They went anywhere.

I also lived through the opposite case, when a true competitor opened nearby and pharmacists left by the dozens (Chapters 1 and 7). Even there, the competitor did not create the reasons people left. It made leaving easy.
That is the lesson I keep coming back to. A competitor does not create your weaknesses. It finds them.
Once you know where people went, the pattern starts to talk. Three readings cover most of what you will see.
If departures cluster, look outside.

Several people leaving the same location in a short window, for the same destination, usually means a competitor is recruiting. Somebody opened a facility, raised pay or started calling your people by name.
If they scatter, look inside.

People leaving at different times for many different places usually means the reason is in your own building. That was our distribution center. Twenty-eight people did not get recruited by 28 different companies. They were pushed, and they took whatever was close.
If they take less money, it was never the money.
A pay cut to leave tells you the working conditions are the problem. You can raise pay and still lose them, because pay was not the reason they went.
These readings are not exclusive. A building with real problems inside will lose people faster when a competitor shows up outside. That is the most dangerous combination.
This example is hypothetical. The numbers are invented to show the method.
Say a 400-person manufacturer lost 24 people last year. The plant manager believes a new competitor across the highway took most of them.
HR builds a simple destination log: date, department, manager, stated reason, where the person went and whether the new job paid more. It comes back like this:
Seven people went to the competitor across the highway. Six of the seven came from second shift in the same department, all within four months.
Twelve people went to 11 different employers, spread across the year and across departments.
Five are unknown.

Now the plant manager has two problems, not one. The cluster on second shift points outside. The scatter points inside, and it is the bigger number. A pay match for second shift might slow the cluster. It will do nothing for the other twelve. Tracing keeps you from spending your whole budget on the story you started with.

blocks.text: How to trace where people go

runs.t: You do not need software to start. You need a spreadsheet, a few honest conversations and a habit.
Start with your last 12.
Pull the last 12 people who left voluntarily in one location or one job family. If three or more went to the same place, you have a competitive pattern.
Ask the people who stayed.
In a team meeting or a one-on-one, ask plainly: Do you know where people have gone? Have you heard how it is going for them? Most teams know. Make it clear nobody is in trouble for staying in touch.
Check public professional profiles.
Many people update their employer within a few weeks. This is public information, and it is often the fastest way to fill in the blanks.
Call a few former employees.
Not to recruit them back. To learn what the new place offers that you do not. People are more candid a few weeks after they leave than they were on their last day.
Record what they gave up, not just where they went.
Did they take more money, the same, or less? Did they change industries? Did they take a longer drive? Each of those tells you how hard they wanted out.
Repeat every quarter.
One trace is a snapshot. Four in a row show you when a competitor enters the market and which departments it is working.

One caution. Tracing where people go is not surveillance. You are not monitoring anyone who still works for you. You are learning from public information and from people who choose to share it. Keep it respectful, and keep the focus on what the company can fix.

blocks.text: The signals of a competitive pull

runs.t: Competitive departures move faster than ordinary turnover. Someone who has taken a phone screen and has an offer in hand has days, not months.
Watch for four of them.
Clusters.
Several departures from one location or one team in a short window.
A common destination.
Former employees showing up at the same company on professional networking sites.
Recruiter activity.
People mentioning calls and messages from the same recruiter or the same company. If one person mentions it, note it. If three do, act.
Behavior changes.
Time off in small pieces, quieter people in meetings, schedule change requests.

The signs that someone is about to leave are the subject of Chapter 6, and how we built Flight Risk by hand is in Chapter 7. What changes in a competitive market is the threshold. In a hot market, a Flight Risk Score of 65 deserves the attention you would normally give an 80. The score has not changed. The world around it has.
The score never goes to supervisors, and it never makes an employment decision. The conversation is still the fix.

blocks.text: Ask your people what the competition offers

runs.t: The people who stay know what the competition is offering, because their friends tell them. So we asked them directly.

We formed an employee advisory council and ran small listening sessions and one-on-one interviews. That work became the start of what we now call Honest Read. How we run those sessions, and why managers should not lead them, is the subject of Chapter 13. The questions about the competition were simple.

blocks.title: Questions to ask about the competition
lines: •  Where they went: What have you heard about other employers people have gone to?
•  What is better: What makes them better?
•  The details: What have you heard about their pay? Their benefits? Their working conditions?
•  The standard: If we want to be the best place to work, what have you heard out there that is better than here?
•  The direct one: What would it take for a competitor to recruit you?

runs.t: That last question is one I like a lot. It is easier to answer than "what do you think of your boss," and it gets to the same place. The answers are your weak spots, ranked by the people most likely to be recruited.
Then we let people get it all out. We did not argue, explain or promise in the room. We wrote it down.
Most of what we heard was small and fixable.

rows: They were disgusting. We painted them.
Broken for months. We fixed them.
"I've had the same gloves for five years." We replaced them.
Our plan did not cover certain conditions and medications. That was bigger. We did what we could.

runs.t: A competitor was not winning on bathrooms. But a person deciding whether to take a recruiter's call compares everything, and broken soap dispensers tell people every day how much the company thinks of them.
The benefits gap was different. It was bigger and slower, and we could not close all of it. We said so. People can live with "we cannot fix that yet" when they can see you fixed the things you could.

blocks.text: Know the market the hard way

runs.t: Asking employees gives you the stories. You also need the numbers.

At the distribution center, we did not guess at market pay. The team researched job postings, called employers and even submitted applications at other companies so recruiters would call back with pay and benefits. Everywhere nearby paid at least $19.50. Our center started people at $18.25. That gap was real, and it was one part of the fix. I go through how we made the case for closing it, and the rest of the turnaround, in Chapter 20.

The same research also changed where we looked for candidates, because some backgrounds fit the work better than others (Chapter 16). Knowing your competition tells you two things: who is pulling your people out, and where your best new people are likely to come from.
You can do a basic version of this yourself this month:
List the five employers your people are most likely to leave for, using your destination log.
Pull their current postings for the roles you hire most. Note posted pay, schedules, sign-on bonuses and benefits.
Read what their employees say about them on public review sites, and what yours say about you.
Compare. Not just on pay. On schedule, predictability, equipment, commute and how people say they are treated.
Once we knew what we were up against, we said so. We told our people directly that we intended to become the best place to work, and that we were going to change things to get there.

That is a risky thing to say. It sets a standard people will hold you to. That is the point. A public promise tells people to look, and then they see the bathrooms painted and the gloves replaced, and the promise starts to mean something.

Then you have to prove it, again and again. We made feedback easy and frequent. Every so often, we asked one open question, "What's on your mind?", and people answered on paper and dropped it in a box. I tell that story in Chapter 13. The short version is that once people believed it was anonymous, they were honest, and their answers told us what to fix next.
Competing back out loud does three things a quiet plan cannot.
It gives people a reason to wait.
Someone halfway out the door may give you another month if they believe change is coming and can see the first of it.
It changes what people tell their friends.
The same texting network that tells you where people went also tells former coworkers what is happening at your place. Give them something good to pass along.
It makes you accountable.
Once you have said it in front of everyone, it is hard to let it slide.
A competitor's pull also exposes something no recruiting plan will fix: whether the people you have can cover for the people you lose.

When our region lost pharmacists to a competitor, we found that many pharmacists from our low-volume stores could not work in our high-volume stores (Chapter 7). Ask yourself the same question before a competitor asks it for you. If your three busiest locations lost a quarter of their people, who could step in? If the answer is nobody, your development program has a gap, and a competitor will find it before you do.
When we built EIP, we turned what we did by hand into a repeatable process.
Public job postings and pay.
We review competitors' own career pages and job boards for the roles you hire, including posted pay, schedules, sign-on bonuses and benefits.
What employees say.
We review employee review sites and public forums for what people say about working at each competitor, and at your company.
Where people go.
We review public professional profiles to see where people from your company and your industry move, and where your best candidates come from.
Validated against outside data.
We check our findings against competitor intelligence from a strategic data partner.

The result shows how you stack up against the employers competing for your people, and where to look for candidates: which competitors, which geographies and which platforms. In our 30-day diagnostic, the Competitive Analysis runs in the first two weeks, alongside the Turn Tax and Flight Risk Score (Chapter 10).
Track where your last 12 people who left went.
If three or more went to the same place, you have a competitive pattern.
Ask the people who stayed.
Use the questions above in small groups, without managers in the room.
Fix the small things first, and tell people.
Bathrooms, equipment, schedules. Visible fixes prove you are listening.
Research the market yourself.
Pull postings, read reviews and compare on more than pay.
Stress-test your bench.
Pick your three busiest locations and name who would cover if a quarter of the people left.
Ask one question often.
"What's on your mind?" On paper, if that is what it takes for people to believe it is anonymous.

label: Chapter 10
title: The 30-day diagnostic
subtitle: How a 30-day diagnostic works, week by week, and why skipping it leads to the wrong program

runs.t: The COO of a staffing company we work with had a retention plan ready before we ever met. The company had about 4,500 employees across six countries.

It was a reasonable plan. A pay adjustment for the front line. A recognition program. A new onboarding video. The CEO liked it, and the budget was waiting for a signature. The only thing missing was proof that it would work, and the COO agreed to a 30-day diagnostic mostly to get that proof before spending the money.

Before day one, the company sent us the HR data its team already exported every month. Nobody had to build anything. We replaced every name with a code before we worked with it. In return the COO got three things: a roadmap for the next 90 days, so the leadership team could see where the work was going; a page of talking points, so leaders could tell their teams who we were and why we were there; and a calendar with the executives' calls already booked.

In week one, the COO spent two hours with me, and so did the head of HR. We asked how people were hired, how they were trained, who trained them, what it cost when someone quit in the first month and what happened to the work when they did. The COO told me later it was the first time anyone had asked them to count what a departure cost instead of guessing. Meanwhile our team was loading the data and scheduling interviews and small listening sessions. By Friday the COO could see the first rough version of who was likely to leave.

In week two, the interviews happened, one on one and in small groups. People talked to an outsider who had no stake in what they said. By the end of the week, the cost of turnover had a dollar figure on it, and the competitive picture showed which employers were pulling people away.

In week three, our Council read everything. Each member wrote an assessment alone, before seeing anyone else's, and then the group met to argue about it. One finding pointed to a need the company could not meet on its own, so the Council brought in a solutions partner, someone members had used and recommended, who already had the findings and could quote exactly what the work would take.
In week four, we took the findings back to the company's people and asked what we had wrong. Then we sat down for the final meeting.

The plan did not survive. Not because it was a bad plan. Because the diagnostic showed turnover was not spread across the company the way the plan assumed. It sat with a few managers on a few shifts, and most of the people who left were not talking about pay. The pay adjustment would have landed evenly on a problem that was not even. The recognition program would have gone to managers who were already doing fine.
Nothing in that final meeting was a surprise. The COO had seen the data every week as it was built, and walked out with a different plan, a roadmap for the next year and logins for the team.
You cannot build a solution until you understand the problem, in this company, with these people, right now.

blocks.text: The plan built on a guess

runs.t: I learned this lesson the expensive way. When I took over customer experience for one of our businesses, there were 47 separate plans in place, and almost none of them moved anything a customer cared about. We stopped all 47 and diagnosed first. That story is in Chapter 4.
The 47 plans were built by smart people who skipped the diagnosis. Each one solved a problem somebody assumed we had.

Retention programs get built the same way. The exit survey describes people who already left. Tenure data describes people who stayed. Neither tells you who is likely to leave next, which managers are driving it, or what it costs. So the program gets built on the most common explanation. Pay is too low. The labor market is tight.
A company-wide fix follows, and it lands evenly on a problem that is not spread evenly.

I saw this twice in my own career. When I ran a region, turnover looked high everywhere. When we split it by district, three districts drove 80% of it (Chapter 2). A region-wide program would have spent most of its money where the problem was smaller.

At a distribution center that ranked 13th of 13 on productivity, everyone assumed pay was the reason people left. Pay mattered. The center started people at $18.25 an hour against a market of about $19.50 to $21. But when we stepped back and listened, money was about a quarter of the conversation. The rest was not seeing a manager for three weeks, getting no feedback and having no career path (Chapter 20). A raise alone would have treated a quarter of the problem.

blocks.text: Shift the infield before the pitch

runs.t: Baseball teams figured out something years ago that most companies still have not. They study what a hitter likes to do, then move the infield before the pitch is thrown. They do not wait to see where the ball goes and then run after it.

Retention analytics works the same way. Most retention programs are built after the ball is in the outfield. Someone good quits, and a program launches in response. A diagnostic flips the order. It tells you where the turnover is going to come from, so you can move your people and your money there first.
That is also why a diagnostic beats a single tool. A pay study tells you about pay. A turnover report tells you who already left. None of them, alone, tells you where to stand.

blocks.text: Two tracks, run at the same time

runs.t: Our diagnostic runs two tracks in parallel, data and people, with someone from your team in the loop every day.
The
data track
builds three things from HR data you already export:
Turn Tax:
the dollar cost of your turnover, across 13 cost categories and up to 250 variables.
Flight Risk Score:
a forward look at who is likely to leave in the next 90 days, scored 0 to 99.
A KPI dashboard:
the numbers your leaders will watch after we leave.
The
people track
runs Honest Read: one-on-one interviews and small listening sessions run by a third party, outside your chain of command.
We run both because each one catches what the other misses. The data shows you where turnover is concentrated. The interviews tell you why. Put together, they tell you where, why and how much.
Four things happen before the first week starts.
You send your data.
The HR data you already export. Names are replaced with codes before we work with it.
We send a 90-day roadmap.
Even if the engagement is 30 days, you can see where the work is going, and that you are not paying for a report that sits on a desk.
We send talking points.
Your leaders can tell their teams who EIP is, why we are there and what to say if someone asks.
We schedule your C-suite.
The calls with your executives go on the calendar before week one starts.

The talking points matter more than they look. When strangers show up and start asking questions, people assume a layoff is coming. A short, plain explanation from their own leader, before we arrive, is the difference between guarded answers and honest ones.

I spend two hours with your COO and two hours with your CHRO. Those conversations fill in the Turn Tax. The costs most executives miss, the slow first weeks, the mistakes and the good person pulled off the line to train, only show up when someone who runs the operation walks through them with you. The competitive analysis starts here too. Our coordinator handles the manual part, reading postings and reviews. The developer handles the part a computer does better. Chapter 9 explains what it looks for.
By Friday, the basics of Flight Risk are in place.

blocks.text: Week two: the picture fills in

runs.t: The interviews and listening sessions finish. The developer compiles what people said into prioritized solutions, so the people track produces a ranked list and not a pile of quotes.

The Flight Risk Score is fully built. The Turn Tax and competitive analysis are done. The KPI dashboard is started. Hire Smart is the one tool not yet ready, because it depends on understanding who your long-tenured top performers are and what they share.

Week three is where our Council comes in. We select the Council members whose experience fits your business best. Each one reviews the data and writes an assessment on their own, before seeing anyone else's. Then they meet and test each other with one question: if this were your company, where would you invest first, and what would you do first?
Independent views first keeps one strong voice from setting the answer for the room. It also catches what the data alone gets wrong (Chapter 7 tells the story of one manager it saved).

If the findings point to a particular need, the Council also brings in solutions partners. These are people Council members have used and recommend, and some sit on the Council themselves. Because they already have the findings, they can quote exactly the work needed. When we sit down with you, the numbers are accurate and nobody is starting from scratch.
That saves weeks. In most companies, a diagnosis ends with a list of needs, and then a new round of finding and briefing a vendor begins.

Hire Smart is built this week, and all tools are finalized by Friday. The developer sets up logins, decides with you who has access to what, and settles where the data is stored and how it is secured.

blocks.text: Week four: test it with your people

runs.t: Before anything goes to the final meeting, we take the findings back to your people and ask what we got wrong. If a fix sounds good in a conference room and makes no sense on the floor, this is where you find out.
Then we update the findings and hold the final meeting.

A weekly one-hour meeting with your sponsor covers progress. Daily stand-ups include someone from your company, not always the same person. You see the data every week, so by day 30 you have watched it being built.

We do it this way on purpose. The big reveal is a bad format for hard news. When a leadership team sees a finding for the first time in a final presentation, the first reaction is often to defend. When they have watched the number take shape for four weeks, the reaction is to act.

runs.t: Who you pick for those sessions matters as much as how many. We want to hear first from long-tenured high performers, because they know where the work breaks and they care enough to say so. Chapter 13 covers how to choose the room and why managers should not run it.

We work from data you already export, so there is no integration project. Names are replaced with codes. In week three we set who has access to what and where the data is stored. The Flight Risk Score is a documented calculation on your own data, tuned and tested as Chapter 6 describes.
Supervisors never see scores. The score never makes an employment decision. It tells leaders where to look and who could use a conversation.

The final meeting runs about two hours, in person or virtual. We walk through the portal and dashboard, every finding and the watch-outs. You get a roadmap for the next 60 to 90 days and for the next year. Everything is shareable, with individual logins for the people you choose.
What happens next is the subject of Chapter 19, which covers the 90 days after a diagnostic and the review cadence that keeps it moving.
You can run a rough version with your own team in a few weeks. It will tell you whether your next program is aimed at the right place. The numbers in this example are hypothetical.
Say you run a 1,000-person company and 300 people left last year.
Split it by manager.

Sort the 300 departures by the manager each person reported to. If you have 60 managers and the turnover were even, each would have lost about five. If eight managers lost 120 between them, you have found where to look first. Then check each of those eight: did they inherit the problem or create it?
Split it by location, job title and tenure.
Averages hide pockets. A location, a shift or a single job title often carries far more than its share.
Pull 90-day turnover on its own.

Early exits point inside the company (Chapter 2). If 100 of your 300 left in the first 90 days, the cause is expectations, selection, training or support, and none of that is fixed with a raise. Chapter 17 covers the first 90 days.
Put a dollar figure on it.
Without a cost, every retention investment looks like an expense. With one, it looks like a recovery. Chapter 3 shows how.
Listen to the people you most want to keep.
Pick ten long-tenured high performers. Ask what gets in the way of doing a great job. Write it down. Do not argue.
Ask your executives one question.
If this were your own money, where would you invest first? Have each one write the answer alone. Then compare the answers to what the data says.
If the data and the executives agree, good. If they do not, you have found the gap that would have sunk your next program.

blocks.text: Questions to ask about any diagnostic

runs.t: Whether you run it yourself, use us or hire someone else, ask these before you trust the findings.
Does it split turnover by manager, location, job title and tenure, or does it report an average?
Does it put a dollar figure on turnover that your CFO would accept?
Does it tell you who is likely to leave next, or only who already left?
Did someone outside your chain of command talk to your people?
Who can see individual-level data, and what will it be used for?
A diagnostic that cannot answer those is a report. A report tells you what happened. A diagnostic tells you where to stand.
Pause the next program until you know where turnover lives.
Split it by manager, location, job title and tenure before you spend.
Put a dollar figure on it.
Weigh every retention investment against what turnover is costing you now.
Listen to the people you most want to keep.
Your long-tenured high performers know where the work breaks.
Show the data while it is being built.
Weekly reviews remove the big reveal, and the defensiveness that comes with it.

•  CHRO: Pull last year's voluntary turnover by manager. Find the three highest. Then check whether each one inherited the problem or created it.
•  COO: List the programs your teams are running to improve retention or experience. Ask which ones are tied to a measured driver. Stop one that is not.

runs.t: A diagnostic tells you where the problem lives. Sometimes it lives in the executive suite, and that is the hardest finding to hear. That is where Part Three begins.

label: Chapter 11
title: When the problem is at the top: leadership self-assessment
subtitle: How leadership decisions drive turnover, and the self-assessment every executive team should run first

runs.t: A division president, who reported to the CEO, wanted to hear directly from pharmacists. It was a good instinct. She asked for a listening session.

She wanted the pharmacists chosen at random, with no help from the field. She did not want district leaders hand-picking their favorites, and I understood why. Leaders who pick the room tend to pick the people who will say what they want heard.

The random list came back with fifteen pharmacists on it. It included a few part-timers, a few people who worked one day a week and a few poor performers. It was not a group built to give a division president the broad view she was looking for.
Only she and a vice president were in the room with them. No field leaders were allowed in. The rest of us on the field team waited in the room next door.

The pharmacists got specific. They talked about register buttons. They talked about why they never got breaks. The biggest theme was understaffing after payroll cuts. One pharmacist working alone was running the register, the drive-through and the phones at the same time.
None of that was a surprise to anyone in the field. Those were the conditions we had been working in.

When the hour was up, the pharmacists came out, said goodbye and headed back to their stores. The president and her vice president stayed behind. Then they came next door, where we had been waiting, and summed up the session for us in one word.
Victims.

The word missed what had happened in that room. The field had been talking about accountability and controlling what you can control. So when the pharmacists sat in a room with the people who could fix the things they could not, they asked for those things: staffing, breaks and equipment. Only corporate could change any of it.
Leadership heard excuses.

Everyone went back to their stores saying the same thing: corporate does not listen, help is not on the way, we are on our own. The session that was meant to close the gap between the top and the front line made it wider.

I do not tell this story to make a villain out of one executive. She did something many senior leaders never do. She asked. But the way the session was built made the outcome almost certain. The wrong people were picked. The people who understood the context were kept out. Nobody went back to the pharmacists. And the conclusion came from two people talking to each other.
A listening session run on the wrong people does more damage than no session at all.

That one word is the reason this chapter exists. Most of what drives people out of a company, from workload to span of control to how change is handled, is decided by senior leaders. Retention starts at the top, and it ends at the top.

blocks.text: Pick the room, then be ready to act

runs.t: The fix for the "victims" session is not to stop listening. It is to listen on purpose.
Pick the people.

You need to hear from your high performers. They care about the job, they know how to make it better, and they are the ones you can least afford to lose. Random selection sounds fair. In practice it often hands the microphone to the people least invested in the answer.
Keep context in the room, but not control.
Field leaders should not run the session, because people will not be honest in front of their boss. But someone who understands the work should hear it and help leadership interpret it.
Decide before you start what you will do with the answers.
If you are not prepared to act on staffing, do not ask about staffing. If you are, say so.
Close the loop with the people who spoke.
They will tell everyone else what happened. Make sure it is something worth repeating.
How we run listening sessions today, and why we use a third party, is the subject of Chapter 13.

blocks.text: The leader who got it right

runs.t: Same company, different part of the business, different leader. He ran what he called roadblock removal sessions. I sat in on one.

He picked about 12 people himself: full-time high performers, some tenured and some new. His view was that poor performers often do not care how the job could be better, so their feedback is worth less. High performers care, so they know where the work breaks.
He asked one question at the start: what gets in the way of doing a great job?

Then he listened. He took his own notes while a colleague took more, as fast as they could write. Every 15 minutes, he stopped and read back the themes he had heard, and asked what he had wrong. People corrected him. He wrote that down too.

He sent his notes to the leadership team during the session. A leadership meeting was already on the calendar. Before the group left the building, someone at corporate was already working on the simple items.
Three of those items stuck with me.
Names in the system.

Call center staff could not change the name the system displayed for them. Some went by a name other than their birth name. One name was spelled wrong, and nobody had been able to fix it. It cost nothing to fix and irritated people every day.
The headsets.
The headsets dug into the side of the head for people with a lot of hair. Instead of telling people to live with it, the team called procurement and sourced better headsets.
The 6 a.m. meeting.

A team on the West Coast started at 6 a.m. to join a live 9 a.m. Eastern meeting. They punched in for a 30-minute meeting, punched out, and came back later for their shift. He replaced the live meeting with a two-minute recorded message pushed to each computer at the start of each shift. It cost nothing and saved money.
Same company, same kinds of problems. One leader told people, in effect, to get up earlier. The other fixed the process.
Instead of telling people they are victims and should get up earlier, you fix the way you do things.
Leaders do not only decide whether to listen. They decide how, and the how can quietly kill the whole thing.
At one point, my company wanted to hear from the people doing the work. So it built a suggestion form.

The form asked employees to estimate the cost of their idea, the timeline and the headcount it would need. Frontline employees had no way of knowing any of that. Most people looked at the form and closed it.

Leadership promised an answer to every suggestion within 48 hours. Then the suggestions came in faster than anyone could review them. The replies turned into templates: we are looking into it. Then they stopped coming at all.
Employees drew the obvious conclusion. The company said it wanted their opinions, and it was paying lip service. People stopped sharing ideas, and many stopped caring.

A promise to listen that you cannot keep is worse than no promise at all. A simpler question would have worked better: what is getting in the way of doing your job well? It needs no cost estimate or timeline, just the problem, from the person who lives with it.

If you are going to ask for feedback, say exactly when and how you will respond, and then keep that promise. If you cannot respond to every idea in 48 hours, do not promise 48 hours. Promise a monthly update on the top themes, and deliver it every month.
Leaders also decide whether bad news can reach them at all.
I once reported to a senior leader who needed to be seen as number one by his own bosses. The system we worked in rewarded how leaders looked to the people above them, and he played that game hard.

When I brought him the numbers on the pharmacists we were losing, his reaction moved through something like the stages of grief: denial, then anger, then frustration. My team kept a running joke about which stage he was in that week. It was a coping mechanism, and not a proud one, but it tells you how predictable the pattern was.

Ideas followed a pattern too. If an idea came from the team, it was a bad idea. If we could make it his idea, it might be good. If we asked what he thought, he said he paid us to figure it out. If he had an answer, it had to happen tomorrow. I learned the hard way not to outshine the king.

When our warehouse staffing work started to succeed, he wanted his own win. His idea was to pay someone to sit at a table near the entrance of our busiest stores, with a tablecloth, brochures and applications, asking shoppers if they wanted to work at the warehouse.

It produced zero applications. The warehouse was being staffed through other means, so the team went along with it to keep the peace. But it cost store payroll in stores that were already telling us they did not have enough people.

It is hard to watch a bad decision and then go execute it. When people learn that bad news is punished and credit is taken, they stop bringing either. That is when leaders lose sight of what is happening in their own company.

Notice what made this possible. It was not one personality. It was a system that measured leaders on how they looked from above. Change what the system rewards and you change what leaders do with bad news.

runs.t: Those numbers usually lead to a manager training program. Training can help. Chapter 12 is all about why the manager is the program.

But look at what managers do not choose. They do not choose their span of control. They do not set their own targets or staffing levels. They do not decide how the next reorganization is rolled out. Senior leaders do. When managers are burning out, the cause is often a decision made several levels above them.

In one large restructuring, my company brought in a top consulting firm to evaluate its people. Managers across the field were asked to update talent profiles and rate their teams. The work was presented as talent planning. It became a large reduction in force.

The consultants worked mostly with corporate, not with the field. Much of what they reported back, the field already knew. When the cuts came, they were broad. About 40% of HR was eliminated, along with about 30% of field leaders.

The leaders who remained were given more stores and more span of control, with no increase in pay. Then came mistakes that anyone in the field could have predicted. Stores were assigned to leaders in a different state. In one case, a person without the required license was put in charge of a state.
Those were not hard mistakes to catch. A district leader looking at the map for ten minutes would have caught the first one. A pharmacy leader would have caught the second. Nobody asked them.
The people closest to the work know where a plan will break. Ask them before the plan is final.
A few years later, leadership split store leadership in two. One leader would run the front of the store, and another would run the pharmacy.
The idea had merit. People with front-store expertise would lead the front store, and pharmacy experts would lead the pharmacy, with one culture across both.

But each leader's store count went from about 15 to about 30, with half of each store. Nearly the whole operation got new teams to manage. And the change rolled out with no change management: no conversation guides, role plays or videos, and little explanation of why.

blocks.title: Stores per field leader, before and after the split
blocks.source: Author's account, approximate; each leader ran half of each store after the split

runs.t: Adding a new structure without explaining why is like handing someone a new kitchen gadget with no instructions. They use it twice and go back to the knife they already trust.
Disagreements and miscommunication followed. It became one of our lowest engagement years.
A good idea, rolled out badly, can do as much damage as a bad idea. Before any change reaches the front line, it needs three things:
A why.
One or two sentences any frontline employee can repeat. If your leaders cannot say why the change is happening, their teams will fill in the blank, and they will not fill it in kindly.
A script.
A conversation guide for every leader who has to explain it, with the hard questions people will ask and honest answers to them. Role-play it before rollout.
A check.
Ask three frontline people, two weeks in, why they think the change happened and how it is going. If the answers do not match the why, you are not done rolling it out.

blocks.text: What a company loses when it cuts

runs.t: I left my own company in a reduction after 20 years. The knowledge that walked out the door with me, and with many others in the same cut, was never counted beforehand. A company that cuts without counting will pay to relearn it later.
We see the same four patterns again and again.
Ego.
Leaders who believe they already know why people leave, or who need every idea to be their own. The data gets collected, but it is used to confirm what leadership already thought.
Knowing the problem but not fixing it.
The diagnosis is clear, then the fix waits for the next budget cycle. By then the people it was meant to keep are gone.
Fixing the symptom, not the system.
A struggling manager gets a performance plan. Nobody asks how they were selected, what standard they were given, or what their own leader modeled.
Blaming the workforce.
"It is the labor market." "People do not want to work." "This industry always has high turnover." Each of these removes leadership from the solution.

Every story in this chapter fits at least one of them. The "victims" verdict was blaming the workforce. The brochure table was ego. The restructuring mistakes came from not asking the field. The front-store split was a good idea undone by skipping the system work that would have made it land.
Retention is a leadership problem. It starts at the top, and it ends at the top.
Before starting any retention program, the executive team should answer four questions, and answer them straight.

blocks.title: Four questions for the executive team
lines: •  Readiness: Are we prepared to hear that part of the retention problem starts with us?
•  Authority: Do we have the budget authority to act on what we find within 30 days?
•  Ownership: Is there one named owner for retention results, who reports to the CEO?
•  Accountability: Are we prepared to make decisions about leaders, not just frontline staff, based on what the data shows?

runs.t: If the answer to any of these is no, that is the first thing to fix. Launching a retention program into an organization that is not ready to hear the findings is not retention work. It is theater.
People rarely say no out loud.
Readiness:
"We know what the problem is. We just need help executing." That usually means the diagnosis has been written in advance.
Authority:
"We will take the findings into next year's budget." By next year, the people you wanted to keep are working somewhere else.
Ownership:
Retention belongs to HR, operations and finance at once, which means it belongs to nobody. Nobody's bonus moves when turnover does.
Accountability:
Every finding about a frontline team gets acted on. Every finding about a senior leader becomes "context."
Do not run the four questions as a group discussion first. The most senior person will answer, and everyone else will agree.
Answer alone.
Each executive writes yes, no or not sure for each question, with one sentence on why. Do it before the meeting.
Collect and show the spread.
Put the answers side by side without names. The spread is the finding. If the CEO answered yes to all four and three of the executive team answered not sure, that gap is the first conversation.
Pick the weakest answer and fix it first.
If nobody owns retention, name an owner before you do anything else.
Ask again in 90 days.
The answers should move. If they do not, the program has not started yet, whatever the calendar says.
This is the same method our Council uses on every diagnostic (Chapter 10). Independent views first keep one strong voice from setting the answer for the room.

It is hard for any leadership team to see itself clearly. That is part of why our Council of current and former executives exists. They have run large operations, made these decisions themselves, and can tell a leadership team what the field will not say out loud.
Ask the field before you finalize the plan.
Run any restructuring past the people who will live with it. They will find the stores assigned to the wrong state.
Check the math on every span of control.
If a leader cannot hold a real conversation with each direct report, the job is not possible.
Give every change a why and a script.
Explain the reason, give leaders a conversation guide, and check how it is landing in the first two weeks.
Count the knowledge before you cut.
Before any reduction, list what each person knows that nobody else does, and decide how it will be kept.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Run the four self-assessment questions with your leadership team, answered alone first. If anyone hesitates, start there.
•  Senior leader: Pick the last major change you rolled out. Ask three frontline employees why they think it happened. If they cannot say, the change was never explained.
•  Manager: Tell your own leader one thing about a recent decision that is making your team's work harder. Be specific, and suggest one fix.

runs.t: Leaders set the conditions. Managers live inside them every day, and that is where the next chapter goes.

label: Chapter 12
title: Managers and accountability
subtitle: Why retention lives or dies with your managers, and how to hold them accountable without breaking them

runs.t: The car had barely stopped at the curb when my boss jumped out.

His own boss had flown in to visit the market, and we were dropping him back at the airport. Before anyone else could reach for a handle, my boss was out of the car and running around to open the rear door. He moved so fast that he stumbled a little on the way.

I remember that stumble because it told me so much about how he spent his energy. He was a Market Vice President, and he was brilliant at managing upward. The people above him loved him. He knew what they wanted to see, and he made sure they saw it.
Below him, it was a different story.
He micromanaged everyone. I sat on a conference call and listened to him berate an hourly employee until she was close to tears. Everyone on that call understood the message. You could be next.
People complained. They used every channel they had. The complaints went nowhere.

Then came the engagement survey. One year, someone gave him a low score. The response that came back down the line was, in substance: if you don't want to be here, leave. After that, people stopped giving honest feedback. They had learned the lesson he was teaching.
So they left. Good people took pay cuts to move into other industries, just to get away from him. It had nothing to do with the company. It had nothing to do with the pay. It was him.

I want to be careful here, because this is not a chapter about one bad boss. He was not the biggest problem. The system around him was. That system measured him on results and promoted him for how he looked to the people above him. Nobody was counting how many good people he cost the company. By every measure the company tracked, he was doing his job.
That is the point of this chapter. Your managers are your retention program. Whatever you measure them on is what they will manage, and if people are not on the scorecard, people will not be managed.

Think about what that Market Vice President was paid to do. He was paid to hit the numbers, and he hit them. He was promoted by people who saw him on their visits, in their meetings and on their calls, and he made sure those moments went well. The people who saw the rest of his week had no vote.

Most companies measure managers on output: sales, margin, productivity, service levels. Those numbers matter, and a manager should own them. The trouble is that they are the only numbers. A manager can lose half their team in a year and still get a strong review, as long as the output held up while they backfilled.

And the output usually does hold up, for a while. That is the trap. Good people do not walk out on the first bad day. They stay, they work harder to cover the gaps, and they quietly start looking. The numbers look fine until the people who were holding them up are gone. By then the manager has often been promoted on the strength of those numbers.
When a manager like that moves up, every other manager watching learns what the company rewards.

I am not excusing behavior. Berating someone on a call is wrong in any system. But if you want fewer managers like that, change what the job is measured on, so that losing good people shows up somewhere it can be seen.
Nobody was measuring how many good people he was costing the company.
You have heard the line that people do not leave companies, they leave managers. The research backs it up.
Gallup has found that managers account for at least 70% of the variance in employee engagement across business units.

In Gallup's 2024 study of people who quit (Chapter 1), 45% said no manager or leader had talked with them about their future in the three months before they left. Better interactions with their manager was one of the most common answers to what could have kept them.
There is a second reason to start with managers. Managers are the most controllable part of retention.

Pay needs a budget. Promotions need open roles. A new building takes years. But a manager who checks in, closes the loop and treats people with respect costs nothing extra. The question is only what you ask them to do with their time, and what you hold them to.

blocks.text: What changed when we stopped ranking people publicly

runs.t: When I took over a struggling region, it was in rough shape. A new competitor had just opened nearby and pulled away many of our pharmacists (I tell that story in Chapter 7). Two district managers quit almost right away. Turnover across the region was running at about 61% a year.
Part of the problem was the crisis. Part of it was how we measured leaders.

Stack ranking was built into the culture. Our company's reports ranked every district from best to worst by default. That is how many leaders led, including the same Market Vice President. The district at number one got recognized. The districts at the bottom got called out in front of everyone.

Think about what that does to behavior in a staffing crisis. A district leader at the top of the list had pharmacists and technicians to spare on a given day. A district leader at the bottom had stores that could not open. Lending people across the line would have helped the company, the patients and the struggling district. It also could have dropped the lender down the rankings. So nobody shared. Everyone held on to their own people, even while stores a few miles away sat closed.
Nobody in that picture was a bad person. Every one of those leaders was doing what the scoreboard told them to do.

So in my region, we ended it. Instead of ranking district against district, we measured our region against other regions. The change took a sentence to explain. Its effect was immediate. Every district leader in the region was now on the same team, competing against someone outside the room instead of the person sitting next to them.
Stores stayed open.
Leaders moved people to wherever they were needed most, without worrying about what it did to their own line on a report.
Talent got shared.
Strong districts helped struggling ones instead of protecting their rankings.
People stayed.
Region turnover fell from about 61% to 18% in one year.

blocks.title: Region turnover, before and one year after ending stack ranking
blocks.source: Author's region, about 3,000 employees, during a competitive staffing crisis

runs.t: Our district leaders felt it too. We had 24 of them, and their turnover had been driven by the stress of constant store-level turnover. Every vacancy in a store landed on a district leader's phone. Once store turnover came down, so did theirs. We went from about four district leaders quitting a year, about 16%, to about 9% within roughly six months, and then to one a year, about 4%.

blocks.title: District leader turnover in the same region (24 district leaders)

runs.t: I want to be clear about what caused what. Ending stack ranking did not fix the region by itself. We were fixing staffing, pay questions and working conditions at the same time. But the ranking had been blocking the one thing we needed most, which was leaders helping each other. Once it was gone, everything else we tried had a chance to work.

If your reports rank managers against each other by default, ask what that ranking teaches them to do. Ask whether it rewards hoarding people. Ask whether a manager who lends their best person to a struggling team for a month gets credit or gets punished.

Then look at what you could measure instead. A region against other regions. A team against its own history. A manager against a clear standard. Any of those can keep the pressure to perform without turning colleagues into rivals.

Some of our district leaders ended up with as many as 28 store managers reporting to them. Some pharmacy leaders had about as many pharmacists. Some districts took four hours to drive from one end to the other.

Do the math on one 30-minute one-on-one a week with 28 people. That is 14 hours a week in one-on-ones alone. That is before the driving, the calls, the visits and the staffing crises. And you are not getting home for dinner.

So it does not happen. The one-on-ones stop. Reviews get rushed. Some leaders in that situation were turning to AI to write their people's performance reviews. I understand why. But nobody who read those reviews felt seen.
Restructures made it worse. One gave leaders more stores with no increase in pay, and a later split took each leader's store count from about 15 to about 30 (Chapter 11 covers both).
If a manager's job cannot be done well, it will not be done well. Before you hold managers accountable for retention, make sure the job is possible.

blocks.text: Run the span math for your own managers

runs.t: You can test this in an afternoon. For each manager, take the number of direct reports and multiply by the time you expect them to spend with each person every week. Then add travel, meetings and the rest of the job.

Take a hypothetical example. Say a manager has 18 direct reports and a standard of a 30-minute weekly check-in. That is nine hours. Add a leadership call, a staffing meeting and two hours of reporting, and you are near 15 hours before any of the work their boss measures. Add three sites an hour apart, and the week is gone.
When the math does not work, you have three honest choices:
Reduce the span.
Add a layer, split the team or move some reports to a peer.
Change the standard.
Weekly time for people who need it most, and every other week for steady, tenured people. Write that down so it is a decision and not a slide.
Remove other work.
Find the reports, meetings and copy jobs that eat a manager's week and cut them. (Chapter 14 is about that kind of friction.)
The choice you cannot make is to keep the span, keep the standard, keep the other work and then blame the manager when the one-on-ones stop.
Most companies already train their managers. Training is not the gap.

Manager training without accountability is like teaching someone to swim and never checking if they get in the pool. You can run a beautiful workshop on coaching conversations. If nobody ever asks whether the conversations happened, most of them will not.

A manager who only talks to people at review time is like a coach who only shows up on game day. If the only feedback is at the scoreboard, it is too late to change the play. The annual review is the scoreboard. The weekly check-in is practice.
So we built a loop. It has four parts, and it runs every quarter.
Every manager gets a short scorecard each quarter. Keep it to a handful of lines:
Their team's turnover against the company average.
How many people on their team sit in the top two Flight Risk bands, Intervention needed (61 to 80) and Critical (81 to 99).
How often they held one-on-ones.
Whether the people flagged for a conversation got one.
Their own manager sees the scorecard too. That matters. A scorecard nobody above you reads is a diary.

One note on the second line. A frontline supervisor should never see an individual's Flight Risk Score. The scores are for the leaders who decide where to spend time and attention, and they never make employment decisions. What a manager of managers can see is the count by team, and whether the conversations happened.

rows: Whether this team is losing people faster than the rest
People in the top two risk bands
How much risk is building on the team right now
Whether the manager is doing the practice, not only the game
Whether the risk turned into action

runs.t: Write it down. Vague expectations do not survive a busy quarter. For example:
Weekly check-ins for anyone flagged as Intervention needed or Critical.
Every Critical person gets a real conversation within the week.
Team turnover no more than five points above the company average without a clear reason and a plan.

The last line has an escape hatch on purpose. Some teams carry turnover that is not the current manager's fault. In Chapter 7, I tell the story of a manager whose team showed 80% turnover. Our Council found he had been brought in to fix a team that was already losing people. A standard with "a clear reason and a plan" protects that kind of manager. It does not protect someone who has no explanation.
Retention shows up in performance reviews and in promotion decisions. A manager who keeps losing good people is not promoted for strong output alone.

This is the part most companies skip, and it is the part that would have changed the story at the start of this chapter. If the Market Vice President's promotion had depended in part on how many good people stayed under him, the people above him would have had to look below him. They would have seen what his teams saw.
A manager with great output and a team that keeps walking out should hear, plainly, that the second fact is holding them back.
Every manager below the standard gets help:
Coaching from someone who has done the job well.
A simple Retention Talk guide, so the conversation with a flagged person has a shape.
A monthly check-in with their own manager until things improve.

The goal is to build the skill, not to punish. Most managers who struggle with retention were promoted because they were good at the work, and nobody ever taught them how to keep people. You can teach that.

blocks.text: All four parts, or none of them work

runs.t: The loop only works if all four parts run. Measurement without consequence is a report. Consequence without support is fear. And fear is how you end up with a team that tells you what you want to hear.

That is the engagement survey from the start of this chapter. Once the answer to a low score was "leave," people wrote what was safe. A company that adds consequences without support will get the same result at scale.
Measurement without consequence is a report. Consequence without support is fear.

blocks.text: How to run the loop in practice

runs.t: A quarter can look like this for a leader who manages managers.
Week one of the quarter.
Pull the scorecards. Read every one before you meet. Sort managers into three groups: above the standard, near it, and below it.
Weeks two and three.

Meet with each manager for 30 minutes. Start with the people, not the numbers. Ask who on the team they are worried about and why. Then look at the scorecard together. If the turnover line is high, ask for the reason and the plan. If the one-on-one line is low, ask what is getting in the way, and believe the answer long enough to check it against the span math.
Every month.
For managers below the standard, hold a short check-in. Ask about the specific people who were flagged: did the conversation happen, and what is the follow-up?
End of the quarter.
Look at who moved. Recognize the managers who improved, by name, in front of their peers.

Two warnings. First, do not rank the scorecards in a list and send it to everyone. You will rebuild stack ranking with a new label. Compare each manager to the standard and to their own last quarter. Second, do not let the scorecard replace the conversation. A number tells you where to look. It does not tell you what you will find.

blocks.text: Questions to ask about your own managers

runs.t: These questions will tell you quickly where you stand:
What is turnover on each team compared to the company average? Can every leader who manages managers answer that without looking it up?
Who was the last manager promoted, and what was the turnover on their team before the promotion?
When a manager lends a strong person to a struggling team, does anything on their scorecard reward it?
When someone gives a manager a low score on a survey, what happens next? Does anyone follow up with the team, or only with the manager?
Which managers are excellent at keeping people? Has anyone asked them how they do it?
If the honest answer to most of these is "I don't know," the problem is not your managers yet. It is that nobody has asked them to manage people, only output.

blocks.text: What this looks like with EIP tools

runs.t: Council View, our monthly metrics review, is built to show where turnover hides behind the company average. It shows which team is losing people while the company-wide number looks fine, and our advisors go through it with leaders each month.

The Flight Risk Score reads the manager relationship as one of its four areas, including things like manager changes, meeting frequency and teammates leaving. It points leaders to the teams that need a conversation now. It does not make decisions about anyone, and supervisors never see individual scores.
Neither tool replaces the loop. They make the first step, measurement, faster and harder to argue with.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Ask each leader who manages managers one question: what is turnover on each of your teams compared to the company average? If they cannot answer, you do not have manager accountability yet.
•  Senior leader: Look at how your reports rank managers. If they list teams from best to worst by default, change the default to a comparison against a standard.
•  Manager: Count your direct reports. Multiply by 30 minutes. If that number is more than you can spend each week, tell your boss, and decide who gets weekly time and who gets every other week.
•  Supervisor: Hold one 15-minute check-in with each person on your team this week. Not about tasks. About how they are doing. Write down one thing to follow up on.

runs.t: A manager who checks in is only half of it. The other half is knowing what to listen for, and who to listen to. That is the subject of Chapter 13.
