label: Chapter 13
title: Honest Read: listening to your people
subtitle: Who to listen to, who should ask the questions, and what to do with the answers

runs.t: The message was a few lines long.

We had started asking our people one open question: what's on your mind? It went out through whatever channel fit the group. Email for some. A text for others. A phone line. For the people who sat in front of a computer all day, a small chat window popped up on the screen. Someone on our HR team read every answer by hand and sorted it.

This one was about a support ticket. It had been sitting for four weeks. A client was waiting on the information inside it, and the employee who wrote in had no way to move it. They had already done everything the process asked of them. The ticket just sat there.
The message went into the pile marked "can do now." A small action team picked it up. The ticket was resolved soon after.
Nobody sent out a memo about it. Nobody needed to. The person who wrote in told the people around them, and those people told others. The word that spread was short: fill it out, it works.

That is the whole idea of this chapter in one small story. People will tell you what is wrong if two things are true. They have to believe the right person is listening, and they have to see something happen. Get either one wrong and you teach people to stop talking.

I have seen what it looks like when the second part fails. In Chapter 11, I tell the story of a listening session with fifteen pharmacists that ended with a one-word summary from the top: "victims." Everything in this chapter is built to keep that from happening.
Would you take investing advice from someone buried in debt? Or from someone who has built wealth?
If you want to get better at golf, you do not study the player who just shot 120. You watch the one who shoots par.

Yet that is not how most companies listen to their people. A random listening session gives every voice in the room the same weight. So does a survey that adds up every answer equally. Both take advice from the low performer as seriously as advice from the person you can least afford to lose.

I am not saying low performers have nothing to say. Some of them struggle because of the same broken process everyone else is fighting. But when you are deciding where to invest, the people who do the job best know exactly where it breaks. They care about the job, so they have thought about how to make it better.
Pick the people, or do not run the session. A random room gives you random advice.

The people you most need to hear from are leaving without being asked. In Gallup's 2024 study of people who quit, only 17% were asked what would keep them (Chapter 1). More than four out of five people who walked out the door were never asked the one question that might have kept them.
When we built a list for a session, we started with full-time high performers. Then we made sure the list had a mix:
Tenured people,
who know how things used to work and why they changed.
Newer people,
who still notice the things everyone else has stopped seeing.
Different shifts and locations,
so one site's problem does not look like everyone's problem, and one site's problem does not get missed.
Do not leave the list to chance. The people you choose decide what you will hear.
At my old company, we tried every group size and every format. Big rooms, small rooms, online sessions, manual notes, typed notes, recordings. We landed on a hybrid.

rows: People build on each other's ideas
Groupthink, or a few people dominating

runs.t: The two formats cover each other's weak spots. In a group, people bounce ideas around. Someone mentions a problem with the schedule, and someone else says, "That's because of the way the handoff works," and a third person says what would fix the handoff. You do not get that in a one-on-one. A one-on-one lets you go deep with a single person and test whether an idea from the group holds up.

blocks.text: What it looks like for a 1,000-person company

runs.t: Take a hypothetical company with 1,000 employees.
About 1% in one-on-one interviews is about 10 people, 30 minutes each. That is five hours of interviewing.
About 4% in small groups is about 40 people. In groups of five, that is about eight sessions of one hour each.
That is roughly 13 hours of listening, spread across a week or two. The cost to the business is about 50 people giving up 30 to 60 minutes each. For what you learn, that is cheap.

When you can, meet in person. People open up more when you make eye contact. You can read body language. You can see where someone gets uncomfortable, and that is often exactly where you need to ask one more question.
A video call hides most of that. People mute themselves, look at another screen, or keep their camera off. You hear the words and miss the rest.

For years we fought with notes. If the interviewer takes notes, they stop listening. If someone else takes notes, they miss half of it. Today, a digital note taker sits on the table and produces the notes and the transcript. The interviewer can watch faces and follow the thread.

If you do not have that, use a second person whose only job is writing, and recap the themes every 15 minutes the way the leader in Chapter 11 did. The recap catches mistakes before they reach a slide, and it shows the room that what they said was heard.
Our standard room had five employees, one advisor and one trained interviewer.

The interviewer is the most important person in that room. A good one knows when to follow up, when to push and when to back off. They can tell the difference between a complaint that has been told a hundred times and a new idea someone is still forming. They keep one person from taking over. They make sure the quiet person in the corner gets asked directly.
Do not ask, "What do you think of your boss?" Nobody wants to criticize their boss to a stranger with a notepad. You will get polite answers or nervous ones.
Ask instead: "What would it take to get a competitor to recruit you?"

That question does a lot of work. It tells you what someone values. It tells you how close they are to leaving. And it does it without asking them to criticize anyone. Some people will laugh and say nothing could. Others will name a number, a schedule or a kind of boss in about two seconds. Both answers tell you something.

blocks.title: Questions that get honest answers
lines: •  What would it take to get a competitor to recruit you?
•  If you had a magic wand, what would you fix about your job?
•  What would you change to make things better for customers?
•  If you had no budget, what would you fix first?
•  What gets in the way of doing a great job?

runs.t: Chapter 5 has the full set of magic wand questions and how they came about.

We also used Gallup's Q12 engagement questions, first in a distribution center and later in our stores. The Q12 tells you where engagement is weak. The open questions tell you why, and what to do about it.
This is the part leaders push back on most. They want to hear it firsthand. I understand that.

When a manager sat in, low performers went quiet for fear of being fired. With a direct manager and the boss's boss in the room, people said everything was great. Anonymous surveys fail for the same reason. If people think their words can be traced back to them, they protect themselves.

It worked better when the room was high performers and the moderator was not their manager. Managers can hear the solutions afterward, but they should not lead the session. They know too much, and the room knows it. A manager who already believes they know the answer will steer toward it, even without meaning to.
The best interviewer is a third party with no stake in either side. Someone who is not associated with the region can ask questions as if they do not know, because they do not.

That is why Honest Read, EIP's interview and listening session service, is run by a third party outside your chain of command. Doing it yourself is not the same. Your people know who signs their reviews.
Keeping managers out of the room does not mean keeping them out of the work. They have three jobs:
Before the session,
help build the list. They know who the strong performers are.
After the session,
hear the themes. Not who said what. What the room said.
After that,
own the fixes that sit inside their control, and report back on them.
Managers who are trusted by their teams tend to welcome this. Managers who resist it usually have a reason worth looking at.
A listening session is a snapshot. If you only listen once a year, you will be surprised the rest of the year. We built two habits to keep the flow going between sessions.
We wanted the fastest path for frontline feedback to reach senior leaders, and for senior leaders to ask frontline questions directly. So we built an employee advisory council.
We were clear about what it was not. It was not a union. It was not a party-planning committee. Its job was to carry the truth up and carry questions down.

The council met monthly for 90 minutes. Half the members carried over from the last meeting, and half were new. That rotation did two things. The carryover half could see progress on what they had raised last time, and could tell the new half what had already happened. The new half brought fresh problems and kept the council from turning into a club.

Decisions got made faster, because senior leaders heard the front line without filters. Before the council, a frontline problem had to pass through a supervisor, a manager, a director and a vice president before it reached anyone who could change it. Each layer softened it a little. The council cut out the layers.
If you want to start one, a few practical choices make a difference:
Pick members the way you pick a listening session:
strong performers, mixed tenure, mixed locations and shifts.
Put a senior leader in every meeting
who can make decisions, not just take notes.
Open each meeting with what happened
to the items from last month. If nothing happened, say why.
Give the council real work.

Later in our program, council members took ideas from our tracking portal, talked to the people closest to the work and fleshed each idea out before it went to leadership. (Chapter 14 tells that part.)
The second habit was the open question from the start of this chapter.

Why an open question, instead of a list of topics? Because it surfaces things you would never think to ask. One frustrated employee wrote in about a broken computer system. When the team looked into it, they found a whole pile of IT issues nobody had reported in one place. A survey with fixed questions would never have found that.
You can also aim the question. "Do you have a way to reduce costs?" works too, when that is what you need.

We set expectations up front. We told people not to expect a personal answer, and that their message was not going straight to the CEO. It was a pulse on where to invest. Being honest about that kept people from feeling ignored when they did not hear back on every note.

At first, someone on the HR team sorted every message by hand. Later, automation did it. Messages went into "can do now" and everything else. A small action team took the "can do now" pile and went and did those items. That is how the four-week support ticket got moved.
Word spread: fill it out, it works.

Compare that with a suggestion form that asks people to estimate cost, timeline and headcount before they can submit an idea, then promises a reply in 48 hours and sends a template. (Chapter 11 tells that story.) One approach asks people to do the company's homework. The other asks what is on their mind, and then does something.

blocks.text: The answer that changed a decision

runs.t: Listening is not only for finding problems. Sometimes it stops you from making a mistake you had already planned.
We had planned an offsite engagement day with free tickets to a theme park. It looked like a good idea on paper. A day off the job, paid for, something fun.

In the listening sessions, people told us something we had not thought about. They already worked full time plus mandatory overtime. They did not see their families enough. A day away from home, even a fun one, was not what they wanted.
So we asked: what if families came?
Interest went up. We added a vote so people could choose the activity. We cut it to four hours so it did not eat a whole day. And we made sure the C-suite attended.

It became a day when families could see who their people work with. That is a different event from the one we planned, and a much better one. We would have spent the same money either way. Only one version would have been worth it.
Every part of this chapter depends on one thing: people seeing that what they said made a difference.

When you fix something, tell the people who raised it. Be specific. A sentence in the shape of "You told us this, we did that, and it starts on this date" does more for your next listening session than any invitation you will ever send.

When you cannot fix something, say so, and say why. "We heard you on the schedule. We cannot change it this quarter because of the contract. We are looking at it for next year." People can live with no. What they cannot live with is silence, because silence sounds like the one-word summary from Chapter 11.
And fix something before people leave the building, if you can. The fastest fix tells everyone the next session is worth their time.
Most listening programs fail for a handful of reasons. Watch for these:
Random lists.
Fairness in who gets invited is not the same as usefulness in what you learn.
The chain of command in the room.
It turns a listening session into a performance.
Asking for complaints instead of solutions.
"What's wrong?" gets you a list. "What would you fix first?" gets you a plan.
Too many promises.
Do not promise a personal reply to every message. Promise that someone reads them all, and that the quick ones get done.
No owner for the follow-up.
If nobody owns the fix, nobody fixes it.
Choose who you hear from.
Start with full-time high performers, a mix of tenured and new. Do not leave the list to chance.
Mix interviews and small groups.
About 1% one-on-one and about 4% in groups of five gives you depth and ideas.
Keep the chain of command out of the room.
Use a neutral interviewer. Share the themes with managers afterward.
Keep a channel open between sessions.
A monthly council and one open question cover most of it.
Fix something before they leave the building.
Then tell them what you fixed, by name.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Pick about 12 high performers from one location and ask a leader outside their chain of command to run a session. Commit to one fix within a week.
•  Senior leader: Pick one channel your frontline people already use and ask one question through it: what's on your mind? Name the person who will read every answer.
•  Manager: Ask one high performer this week what it would take for a competitor to recruit them. Write the answer down, and do one thing about it.
•  Supervisor: Find one small thing your team has asked about more than once. Fix it or escalate it today, and tell them what happened.

runs.t: When you listen this way, most of what you hear will not be about pay or strategy. It will be about the small things that slow people down every day. Those are the subject of Chapter 14.

label: Chapter 14
title: Everyday friction: the small fixes
subtitle: The small, everyday problems that wear good people down, what fixing them costs, and how to keep the fixes coming

runs.t: The plan looked like a clear win.

In one part of the company, our call center reps took a lot of easy calls. How much is my prescription? When will it be delivered? A machine could answer those. So we brought in voice AI to take the easy calls, and freed our reps to focus on the customers who needed a person.
The tool did what it was supposed to do. The easy calls went away. Then two problems showed up that nobody had planned for.

The first showed up on the scorecard. Handle time went up on every call. The easy calls had been short and friendly. They had kept everyone's average down. Without them, every rep looked worse, even though nobody was working any slower.

The second problem showed up in people. When every call is a hard call, you start to dread the phone. There was no easy call coming to give anyone a breather. Reps started leaving calls on hold and not disconnecting. They were taking their own break before the next big problem landed.
Nobody had told them to stop working. They were finding a way to survive the shift.
The tool worked. The metric did not. We had kept score with handle time for years, and it had quietly become the biggest source of friction in the job.
That is the first lesson of this chapter, and it surprised me. Friction is not always a broken headset or a slow computer. Sometimes it is the way you keep score.
We did not pull the voice AI out. It was doing its job. We changed what surrounded it.
We moved from handle time to first call resolution.

The question became whether the first person solved the problem. Customer experience went up. Transfers dropped. And total time on the phone fell, even though each call ran longer. Every transfer had added minutes of a customer explaining the problem all over again to someone new.
We automated call notes and case updates.
The automated notes were better than what reps had time to write, and they gave time back on every call.
We added tiers between rep and supervisor.

Before, there was nothing in between. The new tiers ran A through F, with mini promotions at B, C, D and E for learning new therapies and skills. Each step paid about 25 cents more an hour, so people moved up in small steps instead of waiting years for one big promotion. (Chapter 15 covers how small pay steps work and where they can break.)
None of those three changes asked the reps to try harder. Each one removed something that was making a hard job harder.
The tool worked. The metric did not.

blocks.text: Check the metric before you blame the tool

runs.t: When a new tool or process makes people miserable, the first instinct is to blame the tool, or the people using it. Before you do either, look at how you keep score.
Ask three questions:
What did this change take away?
In our case, it took away the easy work that had been propping up the average.
What is the scorecard still rewarding?
If the scorecard was built for the old job, it will punish people for doing the new one.
What are people doing to cope?
Calls left on hold were a signal, not a discipline problem. Coping behavior tells you where the friction is.

blocks.text: The friction everyone learns to live with

runs.t: Most friction is not dramatic. It is the stuff people stop mentioning because they have mentioned it before.

rows: An hour on a call, waiting for your name, while most people work on something else.
Rebuilding a dashboard that already exists into slides, because executives want slides.
Slow scanners, computers without enough memory, programs that could make people faster but are not installed, and broken headsets. In a call center, broken headsets are just not a good look.
Tickets that sit for weeks. Clearing ours removed one of the biggest holdups we had.

runs.t: Each item on that list is small on its own. That is why it survives. No single slow scanner is worth a meeting. But people do not experience friction one item at a time.

A good employee can put up with a slow computer. They can put up with a pointless meeting. When it is the slow computer and the pointless meeting and the ticket that has been open for a month and the headset that hurts, the message adds up to something bigger: nobody here is paying attention to what it takes to do my job.
That message is what pushes people out. Not any one item.

In Chapter 9, I wrote about what our people raised when we finally asked: bathrooms that were disgusting, soap dispensers broken for months, and one person who had worn the same gloves for five years. We fixed all three. None of it was expensive. All of it told people someone was paying attention.
The cheapest friction to fix is often the friction nobody has bothered to report up the line.

The roadblock removal sessions in Chapter 11 are the model: a name the system spelled wrong, headsets that hurt and a 6 a.m. meeting replaced by a two-minute recorded message. None of them cost anything, and one saved money.
Most complaints about work are complaints about process. Treat them that way.
There is one kind of friction that does not show up on any equipment list, and it may be the most expensive. It is the coworker who does not pull their weight, and the manager who lets it slide.

Good people notice. They notice who calls off and who stays late. They notice who leaves work for the next shift. When nothing happens to the person who is not doing the job, the good employee draws a conclusion: why should I work this hard for the same pay? (Chapter 20 shows how this played out in a distribution center.)
A toxic employee is like a bad tenant. You are better off with an empty unit than a tenant who damages the place. An empty seat costs less than a toxic one.

Managers keep a toxic or poor performer for understandable reasons. They are short-staffed. Hiring takes weeks. Something is better than nothing. But the math changes when you count what that person is costing in the good people around them. One empty seat is a problem you can see. Two strong people quietly looking for other jobs is a problem you cannot see, until they are gone.

This does not mean firing everyone who has a bad month. It means dealing with it. A clear conversation, a clear standard, a clear timeline and a real decision at the end. The good people on the team do not need to know the details. They need to see that someone noticed.

blocks.text: What the fixes cost, and what they returned

runs.t: Some fixes look like a pure expense on paper. An old scanner still works, just slowly, so a new one shows up in the budget as new spending. Nobody gets in trouble for keeping an old scanner.
But when we paid for the upgrades people asked for, they did their jobs faster. Support tickets and software issues dropped. Almost every fix that came from the people was net positive.

items.label: minimum return on nearly every fix people asked for (author's career)
return on the best fixes (author's career)
cost of the name fix and the recorded message

runs.t: Those fixes were one of the two levers behind $104 million in operating profit in that part of the company. The other lever was keeping the good people. The two are connected, and Chapter 4 explains how. Friction drives people out, and people walking out creates more friction for the ones who stay.

blocks.text: How to make the case for a paid fix

runs.t: A friction fix that costs money has to compete for budget. It will lose if you only show the cost. Show the return.

Take a hypothetical example. Say 40 people each lose ten minutes a day to a slow scanner. Over about 250 working days, that is more than 1,600 hours a year. Put your own loaded hourly cost on those hours and compare it to the price of new scanners. Most of the time, the scanners pay for themselves in the first year, before you count fewer errors and fewer people frustrated enough to start looking.
For each paid fix, estimate three things:
Time saved,
per person, per day.
Tickets or errors avoided,
per month.
Who it touches.
A fix for your highest performers or your hardest-to-fill roles is worth more than the time math alone shows.

Then add what it costs when someone leaves. The Turn Tax puts a dollar figure on that across 13 cost categories and up to 250 variables. Once you know what one departure costs, a fix that keeps even one strong person from leaving often pays for itself on that alone. (Chapter 3 walks through the full cost of turnover.)
Fixes do not happen because someone wrote them down. They happen because someone owns them.
We started with a plain Excel file. No visuals. Just the idea, the owner and the status. It was not pretty, but everyone could see what had been raised and who had it.
Then we built a portal with about nine icons, for themes such as technology, training and career. Employees could click in to see the themes and vote ideas up or down.
The portal had a catch. People voted only if they had time to go in, and most did not. Participation was weak.

The employee council filled that gap. (Chapter 13 describes how the council worked.) Council members took the ideas, talked to the people closest to the work and fleshed each one out before it went to leadership. A one-line idea like "fix the scanners" came back as a description of which scanners, which sites, how much time was lost and what the people using them thought would work.

blocks.text: A simple tracker you can start this week

runs.t: You do not need a portal to start. A spreadsheet with these columns will do:

rows: What gets in the way, in the words of the person who raised it
A team or location, not necessarily a name
Technology, equipment, process, training, career, facilities
Open, in progress, done, or not doing (with the reason)
Yes or no: did the people who raised it hear what happened?

runs.t: The last column is the one most trackers leave out, and it is the one that keeps people raising ideas. A fix nobody hears about earns you nothing for next time.

Review the tracker on a fixed schedule. A short weekly look by the owner of each open item. A monthly look by a senior leader at anything older than 30 days. Anything marked "not doing" should have a reason someone could say out loud to the person who raised it.

blocks.text: The small fix with the biggest effect

runs.t: Of everything we fixed, the one that mattered most cost almost nothing: a visual career map.
It started with a simple idea. Tell people they have a bright career here, and then show them the path.

We sat down with people and put a dot where they were and a dot where they wanted to be. We asked whether they wanted a promotion, and when. Then we worked backward from that goal and mapped the steps between the two dots.

Now a person could see they would be promoted in a year and a half, and exactly what to do before then. The conclusion they drew was simple: I have an opportunity here, and I do not need to go look elsewhere.

That one conversation did more than most programs I have seen. It turned a vague hope into a plan with dates. And it answered the question that sends so many good people to job boards: is there a future for me here?
A career with no visible path is friction too. It is just harder to see than a broken headset.

blocks.text: How to draw a career map

runs.t: You can do this with a sheet of paper and 30 minutes.
Draw the first dot.
Where is this person today? Role, skills, what they are strongest at.
Ask where they want to go.
Do not assume. Some people want the next title. Some want a different kind of work. Some want to get better at the job they have. All three are fine.
Ask when, and draw the second dot.
Write the goal and the date. "Someday" is an answer too, and it tells you something.
Work backward.
What skills, experience or certifications stand between the two dots? Put them in order, with rough dates.
Agree on the next step.
One thing to do in the next 90 days.
Check in on it.
At every one-on-one, look at the map for a minute. Is the next step on track?

Two cautions. Do not promise a promotion you cannot deliver. The map shows the path, not a promise. And do not draw the map once and file it. A map nobody looks at again becomes one more promise that went nowhere, and that is its own kind of friction.
If you want to find the friction in your own business, you can run a short audit in about two weeks.
Week one: ask.

Pick a small group of strong performers in one area. Ask the questions from Chapter 13: What gets in the way of doing a great job? If you had no budget, what would you fix first? Open your ticket system and sort by age. Look at the meetings on your own calendar that you could cut.
Week two: sort and act.
Put everything into the tracker. Mark what is free. Do the free items that week. Assign an owner and a date to everything else. Then tell the people who raised each item what is happening.
Questions to ask along the way:
What is the oldest open ticket in IT and facilities, and why is it still open?
Which recurring meetings could be a two-minute message instead?
What report is being rebuilt by hand each week from data that already exists somewhere?
Which metric, if we dropped it tomorrow, would make the job easier without hurting results?
Who on each team is not pulling their weight, and does their manager have a plan?
You will find more than you can fix at once. That is normal. Start with the free fixes, then the fixes that touch your hardest-to-fill roles.

blocks.text: Where the Flight Risk Score sees it

runs.t: Friction is one of the four areas the Flight Risk Score reads, along with the manager relationship, career and tenure, and pay. It is a documented calculation, not AI, and supervisors never see the scores.
When friction is driving risk on a team, the score points leaders to that team. It does not tell you which headset is broken. For that, you still have to ask the people who wear them.
Check whether a metric is causing the friction.
When a new tool or process makes people miserable, look at how you keep score before you blame the tool.
Ask the people who do the work well.
Pick high performers, ask what gets in the way and recap what you heard before they leave the room.
Deal with the poor performer.
The good people around them are watching.
Count the return, not just the cost.
For each paid fix, estimate time saved and tickets avoided. Most will pay back.
Track every idea in one place, with an owner.
Start with a spreadsheet, and report back on each one.
Give every person a career map.
Two dots and the steps between them.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Ask for the age of your oldest open IT and facilities tickets. Anything over 30 days is friction someone has already reported.
•  Senior leader: Pick one recurring meeting. Cut it, shorten it or replace it with a short recorded message.
•  Manager: Ask your team what one thing slows them down every day. Fix or escalate one item, and tell them what you did.
•  Supervisor: Sit down with one person and draw their career map: where they are, where they want to be, and the next step.

runs.t: Some friction can be fixed with a headset or a recorded message. Some of it shows up on a paycheck. That is the conversation most companies avoid, and it is the subject of Chapter 15.

blocks.text: Stories and figures come from the author's career at a Fortune 10 company. Names, places and identifying details are withheld. The 3x to 15x returns and the $104 million in operating profit are from another part of the same company.

label: Chapter 15
title: Pay: when and how to talk about it
subtitle: Pay is rarely the first reason people leave, but it is often the last straw

runs.t: During a stretch of heavy turnover, my phone rang with news I did not want. One of our emerging district leaders had an offer.

She ran the highest-volume pharmacy in the company. Everyone loved her, and she had a bright future with us. A federal health agency wanted her to lead its pharmacy. The job came with a large team and about $10,000 a year more than we were paying her.
Her boss called me, and I drove over that day.
We did what most companies do. We went straight to pay, and we made her the highest-paid pharmacist in the company.
Then she told us it was not about the money.

Technician hours kept getting cut. She did not have the support to do the job the way she knew it should be done. She was running the busiest pharmacy we had without the help it needed. What she wanted was a part-time technician.

She stayed. I was relieved, and so was her boss. But the raise we gave her cost far more than that technician would have. We solved a problem she did not have, because pay was the only lever we were used to pulling.
It taught me something I have carried ever since. Pay was on the table because she had an offer. The reason she was listening to offers was somewhere else.

blocks.text: The last straw, not the first reason

runs.t: In Chapter 1, I wrote about pharmacists who took pay cuts to leave us. That should end the idea that turnover is always about money. It does not end the pay conversation, though. It changes where the conversation belongs.

Pay is rarely the first reason someone starts looking. It is often the last straw. A person who is unhappy with their manager, stretched thin by the workload, or stuck with no visible next step starts to wonder what else is out there. Then they find out they are underpaid. That settles it.

Gallup's 2024 study of people who quit (Chapter 1) shows both sides. When asked what could have kept them, more pay or better benefits was the most common answer, about 30% of the actions they named. Yet 45% said no manager or leader talked with them about their future in the three months before they left.

Put those two findings side by side. Pay matters, and nobody is asking. Most companies have a pay problem and a conversation problem at the same time, and they try to fix the first one without ever starting the second.

blocks.text: What your pay says when you are not in the room

runs.t: There is an old line about minimum wage. It is the company saying, if I could pay you less, I would.

Most leaders would never say that out loud. But pay talks even when nobody is talking. A wage set at the lowest number you can fill the job with sends a message to every person who earns it. They hear it every two weeks.

The opposite mistake sends a message too. Picture an apartment building where every unit rents for the same price, whatever the floor or the view. The best tenants, the ones in the corner units with the light, figure out that they are paying the same as everyone else for something better. They leave the moment they find a building that charges for quality. Pay your top and bottom performers the same and you get the same result.
Neither message is one you mean to send. Both are easy to send by accident when pay is set once a year by a formula and never looked at again.

blocks.text: Small steps instead of one big jump

runs.t: Our old path for frontline roles was one jump. You got promoted, earned about $3 more an hour, and waited two years for the next chance. In between, your paycheck stayed where it was, however much you learned.
In the call center, a representative went straight to supervisor with nothing in between. If there was no supervisor opening, there was no next step.

We replaced it with a skill track that ran from A through F. Each new skill, such as learning a new therapy, was worth 25 or 50 cents an hour. The steps at B, C, D and E worked like small promotions. People felt the company was investing in them.
I think of it like the military. Rank moves quickly, and each rank has levels inside it. Nobody waits years for one promotion and hears nothing in between. Frontline jobs can work the same way.
We never called it skill-based pay at the time. That is what it was.

blocks.text: Where it broke, and the fix

runs.t: The first version had a hole. Some people learned skills only to earn the raise. Even poor performers collected the steps, because the steps were tied to finishing training and nothing else.
We added two rules. You had to be at meets expectations or better to earn a step. And you had to use the skill. If you stopped using it, you could lose the pay.

We never had to take money away from anyone. The rule alone removed the reason to game the system. People who wanted the steps now had a reason to use what they learned, and the team got the coverage the skills were supposed to provide.

blocks.text: How to build a step ladder

runs.t: You do not need a compensation consultant to start. You need the job, the people who do it best and a calculator.
List the skills that make the job easier for everyone else.
Not tasks every new hire learns in week one. The skills that let someone cover a hard station, train a new person, handle an upset customer or run a piece of equipment nobody else can.
Put them in order.
Which skill do people need first? Which ones build on others? That order is your ladder.
Price each step small.
Our steps were 25 or 50 cents. The size matters less than the rhythm. A step every few months beats a big raise every two years.
Attach the two rules.
Meets expectations or better to earn a step, and the skill must be in use to keep it.
Show the ladder to everyone.
Post it. Put it in the offer letter. A ladder people cannot see does not keep anyone.

A hypothetical shows the math. Say a role starts at $17 an hour and has six skill steps at 50 cents each. A person who climbs all six in their first two years ends at $20. The company paid the same $3 it used to pay in one jump. The difference is that the person got a reason to stay at every step along the way, instead of one reason at the end that many of them never reached.
We also talked about layered job titles: entry manager, manager, senior manager, executive manager.

Companies already do this with vice presidents. A VP who has been a VP for ten years with no change in title will leave, so companies invent senior VP and executive VP to give them somewhere to go. The same logic holds for shift supervisors and entry-level roles. People want to see that they are moving, even when the work looks similar from the outside.
We were too big to make the change. A smaller company may find it easier.

blocks.text: Pay compression: rolling the dice on loyalty

runs.t: A 10-year employee at my company got about 3% a year. New hires came in higher. Executive leadership said openly that they were rolling the dice that tenured people would not quit.

The policy made that bet easy to keep making. The company paid the middle of the market, not the best and not the worst. There were three pay bands for the whole company and little adjustment for local markets. To pay one person more, a leader had to file a petition and justify it, and it was a long process. Most leaders did not try.
Then a new hire mentioned their pay to the trainer. It was a casual comment. The number was 20% above what the trainer made.

Think about where that leaves the trainer. The person teaching the job was now the cheapest person on the team, and they knew it. They still had to show up the next morning and teach the new hire everything they knew.

Years later, the company merged with another company that paid much more for the same roles. Our people got raises to reach parity, and job titles were lined up. It was the right correction. It also showed what we should all have known. We were underpaid.
When new hires start above the people training them, the company is betting tenured people will not quit.

blocks.text: How to find your compression before a new hire does

runs.t: Compression hides in plain sight, because nobody runs the report. Run it.
Pull every role where at least one person has five or more years in the job.
For each of those roles, list everyone hired in the last 12 months and their starting rate.
Flag every tenured person who earns less than a recent hire in the same role.
Start with trainers, leads and anyone who onboards new people. They are the ones most likely to find out, and the ones you can least afford to lose.
The list is usually shorter than leaders fear and longer than they hoped. Either way, you want to see it before your trainer hears it in the break room.

blocks.text: Cost-of-living bands and the hardest places to staff

runs.t: Starting pay was set in three bands. Band A covered the highest cost-of-living areas, B the average, and C the lowest.

On paper that looks fair. In practice, the low-cost areas are the hardest to staff. A high-cost city might get 20 applicants for a job. A remote town might get none. Remote areas also received smaller raises, so nobody had a reason to move there.
If you price a job only by what it costs to live nearby, you will underpay in exactly the places where you have the fewest people to choose from.
A better question for every location is how many qualified applicants you get per opening. Where that number is low, the price of the job should go up, whatever the local rent looks like.

Some of our remote stores were among the busiest in the region but sat in the lowest pay band, so no pharmacist wanted to move there. To fill them, pharmacist sign-on bonuses climbed from $10,000 to $20,000 and eventually as high as $100,000.
It filled some stores. It also taught our loyal people a lesson we did not intend.

New hires could out-earn people with years of tenure, and the tenured people were the ones training them. Some realized they could quit, come back and earn more than if they had stayed. We had built a reward for leaving.

We later added a two-year hold to the bonuses after some early hires quit within a month. The hold fixed the fastest exits. It did nothing for the pharmacist who had stayed through the worst of it and watched a stranger walk in with a check larger than her raise.
Whatever you pay to attract people, check what it tells the people who already stayed. A sign-on bonus is a message to two audiences. Most companies only write it for one.

blocks.text: The raises that worked, then leaked

runs.t: We tried to get ahead of it. Using local pharmacist counts to show how thin the labor market was, we asked for proactive raises in the hardest markets. Some were approved, and the people who got them were grateful.
Then word spread. Some pharmacists had received raises and others had not. The ones left out asked a fair question: why not me?
We had done a good thing in a way that created a new grievance.

The lesson: make it individual and confidential. Handle pay as a series of one-off decisions about specific people, each with a reason you can explain, instead of one sweep that everyone will compare. I am still thinking about the best way to run this at scale. What I know is that a broad sweep invites a broad comparison, and a broad comparison always finds someone who lost.

blocks.text: The distribution center: pricing the job with evidence

runs.t: The distribution center that supplied my stores is the full story of Chapter 20, including the pay case. The short version: starting pay was $18.25 an hour against a market of about $19.50 to $21, and money was only about a quarter of what people talked about. We proved the gap with postings, calls and applications to other employers, traced where people went, and proposed a start at $19.50, rising to $21 and up to $25 after 90 days.

Notice the order. We did not ask for a raise because people were unhappy. We showed the market rate, the destinations, the gap and a structure the company could accept. That is how a pay change gets approved in a company that says no to most of them.
A raise handed over without a conversation about growth is like a birthday card with cash and no note. The money is appreciated. It does not tell the person you see what they are doing.
That is what we did with the pharmacist at the start of this chapter. We handed her the cash. We almost skipped the note entirely, and the note was where the answer was.
When someone has an offer, or when you suspect they are looking, start with questions before you start with numbers.
"If the pay were equal, would you still want to go?"
"What would you change about this job if you could change one thing?"
"Where do you want to be in two years, and do you see a way to get there here?"

Then listen. If the answer is pay, you will hear it, and you should fix it. If the answer is a technician, a schedule, a manager or a path, you just found something cheaper and more durable than a raise.
Pay is the easiest lever to see and the most expensive to pull. When someone is at risk, EIP looks at four things, in this order.
The manager.
Does this person see their manager, get feedback and know where they stand? This is where most people who leave start leaving (Chapter 12).
The career.
Can they see the next step and what it takes to get there? A career map is often enough (Chapter 14).
The work itself.
What makes the job harder than it needs to be? Staffing, tools, schedules and support, like the technician the pharmacist wanted.
The pay.
Is it fair against the market and against peers in the same role? If not, fix it, and fix it before they ask.

Pay is last on the list because the other three are cheaper and usually closer to the cause. When pay is the problem, it is a problem you cannot talk your way around, and no amount of recognition will cover it.

The Flight Risk Score reads pay as one of its four areas, so it can tell you, for a given group, whether pay is the driver or one of the other three. The Turn Tax puts a dollar cost on losing a person, so you can weigh a pay adjustment against it. For the pharmacist, the comparison would have been easy. A part-time technician was a small number next to replacing the leader of our busiest pharmacy.
Replace one big raise with small, frequent steps.
Tie each step to a skill the person must use, and require meets expectations or better to earn it.
Find your compression before a new hire does.
Start with trainers.
Price hard-to-fill places by applicants per opening,
not only by cost of living.
Check every bonus against your loyal people.
If a new hire can out-earn a five-year employee, fix it before the five-year employee does the math.
Make pay adjustments individual and confidential.
Decide person by person, document the reason, and have the conversation in private.
Ask before you pay.
When someone has an offer, find out what they would change if pay were equal. It may cost less than the raise.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Ask HR for one list: every employee with five or more years who earns less than a hire from the last 12 months in the same role. Review it with your COO.
•  Manager: For each direct report, write down the one thing other than pay that would make them stay. If you do not know, ask them this week.
•  Supervisor: If you think someone on your team is underpaid and pulling back, raise it with your manager before they raise it with you.

runs.t: Pay can be fixed after someone is hired. Many of the problems that end in a resignation start earlier than that, with who we hire and how we choose them, which is where the next chapter goes.

The step ladder example with a $17 starting rate is hypothetical and is not drawn from any company's results.
All other stories come from the author's career at a Fortune 10 company. Names and identifying details are withheld.

label: Chapter 16
title: Hire Smart: hiring people built to stay
subtitle: A lot of turnover is decided before day one, and the answer is already on your payroll

runs.t: For years, we interviewed the way most companies still do.
Tell me about your strengths. Tell me about your weaknesses. Where do you see yourself in five years?

Those questions had probably been passed down since the company was founded. In Chapter 2, I mentioned the interview guide I kept from my days as a store trainer. It barely changed in 20 years. None of the questions told us whether someone would succeed in the job, and none of them told us whether that person would still be there in a year.

Then my region became one of the pilots for a redesign of how we interviewed and hired. We stopped asking people to describe themselves. We started looking at the people who had already succeeded and stayed, and we wrote down what they had in common.
That work rolled out across the company. It was Hire Smart before it had a name.

blocks.text: A lot of turnover is hired in

runs.t: If the job you described is not the job they get, or the person was never a fit, no retention program will save the hire. You can fix the manager, the friction and the pay, and some of those people will still leave, because they were never going to stay.
Hiring off a resume is like buying a car based on the brochure. It looks great on paper. You do not know how it drives until you are already behind the wheel.
Most hiring processes are built to answer one question: can this person do the job? That question matters on day one. It says almost nothing about whether they will still be doing it in year three.

Leadership IQ's widely cited study of more than 5,000 hiring managers found that 46% of new hires failed within 18 months. It also found that 89% of those failures came down to attitude, motivation and fit, not technical skill. The study is from 2005. Most hiring processes have not changed much since.

runs.t: Posting a job without knowing what good looks like is like casting a movie without a script. You will get people who can act. You will have no idea if they are right for this part.
Every workforce sorts into four groups by two questions. Do they perform? Do they stay?

rows: Avoidable loss. The people you most regret losing.
An accountability gap. Managed around, not managed.

runs.t: Most companies hire for the top row, high performers, and hope they stay. The goal is one box: people who perform and stay.
The other boxes are worth a minute.
The top left is where the money goes. These are the people Chapter 8 warns about, the ones with options.
The bottom left looks like a problem and often is not. A poor performer who leaves early is a hiring miss, but the departure itself costs you less than keeping them would.

The bottom right is the box nobody talks about. These people stay for years and never meet the bar. They are managed around instead of managed, and your best people are watching (Chapter 8). Hiring more people who land in this box makes every other problem worse.
Your best long-tenured people are in the top right for a reason. They came in with something. Most companies have never found out what it was.

blocks.text: Find the 3 to 5 traits your best people share

runs.t: Your long-tenured high performers share a handful of traits. These are traits, not skills. How they handle a bad day. Whether they find meaning in repetitive work or need constant change. What they do when something breaks and nobody is around to ask.
These traits are specific to your company and your work. A distribution center will not share them with a hospital. You have to find your own.
Pull the right list.
Everyone with three or more years of tenure who is also rated in your top performance tier. You need both filters. Long tenure alone is not the goal, because the bottom right box has long tenure too.
Talk to them.

In person, not through a survey. Ask what they knew about this kind of work before they started, why they said yes, what their first 90 days were like when something went wrong, and what almost made them leave in year one.
Look for what repeats.
You will usually find 3 to 5 traits that show up in nearly every conversation and are missing in the people who left early. They are almost never what the job posting asks for.
Rebuild the front end around them.
Where you recruit, what the posting says, the interview questions and how answers are scored.
Measure it.
Track how many new hires are still there at 90 days and at one year, for people hired the new way against people hired the old way.
You can start this without any software. Ten conversations with your ten longest-tenured high performers will give you a first draft.

blocks.text: What to listen for in those ten conversations

runs.t: The answers that matter most are usually stories, not adjectives. If someone says they are patient, ask for the last time patience mattered. If they say they love the work, ask what part they would miss if it went away.

Listen for the moment that almost made them quit. That moment is often the most useful thing in the interview, because it shows you the trait that carried them through it. To take a hypothetical, one person might say they stayed because a peer covered for them during a hard month. Another might say they liked solving the problems nobody else wanted. Those are two different traits, and they lead to two different hiring questions.
Write down their words, not your summary of their words. When the same phrase shows up in four or five conversations, you have found something.

blocks.text: What we did: a hiring redesign that went company-wide

runs.t: The pilot in my region produced two short lists.

blocks.title: What we hired for
lines: •  Pharmacy: Handles change well. Handles upset customers with empathy. Has a flexible schedule that includes nights and weekends. Gets along with others, because the work is side by side all day. Enjoys the medical side of the job, like medications and medical terms.
•  Front store: Dependable, honest and wants to take care of customers.

runs.t: Notice what is missing from that list, such as years of experience or a specific piece of software. Those things matter for some roles, and you can check them on the application. The traits on the list were the ones that told us who would still be there.

blocks.text: We stopped asking people to describe themselves

runs.t: We never asked, "Are you dependable?" Everyone says yes.

We asked behavioral questions instead. Tell me about a time when. What would you do if. A question about the last time a schedule changed on short notice tells you more about flexibility than any self-rating.

Judging a candidate on charisma is like hiring a chef because he is a great talker in the dining room. Charm gets him through the interview. It does not tell you if he can run the kitchen at seven on a Friday night. Behavioral questions move the interview into the kitchen.

For the medical side, we talked through medications and medical terms with candidates to see whether it interested them. We were not testing what they knew. We were watching whether they leaned in. If someone did not enjoy that part, they were not going to enjoy the job.
A good question is only half the work. The other half is knowing what a strong and a weak answer sound like, so two interviewers hearing the same answer give it the same score.
For each trait, write down three things before anyone interviews:
The question.
One behavioral question per trait.
A strong answer.
What a person with the trait tends to say. For "handles change well," a strong answer names a specific change, what the person did in the first hour and what they did differently afterward.
A weak answer.
What a person without it tends to say. A weak answer stays general, blames the change or describes waiting for someone else to fix it.
Train interviewers on those examples. Then compare scores across interviewers every few months. If one interviewer scores everyone high, the guide is not the problem.

blocks.text: Sample questions for the traits we hired for

runs.t: These are the kinds of questions that fit the pharmacy list above. Use them as a pattern, then write your own around your traits.
Handles change well:
"Tell me about the last time your schedule or your duties changed with little notice. What did you do that first day?"
Handles upset customers with empathy:
"Tell me about a customer who was angry about something you could not fix. What did you say, and how did it end?"
Gets along with others side by side:
"Tell me about a coworker you found hard to work with. How did you make the shift work?"
Flexible schedule:
Ask it straight. "This job includes nights and weekends. Walk me through how that fits your life right now." A clear answer in the interview saves a resignation in month two.
Fit was half of it. Speed was the other half.

Getting hired went from about two weeks to one. Onboarding paperwork, background checks and drug tests went from about 30 days to 15. Time from applying to starting went from roughly six weeks to three.

Every week between yes and day one is a week a better offer can arrive. The people you most want to hire are the ones most likely to get that offer. A slow process filters for the candidates nobody else wanted.
It worked well enough that it rolled out to more than 1,200 stores, and then across the company.
The same thinking helped cut early losses among seasonal hires in another part of the company from 42% to 15% (Chapter 3).

Hire Smart matching works like casting by chemistry read. Two actors can both look right for the part on their headshots. You do not know who plays well opposite the rest of the cast until you put them in a scene together.
Most interviews are headshots. A candidate meets one manager, in one room, for thirty minutes. The manager decides whether they look right.

At the distribution center that supplied my stores, we added peer interviews. New hires were interviewed by the people they would work beside, not only by the center's leader. Candidates met their future colleagues and their trainer before they ever started. The peers saw how the candidate talked to people like them. The candidate saw who they would spend their days with. Both sides got a chemistry read. Chapter 17 picks up what that did for a new hire's first day.

blocks.text: Tell the truth in the job posting

runs.t: That same distribution center had turnover of 97% when I got involved. Chapter 20 tells the whole story. One of the causes was the hiring pitch.
Recruiters told candidates: come work for us. It is a big name and a family culture. We will take care of you. Work 40 hours, and pick up overtime if you want it.

Then new hires showed up. Their supervisor was on the line, short-staffed and stressed, with no time to train anyone. The overtime was not optional. It was mandatory, on Saturdays, and refusing it could get you written up and eventually let go.
The pitch described the company people wanted to work for, not the job they were walking into. New hires found out the difference in the first week, and many of them left.
I do not think anyone set out to mislead. The pitch was built to fill seats, and the cost of it showed up later, on the floor, in someone else's numbers.

An honest posting will get you fewer applicants. It will get you the right ones. Describe the hard parts: the schedule, the overtime, the physical demands, the pace. The people who still apply are the people who will stay.
Start with your highest-turnover role. Rewrite one posting this month.
Ask three people who do the job well to read the current posting.
Ask what is missing and what is wrong.
Lead with the work.
What a normal shift looks like, start to finish.
Name the hard parts.
If there is mandatory overtime, say when and how often. If the job is on your feet for ten hours, say so.
Say what you offer in specifics.
The pay range, the step plan if you have one (Chapter 15), the schedule, the career path.
Have operations write it, and HR check it.
At the distribution center, job descriptions had been written by HR. Operations rewrote them to match what the job needs.
Then watch two numbers for the role: applicants per opening and 90-day retention. The first may fall. The second is the one that pays.

At the distribution center, certain backgrounds worked and others did not. People from a large e-commerce fulfillment employer struggled, because the center's technology felt like going back in time. They were good workers, but the job felt like a step backward every shift.

That is a fit question, not a skill question. Look at where your long-tenured high performers came from before they joined you. Then look at where your early departures came from. If a source keeps sending you people who leave in 60 days, stop paying for it, however many applicants it produces.
The distribution center did not have enough people to run interviews, so the head of the warehouse was interviewing frontline candidates himself. He did the final interview for everyone.

Every hour he spent interviewing was an hour he was not leading, training or running the operation. The goal became getting bodies in the door. That is how a hiring problem turns into a turnover cycle. The leader is too busy hiring to lead, so people leave, so he has to hire more.
Peer interviews helped here too. The leader was no longer the only person deciding who got in, and the people who knew the job best had a say.

blocks.text: Do not pay new people more than loyal people

runs.t: A sign-on bonus is a hiring decision with a retention cost. When ours climbed as high as $100,000, tenured people learned they could earn more by quitting and coming back (Chapter 15).

blocks.text: Measure the new way against the old way

runs.t: You will not know whether any of this works unless you split your hires into two groups and watch them.

Take a hypothetical company that hires 300 people a year into one frontline role. From the day it starts the new process, tag every hire as old process or new process. Then track three things for each group:
How many accepted the offer and showed up on day one.
How many are still there at 90 days.
How many are still there at one year, and how they are rated.

The 90-day number will move first. It is the number Chapter 2 asks every CEO to watch. When new hires leave early, the cause is usually expectations, selection, training, support or a gap between what was promised and what they found. Most of those are hiring problems.

Put a dollar figure on the difference with your Turn Tax. If the new process keeps even a handful more people past day 90, the savings show up in fewer interviews, less overtime and fewer trainers pulled off the line, and the case for keeping the new process makes itself.
Find your 3 to 5 traits.
Ten conversations with your longest-tenured high performers.
Rewrite one job posting.
Your highest-turnover role. Describe the job as it is, including the hard parts.
Add one question per trait.
Train interviewers on what a strong and a weak answer sound like.
Add a peer to the interview.
Let candidates meet the people they will work beside.
Cut the wait.
Every week between yes and day one is a week a better offer can arrive.
Check your sources.
Recruit where your long-tenured people came from, and stop paying for sources that send people who leave early.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Pull 90-day retention for your highest-turnover role. If more than one in five new hires is gone by day 90, the problem starts before the offer letter.
•  Manager: Write down what your two or three best long-tenured people did differently in their first month. Focus on behavior, not skills. That is the start of your profile.
•  Supervisor: Read the job posting for your own team's role. Mark every line a new hire would find out is not true in their first week. Send it to your manager.

runs.t: Hiring the right person is the first half. The next chapter is about the second half: what happens between the offer and day 90, when that person decides whether you meant what you said.

label: Chapter 17
title: Onboarding: a new hire's first 90 days
subtitle: The first 90 days decide whether a new hire stays, and most companies leave them to chance

runs.t: Sixteen years into my career, I changed jobs without changing companies.

I had spent my whole career to that point running stores. Now I was moving into a different business unit as an executive director, leading client retention and customer experience. Same company name on the badge. It might as well have been a different company. The work was different, and so were the people.
I showed up on my first day ready to learn. My new boss did not meet me that day, or the next.
On day two, he called to check in. We talked for 30 minutes. We talked about golf, and we talked about guitars. We did not talk about the job.
There was no learning plan. There was no list of who to meet. The guidance, when it came, amounted to this: go meet people, and you will figure it out.

So I did. I built my own learning plan. I worked out who I needed to know and introduced myself to them one by one. Other people who joined that team later told me the same story. It was how things were done there.

What nobody saw was what went on in my head during those two weeks. I kept asking myself whether I was doing well. I wondered whether my boss was out of the loop or just did not care. I did not start that role engaged. I started it feeling like I was taking up space.

It worked out. I ended up contributing a lot in that role, and some of the work in Chapter 4 came out of it. Years later, the same boss was the one who let me go. I mention that only because it is part of the record. The bigger point is about the system around him. Nobody measured how a new leader's first two weeks went, so nobody had a reason to plan them.
If that can happen to someone 16 years into their career, imagine what it does to a 22-year-old in their first real job.

blocks.text: The map of the wrong city

runs.t: Gallup has found that only 12% of employees strongly agree their organization does a great job onboarding new people.

That number should bother any leader who has signed off on a recruiting budget. You spend money and time to find someone, convince them, screen them and make the offer. Then, at the moment they are most open to learning how you work, most companies hand them a packet and point them at a desk.
A generic onboarding packet is like handing someone a map of the wrong city. It is technically a map. It just does not get them anywhere, and now they think it is their fault they are lost.

A new hire who is lost does not blame the packet. They blame themselves, or they decide the company does not care. Either way, they start their job with a question in their head that nobody is answering. Did I make a mistake coming here?

items.label: of employees strongly agree their organization does a great job onboarding (Gallup)
days for onboarding paperwork, background checks and drug tests after our hiring redesign
days from application to start at the distribution center

blocks.text: Why the first 90 days are a company problem

runs.t: In Chapter 2, I listed the six numbers a CEO should watch. The first one is 90-day turnover, and it is first for a reason.

Nobody goes through all the steps of getting a job only to quit right away. They applied, interviewed, waited for the checks and turned down other options. When someone walks away inside 90 days, the cause is almost always something the company controls: expectations, selection, training, support, or a gap between what was promised and what they found.
Chapter 16 covered selection. This chapter covers the rest.

Most companies do not track any of it. Recruiting measures time to fill and stops at the offer. Operations measures output and starts counting once the person is trained. The space in between belongs to nobody, and that is where a lot of new hires quietly decide to leave.

blocks.text: Day one at the distribution center

runs.t: The distribution center that supplied my stores (Chapter 20) showed me how fast a bad first day can undo a hire.
Recruiters sold a family culture and optional overtime. Day one was mandatory Saturday overtime, with a supervisor on the line who had no time to train anyone.

The center hired about 75 people at a time and hoped 20 would still be there a month later. Someone hired yesterday did not show up today. Chapter 16 covers how we fixed the pitch. The other half of the fix was what happened between yes and that first Saturday.

blocks.text: Day one starts before day one

runs.t: The first thing we changed was the wait.

At the distribution center, it took roughly 35 to 40 days to get from application to a start date. In that time, a good candidate could take another job, change their mind or stop answering the phone.

We cut it to about 10 days, a best-in-class pace. We did it mostly by overlapping steps that used to run one after another. If the first meeting showed that someone was hireable, we ordered the background check right away. It took about seven days. If we ended up not hiring the person, we lost about $30.
That is the whole trade. Thirty dollars of risk on a check that might not be needed, against weeks of delay that cost us people we wanted. It was an easy call once someone wrote it down.
The store hiring redesign in Chapter 16 did the same, cutting onboarding paperwork and checks from about 30 days to 15.

blocks.text: How to shorten your own wait

runs.t: Map every step from application to first shift. Write down how long each one takes and who owns it. Then ask three questions of each step.
Does it have to wait for the step before it?
Most background checks, drug tests and paperwork can start as soon as you know you want the person.
What does starting it early cost if you do not hire?
Compare that to the cost of losing the candidate. At the distribution center, the answer was $30.
Who is waiting on whom?
Many delays are a form sitting in an inbox. Name an owner for each step and a deadline.

Then stay in touch during whatever wait is left. A short call or message from the person's future supervisor between the offer and day one tells the new hire someone is expecting them. It costs a few minutes.
The second thing we changed was who the new hire knew on day one.
We added peer interviews (Chapter 16), so candidates met their future colleagues and their trainer before they ever started.
So when they walked in on day one, they started with a friend. They had a face to look for, someone who already knew their name and had already decided they wanted them on the team.

That changes a first day. A new hire with a friend on the floor has someone to ask where the break room is, what the supervisor is like and how the scanners work. They have someone to eat lunch with. They have one person who would notice if they did not come back.

You do not need peer interviews to get some of this. Assign every new hire a named person before day one, someone who does the same job and does it well, and tell the new hire who it is. Ask that person to meet them at the door.

blocks.text: A flight with no pilot announcements

runs.t: Onboarding someone without check-ins is like putting them on a flight with no destination and no pilot announcements. They do not know how long the trip is, what is ahead, or whether the skies will be calm or rough.
That was my two weeks. I knew the plane had taken off. I had no idea where it was going or whether I was doing anything right.

Most new hires get the same flight. They hear from their manager on day one and at their first review. In between, silence. They fill the silence with their own guesses, and the guesses are usually worse than the truth.
The fix is a schedule of short check-ins at the points where new hires are most likely to drift.

EIP builds post-hire check-ins into Hire Smart at six points: the first day, the end of the first week, the end of the second week, and days 30, 60 and 90. Each is a few questions. The point is to ask what is going on and how we can help, and to use the answers to fix onboarding for the next person.

rows: Did today match what you expected? Did you know where to go and who to ask?
Gaps between the pitch and the floor
What has been harder than you expected? Has anyone shown you how your work will be measured?
Do you know who to go to when something breaks? Is there anything you need that you do not have?
Do you know how you are doing? Has your manager given you feedback?
Can you see what your next step here would be?
Knowing what you know now, would you take this job again? What would you tell a friend about it?

runs.t: A few rules make the check-ins work.
Do not use them to grade the new hire.
The check-ins measure the onboarding, not the person. If people think their answers go into a file, they will tell you everything is great.
Read them by manager and by start date.
One unhappy answer is a conversation. The same answer from five people under the same supervisor is a pattern.
Close the loop.
When a week-one answer leads to a fix, tell the next group of new hires it was fixed because someone said so.

The check-ins work best when the new hire's direct supervisor is not the one collecting the answers. A new person will not tell their boss, in week one, that their boss has not trained them. Send the questions by text or a short form, or have someone outside the team make a two-minute call. The supervisor should see the themes, not who said what.
Then act on what comes back, fast. A new hire who says in week one that they still do not have a login, and has one by Thursday, learns something about the company that no welcome video could teach.

Say a company brings on 40 new frontline hires in one quarter under eight supervisors. Most of the day-one answers are fine. At week one, six people say nobody has shown them how their work is measured. Four of the six report to the same supervisor.

That is not a new-hire problem. It is a training gap on one team, found in the second week instead of in an exit interview three months later. Without the check-in, the first sign would have been four resignations.
These check-ins are the new-hire version of the listening in Chapter 13. The difference is timing. You are asking while the person can still be kept, not after they have decided.
This is the plan EIP recommends. It is a starting point, not a result I am claiming. Adjust it to your work, then measure it against how you onboard today.
Shorten the wait. Start the background check, drug test and paperwork as soon as you know you want the person.
Name a peer partner, someone who does the job well, and tell the new hire who it is.
Have the direct supervisor call or message once before day one.
Send a one-page note: where to go, what time, who will meet them and what the first week looks like. If there is mandatory overtime, say so here.
The supervisor meets them in person. If the supervisor cannot, the second-level manager does. Nobody starts with no one there.
Give them the plan for the first two weeks in writing: who they will meet, what they will learn and when their manager will check in.
Pair them with their peer partner for the day.
Run the day-one check-in before they leave.
Training happens with a named trainer who is not also expected to carry a full load that week.
The supervisor checks in at least twice, for ten minutes, about the work.
Show them how their work is measured, and what good looks like in week one versus month three.
Run the week-one check-in.
They should be doing part of the job on their own, with their peer partner nearby.
Make sure they have every tool, login and badge they need. Missing equipment in week two tells a new hire the company was not ready for them.
Run the week-two check-in, and fix whatever it turns up before week three.
A real one-on-one with their manager. How are you doing, what is hard, what do you need?
Show them the career map for their role (Chapter 14) and, if there is one, the pay step plan (Chapter 15).
Run the day-30 check-in.
Give specific feedback on one thing they do well and one thing to work on.
Run the day-60 check-in.
A 90-day conversation. Confirm what they have learned, what comes next and when they can expect the next step.
If you use a 90-day pay step, deliver it on time. A late step tells the person the promise was soft.
Run the day-90 check-in, and compare their answers to the ones they gave on day one.

That is a lot of check-ins. Each is short. Add them up and a supervisor spends maybe a few hours per new hire over three months. Compare that to what it costs to replace someone who quits in week three.

blocks.text: Experienced hires and internal moves need this too

runs.t: Most onboarding programs are built for entry-level hires. My two weeks of silence happened to a 16-year employee moving inside the same company.

Internal moves and senior hires often get the least onboarding of anyone, because the company assumes they will figure it out. But a leader who spends their first month figuring out who matters is a leader who is not yet leading.
For senior hires and internal transfers, keep the same structure and change the content:
A list of the 10 to 15 people they should meet in the first two weeks, with a sentence on why each one matters.
One meeting with their new boss in the first two days, about the job, with the first 90 days written down.
A short list of what the business needs from them first.
The same check-ins at day 30, 60 and 90.
None of that costs money. It costs someone deciding that a new leader's first two weeks are worth an hour of planning.
You cannot fix onboarding you do not see. Track these four things for every role:
No-shows.
Offers accepted against people who showed up on day one.
90-day turnover,
by role, by manager and by start month.
Check-in answers,
by manager and by question, over time.
Time from application to start,
by step.

Then put a dollar figure on it. A Turn Tax calculation shows what each early departure costs across interviews, paperwork, training time, mistakes and the trainer pulled off the line. Most leaders who see that number stop thinking of onboarding as an HR program and start thinking of it as an operating cost they control.
Shorten the wait.
Overlap steps, start checks early and name an owner for every delay.
Give every new hire a friend.
Peer interviews if you can, a named peer partner if you cannot.
Give every new hire a plan and a person.
Who to meet, what to learn and when the manager will check in, in writing, on day one.
Check in at day 1, week 1, week 2, and days 30, 60 and 90.
Short questions, read by manager, used to fix the process.
Onboard your internal moves and senior hires.
Sixteen years in, I still needed a plan.

blocks.title: Take action this week
lines: •  CEO: Ask for 90-day turnover for your three highest-volume roles, by manager. Ask who owns the time between the offer and day one.
•  Manager: Map every step from application to first shift for one role. Find one step you can start earlier.
•  Supervisor: For your next new hire, write a one-page plan for their first two weeks: who they meet, what they learn, when you check in. Name a peer partner and hand them both the plan on day one.

runs.t: Every fix in this part of the book works only if someone decides it will last. Part Four is about making that decision, starting with the ten choices leaders make that keep the gains or let them fade.
