label: Chapter 18
title: The ten decisions that keep the gains
subtitle: Why retention gains fade, the ten choices that keep them, and a scorecard for the executive team

runs.t: Over 20 years in operations, I moved from role to role. Each move followed the same pattern. I would spend a couple of years with a team, we would do the hard work of bringing turnover down, and then I would hand the keys to someone else and go start over somewhere new.
And I paid attention to what happened after I left.

In some places, the gains held and kept growing. The next leader kept the reviews on the calendar. They kept asking the front line what was in the way, and they kept fixing it. The numbers kept improving after I was gone.

In other places, the gains faded. It never happened in one dramatic moment. The monthly review got pushed a week because something urgent came up. Then it got pushed again. Then it quietly dropped off the calendar. The small fixes stopped. Nobody announced that the work was over. People on the front line noticed anyway, the way they always notice, and the old turnover numbers came back.
The teams were similar. The tools were the same. The training was the same. The difference was the leader who came after me.
That taught me something I did not want to learn. Nothing about the problem had been solved for good. The behaviors that produced the gains had stopped, so the gains stopped too.
This chapter is about how to keep that from happening to you.
I think about retention the way I think about fitness.

Getting in shape is hard. The first months hurt. You change your schedule, you give things up, and progress is slow. Then one day you look in the mirror and you like what you see. You feel good. And because you feel good, you decide you do not need to work out as much.
So you skip a week. Then two. You lose muscle. One day you try to run the distance you used to run without thinking, and you cannot. Now you are starting over.
Staying fit is easier than getting fit the first time. You do not need the same intensity. You do need to keep showing up.

Retention works the same way. The first push takes energy, attention and some money. Once the numbers turn, keeping them there costs far less. It still costs something. The meetings still have to happen. Someone still has to look at the numbers and ask what changed.
Retention is a long war, not a short battle.

The goal is not a good quarter. The goal is a culture where people expect to stay, where outsiders fight to get in, and where your company is the obvious place to build a career. You do not get there by winning one battle and going home.
The most common reason the work stops is a change at the top.
A new leader arrives, often in HR, and looks at the retention work one of two ways. Some leaders love it, because a program that is working makes them look good.

Others see a threat. A retention program that works can look like proof that the company no longer needs them, or that the person before them did something they cannot match. So the program gets "reviewed." Then it gets "paused while we assess priorities." Then it is gone.

I do not say this to blame anyone. A new leader is under pressure to show their own impact fast. The system usually rewards a new initiative with your name on it more than it rewards keeping someone else's program alive. If you want the work to survive a handoff, you have to design for that pressure, not hope it goes away.

The rest of the C-suite tends to be easier. CFOs like this work because they can see the dollar return. Once turnover has a price, every point of improvement shows up as money kept (Chapter 3). COOs like it because operations get better. There are fewer open shifts, training goes faster and output gets steadier.
As long as the C-suite stays stable and nobody arrives who feels threatened, the gains keep building. The risk sits in the transitions.

blocks.text: Questions to ask before a leadership change

runs.t: If someone who owns part of this work is about to leave, or a new leader is about to arrive, ask these questions out loud, in the room:
Who owns retention results after this person leaves, by name?
Is the next monthly review already on the calendar, and who runs it?
What would make this person see the program as theirs, not someone else's?
What number would tell us, three months from now, that the work has stalled?
If nobody can answer the first question, you have found your biggest risk.
I want to be specific about what is at stake, because "keep the program going" can sound like a soft request. It is not.

items.label: annualized turnover at one distribution center, in about a year
pharmacist turnover in one region, with 18% within about three months
net promoter score over two years, in another part of the company

runs.t: Those results came from the same kind of work described in this book. The distribution center saved roughly $38 million (Chapter 20). The rise in net promoter score came with $104 million in operating profit (EBIT) from throughput and productivity (Chapter 4). The pharmacist turnaround started in a war room (Chapter 7).
The ones that held, held because somebody kept showing up.
Over the years I boiled the work down to ten decisions. Every one of them is made by the executive team. None of them needs a large budget to start. Most of them cost a meeting and a little courage.
Each decision points to the chapter that goes deeper.

blocks.text: 1. Put a dollar figure on turnover

runs.t: Most CEOs can name the costs that show up on an invoice. They miss the slow first weeks, the mistakes, the good person pulled off the line to train and the overtime, which lands in a budget line with no label that says "turnover."

The Turn Tax™ counts 13 cost categories, using up to 250 variables, and puts the number where the CFO can see it. When I did this math for my own results, using the most conservative inputs I could defend, it came to more than $18 million a year in turnover cost avoided (Chapter 3).
How to run it: ask your CFO what one voluntary departure costs in your highest-turnover role. If the answer takes longer than two days, you do not have this decision in place yet.

blocks.text: 2. Run the company on six numbers

runs.t: My region once won its first award for payroll control while our stores were barely staying afloat. We made payroll because turnover was so high we could not staff the stores (Chapter 2). The dashboard said we were winning.
Watch six numbers instead:
90-day turnover
Turnover by manager
The Turn Tax
Flight Risk
The top three items from Honest Read
High performer turnover
How to run it: put all six on the same page as revenue, safety and operations. If they live in a separate HR report, they will get separate attention, which usually means less.

blocks.text: 3. Talk this week, not after the resignation

runs.t: When people quit, their leaders are often shocked. The people who work beside them every day are not. They saw the signs weeks before (Chapter 6).

The Flight Risk Score™ scores each person from 0 to 99 for the next 90 days. Anyone in Intervention needed (61 to 80) or Critical (81 to 99) gets a Retention Talk. Critical means a conversation this week, not next month.

Two rules hold this decision together. Supervisors never see the scores. And the score never makes an employment decision. It tells senior leaders where to look and who to talk to. The talking is still a human job.
How to run it: at your next review, ask how many people are in the top two bands, and how many of them have had a conversation. The second number should match the first.

A president once ran a listening session with fifteen randomly picked pharmacists and summed up what she heard in one word: "victims." Everyone went back to their stores convinced corporate did not listen (Chapter 11).
Do not weight a poor performer's feedback the same as a high performer's. Pick high performers, use a moderator who is not their manager, and act on what you hear (Chapter 13).
How to run it: before the next listening session, look at the list of names. If you cannot say why each person is in the room, change the list.
One leader sourced better headsets for people whose old ones hurt and replaced a 6 a.m. meeting with a two-minute recorded message (Chapter 11).

The simple fixes people asked for returned 3 to 15 times their cost (Chapter 14). Almost none of them needed a committee. They needed someone with the authority to say yes, and the habit of telling people when it was done.
How to run it: ask for the age of your oldest open IT and facilities tickets. Anything over 30 days is friction someone has already reported and nobody has fixed.

One of our best pharmacists got an offer from a federal health agency for about $10,000 a year more. We made her our highest-paid pharmacist. Then she told us it was never about the money. She needed technician support to succeed (Chapter 15).
Pay matters. It is rarely the whole story. Use market data and small, skill-linked raises so the pay conversation happens before the offer letter, and listen for what sits under the pay question.

Promotion works the same way. Promoting without a real path is like a ladder with the top three rungs missing. People can see where it goes. They just cannot get there, so eventually they find a ladder that reaches the roof. Small steps and a visible career map keep people climbing yours.
How to run it: ask HR for every employee with five or more years who earns less than someone hired in the last year in the same role. That list is where your next resignation is coming from.

Averages hide pockets. A company at 4% turnover can be at 1% everywhere except under three managers (Chapter 2). The program you buy will not fix those three teams. The managers above them will, or nobody will.
Look at turnover by manager, set one standard, and back it with measurement, consequence and support (Chapter 12).
How to run it: ask every leader who manages managers what turnover is on each of their teams compared to the company average. If they cannot answer, you do not have manager accountability yet.

In another part of the company, we said the customer was number one, but bonuses went to the people who got off the phone fastest (Chapter 4). People did what we paid them to do. When we rebuilt reporting, training and incentives around what customers valued, the score followed.
Leaders set the targets, the spans and the incentives. If those reward the wrong thing, no amount of frontline effort will fix it (Chapter 11).
How to run it: write down the three things your company says matter most. Then write down what your bonus plan pays for. Put the two lists side by side.

blocks.text: 9. Hire for the people who stay

runs.t: At the distribution center, we hired 75 people and hoped 20 would still be there in a month. We cut the wait to start to about 10 days and added peer interviews (Chapter 20).
Hire Smart™ builds hiring around the 3 to 5 traits your long-tenured top performers share (Chapter 16). Then the first 90 days on the job decide whether those good hires stay (Chapter 17).
How to run it: pull 90-day retention for your highest-turnover role. If more than one in five new hires is gone by day 90, the problem starts before the offer letter.
This is the decision that protects the other nine.

Four structures keep the work from depending on anyone's enthusiasm: one named owner, reviews on the calendar, retention metrics in the main dashboard, and a trigger set in advance that restarts the work when a number slips. Put them in place before the first leader moves on. Chapter 19 shows how to install them in your first 90 days.
The gains that last belong to a system, not to one person's energy. That includes mine. It includes yours.
How to run it: for every leader who owns part of this work, write down who takes it over if they leave tomorrow.
Knowing the ten decisions is not the same as making them. The scorecard turns the list into a conversation your leadership team can have in an hour.
Score each decision from 1 to 5. A 1 means you have not started. A 5 means it is running without anyone having to push it.

All six are on the main leadership dashboard every month

blocks.text: How to run the scoring session

runs.t: The way you run this matters as much as the score.
Score separately first.
Hand each executive a blank sheet. No talking until everyone is done. If the CEO scores out loud first, the room will drift toward the CEO's numbers.
Then compare.
Put every score on one page, side by side.
Talk about the gaps before the averages.

Where two people differ by two points or more, stop and talk that through before anything else. A CFO who scores pay a 4 and a COO who scores it a 2 are looking at different evidence. Find out what each one is seeing.
Agree on one number per decision.
Not an average. A number the room can defend.
Keep the sheet.
You will score again in six months, and the change is the point.
Under 30:
Start with your two lowest decisions. Most companies begin here, and the early fixes are often cheap.
The structure exists but execution is uneven. Look for decisions that depend on one person.
Above 40:
Protect it. Plan now for what happens when a key leader moves on.
This is a hypothetical. It does not describe a client.
Say a 1,000-person company scores itself at 27. Its lowest scores are a 1 on the dollar figure and a 2 on talking this week. It scores itself a 4 on pay, because it gave a raise last year.

The temptation is to start with whatever feels most urgent. The scorecard says start with the two lowest. So the CFO gets the first one: build a Turn Tax for the two highest-turnover roles within 30 days. The CHRO gets the second: a list of everyone who should be having a Retention Talk, and a date for each one.
They do not launch a new program or buy anything. They make two decisions, give each one an owner and a date, and book the next review.
Six months later, they score again. If the dollar figure is now a 3 and the Retention Talks are a 4, the company has moved four points without spending much at all.
Score the ten decisions this month.
Do it as a leadership team, and keep the sheet.
Name one owner.
One person, by name, who owns retention results and can act without waiting for approval.
Book the next twelve reviews.
Put them on the calendar now.
Write down your trigger.
Pick the number that restarts the work, and fund the response in advance.

None of this is complicated. That is the trap. Because it is not complicated, it feels optional, and the first busy month it gets skipped. The companies that hold their gains are the ones that treat these decisions like the monthly close: not exciting, not optional, and never skipped.

label: Chapter 19
title: The 90-day quick-start plan
subtitle: What to do in the 90 days after the diagnostic, who owns each piece, and how often to look

runs.t: Over 20 years, I sat in a lot of rooms where a problem had just been explained well. The data was on the screen. The causes were clear. Everyone nodded. Then the meeting ended, people went back to their calendars, and the urgent work of the week swallowed the important work of the year.
The rooms I remember fondly are the ones where something moved before people left the building.

In one of them, a leader ran a session to find out what got in his team's way and sent his notes to leadership while it was still going. A leadership meeting was already on the calendar. Before the group walked out, he had someone at corporate working on the simple items (Chapter 11).

In another, we had set up a channel where employees could tell us what was on their mind. Someone wrote that a support ticket had been sitting for four weeks while a client waited. It was fixed soon after. The word spread on the floor faster than any memo could have: fill it out, it works (Chapter 13).
Neither of those moments was expensive. What they had in common was speed, a named person who acted, and a calendar that was already set. That is most of what this chapter is about.

Chapter 10 walked through a 30-day diagnostic. At the end of it, you have a dollar figure for your turnover, a list of who is likely to leave, the top three things your people want fixed, and a ranked list of where to start. This chapter covers the 90 days after that. It is EIP's recommended plan: the order to do things in, who owns each piece, and how often to check.

blocks.text: Why the 90 days after matter more than the 30 before

runs.t: The diagnostic does something you cannot take back. It asks people what is wrong.

Somewhere around 50 of your employees, in a 1,000-person company, sat in an interview or a listening session and told someone outside their chain of command what gets in their way. They went back to their teams and talked about it. Now everyone is watching to see what happens next.

If nothing visible happens in the first few weeks, you have taught your people that talking to leadership is a waste of time. That lesson is hard to unteach. Chapter 5 covers what years of surveys with no follow-through do to trust. A diagnostic with no follow-through does the same damage, faster, because people were asked face to face.

The second reason is urgency. In my experience, urgency carries a retention effort for about the first six months. After that, a new crisis takes the meeting slot. The 90 days after a diagnostic are when you have the most attention you will ever have. You want to spend it on two things: visible fixes, and structures that keep the work alive after the attention moves on.
You will have more fixes than you can do at once.
So sort them. Ask two questions about every fix. Is it quick or long-term? Is it free or costly? That gives you four boxes:
Quick and free:
do now.
Quick and costly:
do soon, with a business case.
Long-term and free:
start now, finish over months.
Long-term and costly:
plan and fund.

Pick the top five to ten. Then bring a few employees in and ask them three questions. If we did these, how would it affect you? What are we missing? How would you rank them? We did this at the distribution center in Chapter 20, and when people saw the plan go in, they said it was what they had asked for.
Once the list is ranked, the 90 days follow a sequence I recommend for almost every company:
Quick friction wins in the first two weeks.
They prove that listening leads to action.
Manager accountability next.
Turnover lives under managers, and managers need time to change habits.
Pay moves after that.
Pay needs evidence and a business case, which takes weeks to build properly.
Hiring changes last in the 90 days.
They protect everything else, and they take the longest to show up in the numbers.
The sequence is not a rule that the other work waits. Long-term work starts early so it can finish later. The sequence tells you where to put your leadership attention first.

Friction fixes are the fastest proof you can give. A broken headset replaced, a pointless meeting cut, a ticket that sat for a month finally closed. Each one tells people that what they said was heard.
They also pay. In another part of the company, the simple fixes people asked for returned 3 to 15 times their cost (Chapter 14). Most cost little or nothing.
The one rule: every fix gets told back to the people who asked for it. A fix nobody hears about earns you almost nothing in trust.
When you split turnover by manager, the problem usually concentrates. Chapter 2 has the math, and Chapter 12 has the story of what fixing it looks like.

Manager work cannot be rushed. A manager who has never held weekly check-ins will not become good at them in one week. Starting this work in week three gives it ten weeks to settle before the quarter ends.

Be careful with the first look at turnover by manager. The highest number is not always the worst manager. Our Council once saw a manager at 80% turnover and found, by asking questions, that he had been brought in to fix a team a low performer had left behind (Chapter 7). Ask whether each manager inherited the problem or created it before you decide anything.
Pay is rarely the whole reason people leave (Chapter 1). It is often part of it, and when it is, you need a case that will survive the CFO.

That takes evidence. Read the job postings near you. Call local employers. Trace where your last 30 former employees went. Find the people with long tenure who earn less than recent hires (Chapter 15). Then price the fix against your Turn Tax, so the raise sits next to what turnover is already costing you (Chapter 3).
Building that case properly takes four to six weeks. Starting it in week five means the decision can be made inside the 90 days.
Hiring changes protect every other gain. If you fix the floor and keep hiring the wrong people the wrong way, you will refill the leaky bucket from the top.

They also take the longest to show up. A new hiring process affects the people who start next month, and you will not know how many of them stayed until 90 days after that. So you start the design inside the plan, launch the changes by the end of it, and judge them in the next quarter.

The pieces: build the profile from the 3 to 5 traits your long-tenured top performers share (Chapter 16), cut the time from application to start, add peer interviews, write honest postings, and set up check-ins at day 1, week 1, week 2, and days 30, 60 and 90 for every new hire (Chapter 17).

Every fix on the list gets one owner, by name. That means one person, not a department or a committee: someone who can act without waiting for approval, and who will be asked about it at the next review.
The roles below are what I recommend. Adjust them to fit how your company is built.
Sponsor.
Usually the COO or CHRO. Owns the whole plan, runs the weekly check-in, and clears roadblocks.
CEO.
Owns the quarterly board update and the Honest Read top three. Decides when a fix needs money.
CFO.
Owns the Turn Tax and the business case for every costly fix.
COO or head of operations.
Owns 90-day turnover by location, friction fixes on the floor, and the operating side of hiring changes.
CHRO.
Owns Flight Risk follow-up, the pay evidence and the hiring process.
Senior leaders.
Own turnover by manager for their own managers.
Managers and supervisors.
Own the weekly check-ins, career maps and new hire check-ins for their own people.
A plan without a review rhythm is a wish. Four reviews keep this one honest. Put all of them on the calendar in the first week, for the whole year, before anything else gets in the way.
Thirty to sixty minutes. The sponsor and the owners of whatever is active that week.
Three questions:
What got done since last week, and did we tell the people who asked for it?
What is stuck, and who can unstick it?
Did every Critical Flight Risk score get a conversation this week?
The last question belongs here because it cannot wait two weeks. Critical means a conversation this week (Chapter 6).

blocks.text: Every two weeks: the KPI review

runs.t: During the first 90 days, I recommend looking at all six numbers from Chapter 2 every two weeks. Two weeks is short enough to catch a problem before it becomes a pattern.

Do not overreact to two weeks of data. Annual turnover will barely move inside 90 days. The numbers that move first are the leading ones: Flight Risk bands, 90-day turnover for the newest hires, and whether the Honest Read items are getting done.
After the first 90 days, settle into the rhythm from Chapter 2.

rows: Monthly, by location and hiring manager
Baseline in week one, update at day 90

runs.t: Once a month, the metrics go in front of people who are not in your building. Council View is EIP's monthly metrics review with our Council of current and former executives.

The value of an outside review is the questions. Someone who is not part of your operation can ask things as if they do not know the answer, because they do not. They notice when a number has been flat for two months and nobody has asked why. They flag early when gains start to slip.

If you are not working with EIP, build your own version. Bring in two or three people from outside the chain of command, maybe board members, maybe peers from other companies, and give them the same numbers every month.
At day 90, the CEO takes the work to the board. How you frame it decides whether it survives the next budget cycle.
Do not lead with what the program costs. Lead with what turnover already costs, and how much of it you are recovering (Chapter 3):
Current Turn Tax.
What turnover costs you this year, across all 13 categories.
Recovery goal.
The share of it you agreed to win back, tracked monthly.
Program cost.
Compared against the recovery, not against other budget lines.
Show three scenarios, because boards trust a range more than a single promise. The percentages here are examples only. Your own goal is set with your partner and tracked every month.
Conservative:
turnover down 15%. Turn Tax times 15%, minus program cost.
Base:
turnover down 20%. Turn Tax times 20%, minus program cost.
Strong:
turnover down 25%. Turn Tax times 25%, minus program cost.

At day 90, you will not have a year of results. Be honest about that. Show what has been done, the leading numbers that have moved, and the date of the next update. Boards forgive slow results. They do not forgive surprises.
This is the plan I recommend for a company coming out of a 30-day diagnostic. Week 1 is the week after the day-30 meeting.

rows: Name the owner and sponsor. Book every review for the year. Tell employees what was heard and what comes first. Critical scores get a conversation.
Do the quick and free fixes from the Honest Read top three. Tell each group what was fixed. Schedule Retention Talks for Intervention needed scores. First KPI review sets the baseline.
Review turnover by manager with each senior leader. Check who inherited the problem and who created it. Start weekly 15-minute check-ins. First Council View.
Set one manager standard. Plan for poor performers. Start career maps. Gather market pay evidence and trace where people went.
Price the pay fix against the Turn Tax. Design small, skill-linked steps. Take the case for approval. Second Council View.
Build the trait profile. Overlap hiring steps. Add peer interviews. Rewrite postings and job descriptions with operations.
Put approved pay moves in place. Launch the new hiring steps and new hire check-ins. Plan the next listening round. Third Council View.
Install the four structures. Write the trigger. Give the quarterly board update.

blocks.text: A hypothetical, to make it concrete

runs.t: This example is hypothetical. It does not describe a client.

Say a 1,000-person company finishes its diagnostic. The Honest Read top three are a broken scheduling tool, a weekly meeting that pulls the night shift in early, and no clear path to the next job. Turnover by manager shows four teams well above the rest. Market data suggests starting pay for one role sits below nearby employers. And 90-day turnover is high in the role with the most hiring.

In week one, the COO cancels the early meeting and replaces it with a short recorded message. IT gets a two-week deadline on the scheduling tool. The CEO sends a short note to everyone who took part in the diagnostic, listing what was heard and what comes first.
In weeks three and four, the senior leaders over the four teams each sit down with the data. Two of those managers inherited the problem. Two did not. The conversations are different.
In weeks five through eight, HR builds the pay case for the one role, and the CFO prices it against what turnover in that role costs. The case goes in as a recovery, not a cost.
In weeks nine through twelve, the hiring process for the high-churn role changes. New hires start getting check-ins at day 1, week 1 and week 2.
At day 90, the CEO tells the board what was done, what the leading numbers show, and what the next quarter holds.
Nothing in that plan is exotic. The difference between a company that does it and one that does not is almost never the ideas. It is the calendar and the owners.

blocks.text: Four structures that keep the gains

runs.t: Chapter 18 explained why retention gains fade. Retention is like fitness: if you stop showing up, you slide back to the start, and the most common reason companies stop showing up is a change at the top.
So the last job of the 90 days is to make the work stop depending on anyone's enthusiasm, including the sponsor's. Four structures do that.
One person owns retention results at each level, with the authority to act. Not a committee, and not "HR" in general.
When that person moves on, name the replacement before they leave. The worst time to find a new owner is after the old one has cleaned out their desk.
Put the monthly review on the calendar a year ahead and do not move it. Treat it like the monthly financial review.
Each review ends with a decision, not a report. If a meeting ends with "thanks for the update," it was a report. Reports get skipped first when the calendar fills up.
Retention numbers sit next to revenue, safety and operations.
If your leadership dashboard has twenty numbers and none of them tells you who is leaving, the six numbers from Chapter 2 belong on it.
Decide now what number restarts the work. For example: if voluntary turnover rises three points in a quarter, a new diagnostic is funded automatically.
The point of the trigger is that the response no longer waits for the budget cycle, or for a leader to decide it matters. The decision was made back when everyone was paying attention.

blocks.text: What goes wrong in the 90 days

runs.t: A few patterns come up again and again. Watch for them.
Doing everything at once.
A list of thirty fixes, all started in week one, means none of them finish. Pick five to ten. Finish them. Tell people.
Announcing without doing.
A town hall about the new retention plan, followed by three quiet weeks, is worse than no town hall. Lead with a fix, then talk about it.
Surprising your managers.

If a manager learns from their own boss's boss that their team's turnover is the highest in the company, in front of peers, you will get defense, not change. Have the first turnover-by-manager conversation one on one.
Letting scores leak downward.
Flight Risk Scores belong to senior leaders and HR. The moment a supervisor sees one, the trust the whole system runs on starts to crack.
Losing the slot.
Some new crisis will come up around month two. It will want the meeting time. Hold the slot. If the review moves once, it will move again.

•  Sponsor: Sort your fix list into the four boxes. Pick the quick and free items you can finish in two weeks and give each one an owner.

•  CHRO: Confirm every Critical Flight Risk score has a conversation on the calendar this week.

label: Chapter 20
title: Case study: one distribution center
subtitle: How a center ranked last of 13 cut turnover from about 97% to about 51% in a year

runs.t: Nobody asked me to fix retention at that distribution center. I found out it had a problem because my stores had empty shelves.
Not a few gaps. Four feet of nothing, then eight feet, then twelve. One of my colleagues lay down on an empty shelf and took a picture of himself, asking where the product was.
Across the street, the competing pharmacy was fully stocked.
The stores had been given an explanation. It was a manufacturer problem. Or it was a port problem. The story made sense, and it let everyone off the hook.
It was not true.
I went to the center and found the leader. He was a 25-year veteran, someone who had seen every kind of bad month a warehouse can have. I asked him what was going on.
His answer took three words. "It's turnover."
Then he explained. They did not have enough people to get the freight out. Boxes in did not equal boxes out. He had already pushed a day and a half of trucks to the next day.

That was the moment the empty shelves stopped being a supply chain story and became a people story. This chapter tells it from start to finish, because it is the clearest example I have of the whole book working in one building.
The numbers at the center told the story before anyone said a word.
They would hire 75 people and hope 20 were still there a month later. Someone hired yesterday did not show up today. The center was running a constant intake just to stand still.
To keep up, Saturday overtime was mandatory until they caught up.

The recruiting pitch had sold a family culture. Day one was mandatory Saturday overtime, with managers working the line and nobody checking in. New hires felt the gap between the promise and the job in their first week, and a lot of them did what you would expect.

The leader did the final interview for every hire. The most experienced person in the building, the one who should have been running the operation, spent his days doing a frontline task because nobody else could be spared. Training barely existed, because the trainers had to work the line to keep the freight moving.
Out of 13 distribution centers in the company, this one ranked 13th on every productivity measure, including throughput.

items.label: the center's rank on every productivity measure, including throughput
people hired in the hope of keeping about 20 a month later
annualized turnover when the work started

runs.t: None of this was a people problem. It was a system that rewarded getting bodies in the door today, and it was running exactly as built.

Hire 75 and keep 20, and 55 people are gone within a month. That is nearly three out of every four. Each of them was recruited, screened, interviewed by the most senior person in the building, background checked and set up in the systems. Some of them were partly trained, by trainers who were pulled off the line to do it. Then they left, and the whole cycle started again.

Now follow the cost downstream. Fewer people on the floor means more Saturday overtime for the people who stayed. More overtime means tired people and less time with family, which is one of the reasons they told us they would leave. Fewer people also means freight that does not move. Trucks get pushed, stores get shorted and shelves go empty. And a customer standing in front of twelve feet of nothing walks across the street to the pharmacy that has what they need (Chapter 4).

None of that showed up on a report labeled turnover. The interviews sat in the leader's calendar. The overtime sat in payroll. The empty shelves sat in the stores' sales numbers, explained away as a manufacturer problem. Each line looked like its own issue. Together they were one problem, and it had a price. That is what the Turn Tax is built to add up (Chapter 3).

The leader had spent years on stage. He was an actor in the play, every day, in every scene. When you are on stage, you cannot see the play. You can only see the next line and the person in front of you.
I told him we were going to go to the balcony and watch the play instead.
So we stopped. We stopped the interviews and everything else, and spent about two hours just watching the operation, the way a stranger would.
Two hours sounds like nothing. For a leader doing a frontline job on top of his own, it was a lot. From the balcony, you see the whole stage at once.
Then we spent the first 30 days listening.
This is where a question I still use started: what's on your mind (Chapter 13).
This was also the first place we used Gallup's Q12 engagement questions, which now have a place in Honest Read.
People told us. Four things came up again and again.
Poor performers were not dealt with.
People who were slow and called off stayed, because the center needed bodies. The good people noticed. Their question was fair: why work hard for the same pay as the person who does not?
Mandatory Saturday overtime.
People could not see their families. They told us, plainly, that they could go anywhere else and get their weekends back.
Pay mattered, but less than we expected.
The center paid $18.25 an hour against a market of about $19.50 to $21. Money was about 25% of the conversation.
The building.
Maintenance had been cut. The break room was dirty and the bathrooms were gross. There was nothing to take pride in.

The other 75% of the conversation sounded like this. I have not seen my manager in three weeks. I get no feedback. I do not know if I am doing it right. There is no career map. Training certifications were check boxes, signed off with nobody coaching.
The fastest way to lose a good employee is to not deal with a bad one.

When you keep people who do not do the work because you are afraid of an empty spot on the schedule, you are telling the people who do the work that it does not matter. They hear it. Then they leave, and you are left with more of the people you were afraid to let go.

blocks.text: Sorting the fixes, then asking the floor

runs.t: By the end of the 30 days, we had more ideas than we could do at once. So we sorted every fix by two questions. Is it quick or long-term? Is it free or costly?

rows: Do now. Example: peer interviews, ordering background checks earlier
Do soon, with a business case. Example: cleaning the building
Start now, finish over months. Example: career maps, rewritten job descriptions
Plan and fund. Example: the pay move, the training program

runs.t: We picked the top five to ten. Then we did the step most leaders skip. We pulled a few employees into a room and showed them the list.
We asked three questions. If we did these, how would it affect you? What are we missing? How would you rank them?

The team helped design the plan. When they saw it go in, they said that was what they had asked for. A plan handed down gets judged. A plan people helped build gets protected, because part of it is theirs.

blocks.text: Rebuilding the front end of hiring

runs.t: The old hiring process was a quiz scored by a system, followed by an email or a call that said "you're hired." To a lot of candidates, it looked like spam.

Someone applies, answers some questions on a screen and gets a message saying they have a job, without meeting anyone or seeing the building. They show up, find out the job is not what they imagined, and leave.
The process was built to be fast. It was fast. And it hurt retention, because it filled the building with people who had no idea what they had signed up for.
We rebuilt it in five pieces.
Application to start went from about 35 to 40 days to about 10.

We did not cut steps. We overlapped them. If the first meeting showed someone was hireable, we ordered the seven-day background check right away, instead of waiting until the end. If we did not hire the person, we lost about $30. That was the whole risk. Against the cost of losing a good candidate to a faster employer, it was nothing.
Candidates met their future teammates and their trainer, not just the center's leader.

That did two things. New hires started day one with a friend, someone whose face they knew and who already had a stake in them succeeding. And the leader got his time back. He stopped doing the final interview for every hire and went back to running the building.

blocks.text: 3. Job descriptions written by the people who do the job

runs.t: The job descriptions had been written by HR. Operations rewrote them to match what the job needs. An honest description scares off some people. Those are often the people who would have quit in the first weeks anyway.

Some backgrounds worked and some did not. People coming from a large e-commerce fulfillment employer struggled, because our technology felt like going back in time. That was not a judgment about those workers. It was a mismatch between what they were used to and what we had.

A clean building. Career maps. Training programs, with trainers who were allowed to train. A rebuilt onboarding process. None of these was glamorous. Together they changed what it felt like to walk in the door.
This work became the origin of Hire Smart (Chapter 16). The idea that hiring should start with what your people who stay have in common came out of this building.
Pay was 25% of the conversation. That still meant it needed fixing. And pay is the one fix you cannot do on your own authority. You have to win the approval.
The center posted $18.25 an hour. But people could earn up to $25 an hour starting. Nobody would have known it from the posting.

So we changed the posting to say "up to $25." It attracted people who knew they could earn more if they performed. Current employees also started asking how to get to $25. That was exactly the conversation we wanted. The career maps showed them how.
To win approval for a raise, opinions would not do. We had to prove the gap.

The team read job postings. They called local employers. They even applied at other companies, so recruiters would call back and tell us the pay and benefits. It was a little unusual. It also produced evidence nobody in a budget meeting could argue with.

Then we traced where the last 30 people who left had gone. Everyone assumed they went to the large e-commerce employer nearby. Only two did (Chapter 9). The rest went to other local employers. That changed who we were competing with, and what we had to match.

blocks.text: Build steps the company could say yes to

runs.t: The data pointed to about $19.50 as the floor, with $21 as a psychological barrier. The company did not want to start everyone at a higher rate. So we built steps.
Starting pay moved to $19.50, rising to $21 and up to $25 after 90 days.

That structure did something a flat raise would not have done. It gave people a reason to get through the first 90 days. And it stopped the 90-day turnover, which was where the losses had been heaviest.
The results did not come all at once. That matters, because a lot of retention efforts are judged too early and abandoned before the work has time to show.

blocks.title: Annualized turnover at one distribution center
blocks.source: Author's career at a Fortune 10 company. Figures are approximate and annualized.

rows: Ranked 13 of 13. Hire 75, keep 20. Mandatory Saturday overtime.
Diagnostic complete. Fixes sorted and plans built with employees.
Plans in place, including faster hiring, peer interviews, new postings and a cleaner building.
Career maps, training and onboarding running.

runs.t: Look at day 30. The number had not moved at all. If anyone had judged the work by turnover at day 30, they would have called it a failure. At day 90 it was still in progress, because the people hired under the new process had not been there long enough to show up in the numbers.
By day 180, turnover was down to about 70%. By the end of the year, about 51%, and the gains held. The center saved roughly $38 million.
Chapter 19 turns this kind of sequence into a plan any company can follow.

blocks.text: What the chart does not show

runs.t: A turnover chart cannot show the leader getting his time back. It cannot show trainers who were finally allowed to train, or a new hire walking in on day one and recognizing a face. It cannot show someone asking their supervisor how to get to $25, instead of asking a recruiter across town.
Those things are why the number moved. They are also why it held.

blocks.text: How to run the same arc

runs.t: The same arc works in a call center, a hospital unit, a store or a plant.
Empty shelves, late trucks and forced overtime are often turnover in disguise. So are missed deadlines, rising error rates and customer complaints about wait times.
Ask: which of our operating problems are we blaming on outside forces? Then ask the leader closest to the work what is going on, and believe the answer.
Stop for a few hours and watch the operation as an outsider would. Then spend 30 days asking people what is on their mind.
Ask: when did the leader of this site last spend two hours watching the work without doing any of it?
Your best people are watching what you tolerate. Every week a poor performer stays with no consequence, you are paying your best people in disappointment.
Dealing with someone does not have to mean firing them on Monday. It means a clear conversation about the standard, a plan with a date, and follow-through when the date comes.
Ask: who is the one person the team is waiting for us to deal with?

blocks.text: 4. Sort the fixes into four boxes

runs.t: Quick or long-term, free or costly. Pick five to ten, then let employees rank them.
The ranking step is the one leaders most want to skip, because it feels slow. It is the step that turns your plan into their plan.

Day 30, day 90, day 180 and one year. Report the number at each point, and report what was done, so nobody quits on the work at day 30 because the number has not moved yet.

label: Chapter 21
title: Your first-week checklist
subtitle: A first-week checklist for every role, and a last word

runs.t: I started my career as a store trainer. I still have one of the interview guides I used back then. Twenty years later, when I left the company, the guide had barely changed (Chapter 2).
Nobody decided to keep that guide the same for two decades. It stayed the same because every Monday, there was something more urgent than fixing it. Then the next Monday came, and the one after that.
That is how most retention problems survive. Nobody chooses them. They last because nobody picks a Monday to start.

This chapter is that Monday. It pulls the "Take action this week" boxes from every chapter into one list, sorted by role. You do not need to do all of it. You need to do some of it, this week, and tell someone you did.
Find your role. Pick three items. Put them on your calendar before you close the book.
If an item does not fit your company, skip it. If you finish your three, pick three more next week. The chapter number after each item tells you where to go if you want the reasoning behind it.
A few rules hold across every role:
Write things down.
A list you made in your head on Monday is gone by Thursday.
Tell people what you did.
A fix nobody hears about earns you almost no trust (Chapter 14).
Talk to a person before you look at a report.
The data tells you where to look. People tell you why.
Keep scores with senior leaders and HR.
If you use a Flight Risk Score, supervisors never see individual scores, and the score never makes an employment decision (Chapter 6).
You set what gets watched, what gets rewarded and what gets funded. Your Monday is about questions. Ask them out loud, and expect an answer by Friday.
Ask your CFO what one voluntary departure costs in your highest-turnover role. If nobody can answer in 48 hours, that is the first problem to solve (Chapter 3).
Look at your dashboard. Count how many of the numbers tell you anything about who is leaving. If the answer is none, ask for 90-day turnover and turnover by manager by next month (Chapter 2).
Ask each leader who manages managers what turnover is on each of their teams compared to the company average. If they cannot answer, you do not have manager accountability yet (Chapter 12).

Before you approve the next retention initiative, ask three questions. Where is turnover concentrated? What does it cost us? Who is likely to leave next? If nobody can answer, diagnose first (Chapter 10).
List your top five performers. For each one, ask when they last had a career conversation and a pay review against market (Chapter 8).
Ask where your last 12 voluntary departures landed (Chapter 9).
Ask HR for every employee with five or more years who earns less than someone hired in the last 12 months in the same role (Chapter 15).
Run the ten-decision scorecard with your leadership team. Give the two lowest decisions an owner and a date (Chapter 18).
Book every review for the next twelve months, and name the sponsor in the same email (Chapter 19).
The two of you see the cost and the operation. Your Monday is about putting turnover where the money and the work are.
CFO:
Run the Turn Tax calculation for one job, using the lowest rate in the range. Write down the source for every input (Chapter 3).
CFO:
Write down a recovery goal for the next board update, framed against what turnover already costs (Chapters 3 and 19).
COO:
Put your turnover trend next to your throughput trend for the last 24 months. Look for where they move together (Chapter 4).
COO:
List the programs your teams run to improve retention or experience. Ask which ones are tied to a measured driver. Stop one that is not (Chapter 10).
Both:
Ask for the six numbers in your next monthly review. If they do not exist yet, ask who will build them (Chapter 18).
You hold most of the data and most of the follow-up. Your Monday is about pulling the lists nobody has pulled.
Pull last year's turnover by manager. Find the three highest, and check whether each manager inherited the problem or created it (Chapters 2 and 10).
Take your last engagement survey. Compare comments from your top performers with everyone else's. If you cannot separate them, that is the first gap to close (Chapter 7).
Find out whether any leader's pay is tied to the engagement score, and ask whether it belongs there (Chapter 5).
List the last 30 people who left one site and find out where each one went (Chapter 20).
Pull the last three internal promotions into leadership. Check how each new leader's team is doing on turnover today (Chapter 8).
List every Critical and Intervention needed Flight Risk score. Confirm each one has a Retention Talk on the calendar (Chapter 18).

blocks.text: The senior leader or site leader

runs.t: You are close enough to see the work and senior enough to change it. Your Monday is about getting out of the play long enough to watch it.
Spend two hours watching your operation without working in it. Write down what a stranger would notice (Chapter 20).
Pick the last major change you rolled out. Ask three frontline employees why they think it happened. If they cannot say, it was never explained (Chapter 11).
Pick one channel your frontline people already use and ask one question through it: what's on your mind? Name the person who will read every answer (Chapter 13).
Look at how your reports rank managers. If they list teams from best to worst by default, change the default to a comparison against a standard (Chapter 12).
You are the program. Your Monday is about the people who report to you, one at a time.
Count your direct reports and multiply by 30 minutes. If that is more time than you have each week, tell your boss, and decide who gets weekly time and who gets every other week (Chapter 12).
Ask each direct report what would make them stay, and write down the one thing other than pay. If you do not know, ask this week (Chapters 1 and 15).
Ask one high performer what it would take for a competitor to recruit them. Write the answer down, and do one thing about it (Chapter 13).
Write down what your two or three best long-tenured people did differently in their first month. Focus on behavior, not skills (Chapter 16).
Tell your own leader one thing about a recent decision that is making your team's work harder. Be specific, and suggest one fix (Chapter 11).
Write the backfill plan for your own team, even if you are going nowhere.
You see people every day. You see the signs first. Your Monday is about one conversation at a time.
Hold a 15-minute check-in with each person on your team this week. Make it about how they are doing, not the task list. Write down one thing to follow up on (Chapter 12).
Name the one person you would least want to lose. When did you last have a conversation with them that was not a status update? Have it this week (Chapter 6).
Ask one person: if you ever left, what would make you go? Make it safe to answer. Then do one thing about it (Chapter 1).
Sit down with one person and draw their career map: where they are, where they want to be, and the next step (Chapter 14).
For your next new hire, write a one-page plan for their first two weeks and name a peer partner (Chapter 17).
Name the one poor performer your team is waiting for you to deal with, and make a plan (Chapter 20).

blocks.text: If you only do three things

runs.t: Some of you will read this list and feel the weight of it. That is fair. So if you do nothing else this week, do these three.
Have one honest conversation with someone you cannot afford to lose.
Ask what would make them stay. Listen to the answer under the answer.
Fix one small thing people have asked about more than once.
Then tell them you fixed it.
Put one number about people next to your financial numbers.
Start with 90-day turnover. It will tell you more than you expect.
None of those costs money. All of them cost a little attention, on purpose, on a day when something else feels more urgent.

runs.t: If you want to see how all of this looks in a specific line of work, Chapter 22 walks through four industries: home health, nuclear and power generation, private equity and contact centers.
When I left my old company, I had already written a backfill plan for my team of 27. The company carried out about 95% of it. My people were taken care of, and I am proud of that.

I think about that plan a lot. It was not clever. It was a list of people, what each of them could do, and where each of them would fit if I was not there. It mattered more than almost anything else I did that year, because it was about people, and because I wrote it before I needed it.

That is most of what this book has been about. Knowing your people. Knowing what it costs when they go. Doing the small, unglamorous things before you need them, so that when the hard day comes, the people who matter most are still there.

When I added up my own results, it came to more than $18 million a year in turnover cost avoided, across about 2,100 people who stayed. I did not do that alone. Those numbers moved because store managers, pharmacists, trainers, supervisors, warehouse leads and call center reps told us the truth, and because enough leaders listened. The credit belongs to them.

I started Experience Improvement Partners to help companies see what they lose when good people leave. I still believe most of that loss is preventable. Not with a big program. With a lot of ordinary Mondays where someone decided to start.
This is yours. Go have the conversation.
Brett Kiley

label: Chapter 22
title: Four industries: home health, nuclear, private equity, contact centers
subtitle: Home health clinicians, nuclear operators, portfolio company talent and contact center agents

runs.t: Leaders I talk with often tell me their business is different. They are right about the details. Schedules, licenses and the competitors calling your people change from one industry to the next.

They are wrong about the reasons people leave. In every job I saw over twenty years, people left because of the manager, because they could not see a next step, because pay fell behind the market or because the work got harder than it needed to be. Those are the four areas the Flight Risk Score reads (Chapter 6).

This chapter looks at four industries that look nothing alike from the outside. The worked examples are hypothetical and use national figures to show the math. EIP publishes a full playbook for each industry on eip360.com, with every source and a 90-day plan. This is the short version.

A few things hold in all four. The 13 Turn Tax categories from Chapter 3 apply everywhere, and only the weights move. Most of the loss happens at a predictable moment. The manager carries the most weight. Somebody can always outbid you on pay, so you win on how it feels to work for you. And the signals already sit in systems the company runs, where nobody reads them together.

blocks.text: Clinical home health: nurses and therapists

runs.t: Home health has more patients than it can serve and fewer clinicians than it needs. The limit on growth is no longer referrals. It is the number of nurses and therapists who stay long enough to carry a full caseload. In most companies retention is a cost question. In home health it is a capacity question.
The work also isolates people. Their manager sits in the office while they drive between patients, and charting follows them home. Nobody intended that. What was designed can be redesigned.

runs.t: A typical agency replaces about one RN in four every year, and research on new home health nurses found most first-year departures came within 180 days. Empty seats turn patients away, as the Texas Department of State Health Services' 2024 nurse staffing study showed. The biggest lever is one agencies already control: RNs with the most stable schedules were 40% less likely to quit.
For nurses, the Turn Tax usually runs from about 80% to 120% of annual salary per departure.

Nuclear is growing again, and all of it depends on a small, hard-to-replace group: the operators.

The pool is tiny. About 3,600 people hold active NRC licenses to operate U.S. power reactors. Every loss is a rebuild that takes years, because site training to license an operator usually runs 18 to 24 months. And federal rules set the minimum crew, so you cannot run lean on licensed people. When one leaves, overtime fills the gap, up to the limits of the fatigue rules.
For a nuclear operator, retention protects the license.

A 2023 Idaho National Laboratory study found turnover among nuclear plant operators rose from 4.1% in 2020 to 7.0% in 2022, and to 10.4% at non-fleet sites, which cannot move people between plants. Average site staffing fell 17.7% from 2011 to 2021, so each departure matters more.
Any plant competing for your operators can match their pay. What it cannot easily copy is how it feels to work on your crews.

The narrow path to senior reactor operator is the one I would watch hardest. Chapter 8 describes what happens when a strong performer is passed over and nobody explains why. Silence after a selection decision is when people start answering recruiters.

For a licensed operator, the Turn Tax usually runs from about 250% to 600% of annual salary. The biggest piece is the replacement's own pay for 12 to 24 months while they train and cannot stand watch.

blocks.text: Private equity: portfolio company key talent

runs.t: In a private equity backed company, the people question runs on a clock. Every line of the value-creation plan assumes someone will carry it out.

Most firms treat talent as a CEO and CFO question. In my experience the deal is won or lost one layer down, with the leaders who run the business every day. Their departures rarely show up in diligence. They show up in year two.

Russell Reynolds studied 196 European PE exits from 2020 to 2025. In 69% of deals the company changed CEO at least once during the hold. A new CEO in year one was associated with exit after 4.4 years on average, against 7.7 years when the change came after year two. That is a correlation, not proof of cause, but late leadership change costs time.

Retention bonuses buy time, not loyalty. In a 2014 Towers Watson global study, 68% of acquirers kept more than 80% of retention agreement signers through the retention period. One year after it ended, only 43% still did.

blocks.text: What we got wrong in an acquisition

runs.t: My company once bought about 1,500 stores from another retailer. The announcement came with new signs and a welcome message. For many of the people joining us, pay and benefits were going to get worse, and they knew it.

We treated retention as one generic welcome. We had no list of who to keep and no plan for what it would take. Some of the talent in those low-volume stores was strong, and some had worked for us before. Each group needed a different conversation, and none got one. We lost good people we should not have lost.

Nobody set out to lose them. Our acquisition process was built around store counts, not people one at a time. If I could go back, I would ask two questions about every key person. How much impact does this person have? What would it take to keep them?
In a deal, look at your talent person by person. Use a personalized plan, not a pizza party and new signs.
For senior leaders below the CEO, the Turn Tax usually runs from about 150% to 250% of annual pay.

Contact centers accept something no other part of the business would: replacing about three in ten frontline people every year, and far more at outsourcing partners. Software now takes the easy contacts and leaves agents the hardest ones, which take experience to handle.

Mean U.S. agent attrition was 29% in 2025, according to a ContactBabel survey of 207 contact center leaders. New agents leave fastest: 22% of U.S. centers lost more than a quarter of new agents within 90 days, up from 12% two survey waves earlier.

Outsourcing runs at another scale. Teleperformance, one of the largest outsourcing companies in the world, reported agent attrition of 67.6% in 2024 and hired 389,220 people to keep its headcount flat.

blocks.text: What we saw: paying for bodies

runs.t: I once led patient experience strategy across a contact center operation of about 7,500 agents, about 3,500 of them from outsourcing partners. Our partners told us their turnover averaged about 30% a month. When we read the contract, we saw why nobody was fixing it. We paid them for enough people in seats on January 1, not for whether those people were good or stayed. We changed the incentive and the payment plan, and their turnover dropped significantly.
Whatever you pay for is what you get. Pay for bodies by a date and you will get bodies by a date.
For contact center agents, the Turn Tax usually runs about 25% to 40% of annual pay, mostly lost productivity and customer impact.

runs.t: Turn Tax™.

EIP's model of what turnover costs a company. It builds the cost of each departure from the ground up across 13 cost categories and up to 250 variables, using the company's own data. The name comes from the idea that turnover is a tax you pay every time someone quits, even though it never shows up as one line on the P&L (Chapter 3).
Flight Risk Score™ (patent pending).

A score from 0 to 99 that shows how likely a person is to leave in the next 90 days. It starts with 19 base variables in four areas: manager relationship, career and tenure, pay, and job friction. EIP weights the variables for each company and adds more where needed. The score is tested against people who already left. It is a documented calculation, not AI, and it does not teach itself. Supervisors never see scores, and the score never makes an employment decision (Chapter 6).
Flight Risk bands.
The four ranges of the Flight Risk Score.

blocks.title: The four Flight Risk bands
lines: •  0-40: Low risk
•  41-60: Worth watching
•  61-80: Intervention needed
•  81-99: Critical

runs.t: Honest Read™.
Interviews and small listening sessions run by a third party, outside the company's chain of command, to hear what employees will not put in a survey (Chapters 5 and 13).
Honest Read top three.
The three things the executive team should do this week or this month to make work better for employees, drawn from Honest Read. One of the six numbers a CEO should watch.
Hire Smart™.
EIP's approach to hiring. It builds the hiring process around the 3 to 5 traits that a company's long-tenured top performers share (Chapter 16).
Council View.
A monthly review of retention metrics with EIP's Council (Chapter 19).
Competitive Analysis.

EIP's review of what the employers competing for your people offer: their posted pay and benefits, what employees say about working there, and where people from your company go when they leave (Chapter 9).
The Council.
EIP's Council of current and former executives. Members review a client's findings independently, then together, and decide which fixes fit best before anything is recommended (Chapter 10).
Solutions partners.

People the Council's members have used before and recommend, some of whom sit on the Council. When a diagnostic shows a particular need, the Council brings them in. Because they already have the findings, they can quote exactly the work needed.
30-day diagnostic.

How an EIP engagement starts. Two tracks run at once for 30 days: a data track that builds the Turn Tax, Flight Risk Score and dashboard, and a people track of interviews and listening sessions (Chapter 10).
Retention Snapshot.

EIP's starting point, by invitation: the same analysis that opens every paid EIP engagement, run on one spreadsheet for one to three job titles that share a pay band, a location and the same kind of work, with first numbers in about 7 days.
90-day turnover.

The share of new hires who leave within their first 90 days. Nobody goes through every step to get a job only to quit right away, so early exits usually point to something inside the company: what was promised, who was chosen, or how they were trained and supported (Chapter 2).
Annualized turnover.

A turnover rate for part of a year, scaled up to show what it would be over a full year at the same pace. A distribution center that loses people at a steady pace for six months can be described by its annualized rate (Chapter 20).
Voluntary turnover.
Departures the employee chooses, such as a resignation, as opposed to people who are let go.
Preventable turnover.

Departures the employer could have stopped with something within its control, such as a conversation, a schedule change, a career step or a better manager. Gallup's 2024 research found 42% of voluntary turnover was preventable (Chapter 1).
High performer turnover.
The rate at which a company loses its long-tenured top performers. One of the six numbers a CEO should watch, because losing the person others stayed for creates a ripple effect (Chapter 8).
Turnover by manager.
Turnover split by the manager each person reported to. It shows whether a company has a company-wide problem or a problem on a few teams (Chapter 12).
Retention Talk.
A conversation with a current employee about what keeps them and what would make them leave, held before they decide to go.
Magic wand interview.

The name my teams used for Retention Talks, after the first question, which asks what part of the job a person would eliminate with a magic wand. The most useful question was the last one, which asks what they would fix if they had no money (Chapter 5).
Exit interview.
A conversation with someone who has already decided to leave. Useful for patterns, but it describes people you have already lost.
Listening session.
A small group conversation, usually five people for one hour, run by a neutral interviewer with no managers in the room (Chapter 13).
Phantom staffing.

When a report shows people as working who are not there. During COVID, paid call-offs with no tracking code made stores look about 95% staffed on paper while they were closer to 60% in reality (Chapter 3).
Pay compression.
When new hires start at or above the pay of people who have been in the same job for years, often including the people training them. It is a bet that tenured people will not quit (Chapter 15).
Cost-of-living band.
A pay range set by the cost of living in an area. Hard-to-staff areas are often low cost, so bands built only on cost of living can underpay the places that are hardest to fill (Chapter 15).
Skill-based pay steps.
Small raises tied to each new skill a person learns and uses, in place of one large raise after a long wait (Chapter 15).
Span of control.
The number of people, locations or teams one leader is responsible for. If a leader cannot hold a real conversation with each direct report, the span is too wide (Chapter 11).
Sign-on bonus.
A one-time payment to get someone to accept a job. It can bring people in, but it rents loyalty rather than earning it (Chapter 15).
Retention bonus.
A payment for staying through a set date, common after an acquisition. It buys time, not loyalty, and the end date can become an exit date (Chapter 22).
Engagement survey.
A periodic, usually annual, questionnaire about how employees feel about their work. Gallup's Q12 is one well-known set of engagement questions (Chapter 5).
Anonymous and confidential.

An anonymous survey cannot link an answer to a person. A confidential survey can, but promises not to. Most surveys that require a login are confidential, not anonymous, and employees know the difference (Chapter 5).
Net Promoter Score (NPS).
A measure of how likely customers are to recommend a company, on a scale from minus 100 to 100 (Chapter 4).
Friction.
The everyday obstacles that make a job harder than it needs to be, such as broken tools, bad meeting times or slow processes. Small fixes to friction are often cheap and fast (Chapter 14).
Career map.
A simple picture of the steps from a person's current job to the next ones, with what each step takes (Chapter 14).
Post-hire check-ins.
Short conversations with a new hire on the first day, after the first and second weeks, and at 30, 60 and 90 days (Chapter 17).
Four kinds of employee.
A way to sort any workforce by whether people perform and whether they stay. The target is the people who perform and stay (Chapter 16).
Preceptor.
In clinical work, an experienced clinician who trains and supports a new hire through their first weeks in the field (Chapter 22).

runs.t: Brett Kiley spent 20 years, from 2004 to 2024, at a Fortune 10 company. He worked in retail stores, a call center, frontline pharmacy and executive leadership. He led teams of up to 3,500 people and a $1.2 billion P&L, and in the specialty business he was responsible for $3 billion in client contract renewals.

He started as a store trainer and rose to region director, responsible for about 3,000 people across several states. He led the turnaround of the distribution center that supplied his stores, and later, as an executive director of customer experience, he led patient experience strategy as Net Promoter Score rose from 24 to 81 over two years. His teams' results added up to more than $18 million a year in turnover cost avoided, across about 2,100 people who stayed. He was the only executive to win both the company's innovation award and its employee experience award in the same year.

After leaving, he built the Six Degree Career Accelerator, a program that helps people get a job offer within 180 days without applying. He then spent two years as a vice president at Ciklum, a global AI solutions company, starting its U.S. healthcare vertical and building custom AI, automation and analytics for clients.
In 2026 he founded Experience Improvement Partners to help companies see what they lose when good people leave, and keep the ones they cannot afford to lose.
Experience Improvement Partners (EIP) is an operator-led retention advisory firm. It helps companies see who is likely to leave and what turnover costs them, then stays with them through the fix.
EIP's work is guided by its Council of current and former executives and operators. The Council reviews every client's findings and decides which fixes fit best before anything is recommended.

Honest Read™
runs interviews and small listening sessions as a third party.
Hire Smart™

Council View
